points.title: TCP communication crosses user space, kernel, NIC, and network
points.body_markdown: Application bytes pass through user space, the kernel, the NIC, and the network. The CPU processes the protocol stack, while the NIC transfers packet data with DMA.

points.title: TCP/IP encapsulation adds headers per layer
points.body_markdown:
Each layer adds information needed by its peer. Encapsulation adds headers but need not copy the payload at every layer.

Ethernet frame [ IP packet [ TCP segment [ application bytes ]] ]

| Layer | Data unit | Main responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Application | Bytes | Application meaning and message framing |
| TCP | Segment | Ports, ordered delivery, and loss recovery |
| IP | Packet | Host addressing and routing across networks |
| Ethernet | Frame | Delivery over the local link |

points.title: The TCP socket interface is kernel-managed
points.body_markdown: Applications use calls such as `socket()`, `connect()`, `send(fd, buf, len, 0)`, and `recv(fd, buf, cap, 0)`. The kernel manages buffers and TCP state for each socket. `send()` accepts bytes locally; the peer application may read them later.

points.title: TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream
points.body_markdown: Read boundaries can differ from write boundaries (e.g., `send("AB")` then `send("CD")` may be read as `"A"` then `"BCD"`). Sequence numbers and ACKs track delivery, and retransmission repairs loss. Flow control protects receiver buffers; congestion control limits network load.

points.title: The kernel transmit path copies payload into the kernel
points.body_markdown:
1. Copy application bytes into a kernel buffer.
2. Process TCP state and protocol headers.
3. Queue packet work and pass it to the driver.
4. Let the NIC fetch packet data with DMA.
5. Retain unacknowledged bytes for retransmission.

The user-to-kernel boundary copies the payload in this ordinary path.

points.title: The kernel receive path separates arrival from consumption
points.body_markdown:
1. The NIC DMAs data into a kernel buffer.
2. An interrupt schedules receive processing.
3. NAPI, GRO, and TCP/IP process the data.
4. TCP makes ordered bytes available to the socket.
5. `recv()` copies bytes into the application buffer.

Packet arrival and application consumption are different events.

points.title: Interrupts and NAPI batch receive processing
points.body_markdown: An IRQ schedules NAPI; the system then polls work in batches up to a receive budget. When work is drained, NAPI completes and interrupts are re-enabled. One interrupt can lead to processing multiple received packets. Notification starts processing; DMA moves the packet bytes.

points.title: TSO and GRO amortize per-packet work
points.body_markdown:
GSO provides software segmentation; TSO delegates it to the NIC. GRO combines received segments before TCP processing. Larger processing units amortize protocol and buffer-management work. Wire packets still obey the MTU, and receive aggregation happens at the host.

| Mechanism | Description |
|---|---|
| TSO (Tx) | TCP Segmentation Offload. Offloads segmentation of "big" packets (up to 64KB) into frames to the NIC. |
| GRO (Rx) | Generic Receive Offload. Aggregates MTU-sized frames into a "big" packet (up to 64KB) before passing them to the TCP/IP layer. |

points.title: Small packets leave little CPU work per frame at 100 Gb/s
points.body_markdown:
100 Gb/s = 12.5 GB/s nominal link rate. Actual throughput also depends on memory, queueing, and offloads.

| Ethernet frame | Wire occupancy | Packet rate | Cycles/frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 B | 84 byte-times | 148.8 Mpps | 20.2 |
| 1518 B | 1538 byte-times | 8.13 Mpps | 369.1 |

Add 8 B preamble/SFD and 12 byte-times of inter-frame gap. Cycles/frame = 3 GHz / packet rate, for one idealized CPU core, calculated at 100 Gb/s nominal MAC rate before payload and processing overheads.

points.title: A modern NIC connects host memory to a packet pipeline
points.body_markdown: PCIe and DMA connect host memory to the NIC packet pipeline. Queue managers track work; engines and the scheduler execute it.

points.title: Descriptors point to packet buffers
points.body_markdown: A descriptor contains a DMA address, length, and flags. The NIC queue state includes ring base, ring size, producer progress, and consumer progress. After the last slot, the index wraps to slot 0. Producer and consumer progress control when slots and buffers can be reused.

points.title: Doorbells notify; DMA moves work and data
points.body_markdown: MMIO writes carry the work descriptors; MMIO accesses device registers or mapped device memory. A doorbell notification can trigger larger DMA transfers. The CPU pushes descriptors, notifies the NIC, and the NIC fetches them, with a separate payload DMA read.

points.title: Transmit: prepare, publish, fetch, send
points.body_markdown:
1–2 Prepare and fill a buffer.
3 Publish descriptors and notify the NIC.
4–5 DMA-read descriptors and packet bytes.
6 Transmit through MAC/PHY.
7 Observe completion and reclaim resources.

Ring colors show logical buffer ownership.

points.title: Receive: post buffers before packets arrive
points.body_markdown:
Software posts available receive buffers before packets arrive.
1–2 Classify the packet and select a queue.
3 DMA-write bytes into a posted buffer.
4–5 Publish completion; software notices it.
6 Deliver packets and refill RX buffers.
7–8 Process, then release or forward.

A free pool allocates and recycles buffers; ring colors show logical buffer ownership.

points.title: Completion records work; interrupts notify software
points.body_markdown:
The NIC DMA-writes completion/status records, and MSI-X provides notification; the CPU can also poll for completed work.

| Queue / ring | Information it carries |
|---|---|
| Descriptor ring | Work to perform or available RX buffers |
| Completion queue | Results of completed work |
| Event queue | Queue events, as in Corundum |
| Software handoff ring | Buffer references between software stages |

points.title: RSS maps flows to receive queues
points.body_markdown: A flow hash (for flows A, B, C) is used with an indirection table to select RX queues 0, 1, 2, which map to cores 0, 1, 2. A stable RSS mapping keeps one flow on one receive queue; CPU affinity maps receive queues to processing cores.

points.title: Queue state drives DMA requests
points.body_markdown:
1. Descriptor DMA: fetch address + length.
2. Payload DMA: use buffer address + length.

TX/RX descriptor queues: software produces, NIC consumes. Completion queues reverse the producer and consumer roles. RX uses its descriptor to DMA-write received payload into host memory.

NIC queue-state RAM (illustrative values):

| Queue | Ring base | Slots | Producer (head) | Consumer (tail) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TX 0 | 0x1000 | 8 | 5 (software) | 2 (NIC) |
| RX 0 | 0x2000 | 8 | 6 (software) | 4 (NIC) |
| CQ 0 | 0x3000 | 8 | 3 (NIC) | 1 (software) |

TX descriptor address = base + (reserved index mod size) × stride. Example: reserved slot 2 = 0x1000 + (2 mod 8) × 16 B = 0x1020.

points.title: Multiple queues and in-flight jobs keep the NIC pipeline busy
points.body_markdown: Multiple TX queues (e.g., queue 0 with jobs J1, J3; queue 1 with J2, J4) supply work to the TX scheduler, and each queue can keep several jobs in flight. Pipeline stages are descriptor DMA, payload DMA, checksum/segmentation, and TX MAC/PHY; at slot 4, all four stages work concurrently. At 100 Gb/s with 64 B frames, 148.8 Mpps corresponds to 6.72 ns/frame.

points.title: Putting the NIC pipeline together
points.body_markdown:
1. Control/time: PCIe HIP, AXIL M, PTP HC, queue state.
2. TX work: TXQ, descriptor fetch, scheduler/control, TX engine.
3. TX bytes: DMA IF, RAM, port DMA, checksum, MAC/PHY, SFP.
4. RX: MAC/PHY, hash, checksum, RX engine, RXQ, host buffer.
5. Results: completion write, TXCQ/RXCQ, EQ, PCIe notification.

points.title: Kernel TCP/IP CPU costs come from protocol handling, copying, and buffer management
points.body_markdown: Host CPU cycles go to protocol handling, copying, and buffer management. These are separate experiments with different workloads and platforms (a long TCP flow at the receiver; 4 KB RPCs at the sender).

points.title: Kernel bypass and offload are separate, combinable choices
points.body_markdown: The software packet path on the host spans user space (application and userspace TCP) and kernel space (kernel TCP or an early XDP hook). Work executed by the NIC includes packet I/O, selected TCP functions, and payload placement. Kernel bypass changes the software fast path; offload changes which functions the NIC executes. The choices can combine.

points.title: Userspace can drive the queues directly
points.body_markdown: In the userspace fast path, TCP logic still runs on host CPU cores. The kernel sets up controlled device and memory access.

points.title: Polling and batching have trade-offs
points.body_markdown: Polling inspects the queue repeatedly; empty checks consume CPU cycles. Polling avoids waiting for a notification, at the cost of idle CPU work. Batching processes packets already available: burst processing amortizes overhead, but waiting to fill a batch adds delay.

points.title: DPDK provides packet I/O, not TCP semantics
points.body_markdown: An application packet loop uses `rx_burst(rxq, pkts)`, processes the packets, then calls `tx_burst(txq, pkts, n)`. An optional software TCP stack can run inside the process. An mbuf holds metadata and a packet-data reference; a mempool handles buffer allocation and recycling. Packet I/O provides packets; an upper layer provides TCP semantics.

points.title: DPDK Buffer Ownership: Device View vs. Software View
points.body_markdown:
- The same packet-data region in host memory has two views:
  - **Device view**: RX descriptor holds DMA address/length and hardware status.
  - **Software view**: `rte_mbuf` holds data pointer/length and software metadata.
- A **mempool** supplies and recycles buffers.
- `rx_burst()` returns mbuf pointers to the application.
- **TX ownership example**: offered m0, m1, m2; accepted = 2.
  - m0, m1: TX PMD owns them; the PMD reclaims accepted buffers after device use.
  - m2: application still owns it; the application must retry or free it.

points.title: XDP: Hook Placement and Verdicts
points.body_markdown:
- eBPF = program; XDP = hook.
- XDP processes packets **before** the stack (native driver XDP).
- Verdicts:
  - **PASS**: continue through kernel TCP/IP.
  - **DROP**: stop processing this packet early.
  - **TX**: send back through the same interface.
  - **REDIRECT**: send to another interface, CPU, or AF_XDP.
- Upper arrows continue to userspace applications and control logic.

points.title: XDP Program Structure, Maps, and Verification
points.body_markdown:
- Program loading path: eBPF bytecode → kernel verifier → admitted program → per-packet execution.
- The C-like excerpt shows:
  - Bounds check: `if ((void *)(eth + 1) > end) return XDP_DROP;`
  - Non-IPv4 check: `if (eth->h_proto != bpf_htons(ETH_P_IP)) return XDP_PASS;`
  - Map lookup: `mode = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&policy, &key);`
  - Policy decision: `return mode && *mode ? XDP_DROP : XDP_PASS;`
- **Map updates change policy without reloading the program**: userspace updates the `policy[0]` entry (0 = pass IPv4, 1 = drop IPv4).

points.title: Offload Candidates Beyond Kernel Bypass
points.body_markdown:
- After kernel bypass: application + userspace TCP still runs protocol code on the host CPU; the NIC does packet I/O and basic offloads.
- Additional functions can move to the NIC **together with their state**; each design chooses a function boundary and a state owner.
- Offload candidates:
  - **Connection management**: SYN / FIN lifecycle.
  - **Established TCP**: SEQ, ACK, windows, fast recovery.
  - **Payload movement**: split / merge, direct placement.

points.title: Offloading Connection Management
points.body_markdown:
- One owner updates connection state at a time.
- Teardown offload requires an eligible close and a state handoff.

points.title: Offloading the Established TCP Fast Path
points.body_markdown:
- **Host / control plane** keeps: connection management, congestion policy, timeout recovery triggers.
- **Application + libTOE**: socket payload buffers in host memory; payload DMA to/from the NIC.
- **Programmable NIC pipeline**:
  - Preprocess: parse + lookup.
  - Protocol: SEQ / ACK / window, fast retransmit.
  - Postprocess DMA: notify application.
- Protocol updates remain **atomic per connection**.
- NIC flow scheduling enforces the software congestion policy.

points.title: Separating Protocol Control from Payload Movement
points.body_markdown:
- Software TCP keeps CC, loss recovery, and delivery decisions programmable.
- The NIC splits headers from payload and moves bytes to application buffers.

points.title: RDMA: Hardware-Based Transport
points.body_markdown:
- **Host** handles: application and setup, work submission, completion handling.
- **RNIC** handles: transport processing, DMA and direct placement, address translation.
- Buffers and queues still use host memory.

points.title: Registered Memory and Access Protection
points.body_markdown:
- Registration of a virtual memory region establishes: mapping + bounds, access permissions, and **lkey / rkey**.
- On a request, the RNIC checks range and access, then DMAs:
  - Valid range + permitted access → DMA allowed.
  - Outside bounds or denied access → rejected.
- Registration follows the **resource lifetime**, not each packet.
- Keys authorize access to the region; they **do not encrypt** its bytes.

points.title: SEND vs. WRITE: Who Chooses the Remote Buffer
points.body_markdown:
- **SEND / RECV**: SEND WQE (src=A, len) → requester RNIC → bytes → responder RNIC, which uses a RECV WQE (dst=B).
- **Ordinary WRITE**: WRITE WQE (B + rkey) → requester RNIC → bytes; no RECV WQE; RNIC checks B / rkey.
- Requester CQE if signaled in both cases.

| | SEND | WRITE |
|---|---|---|
| Remote buffer | Receiver via RECV | Requester via WRITE |
| Remote receive WQE | Required | Unused |
| Remote receive CQE | RECV completion | None for ordinary WRITE |

points.title: RDMA READ: Request and Response
points.body_markdown:
- Local application posts READ WQE: B, rkey, len; destination D.
- Requester RNIC sends READ request; responder RNIC DMA-reads B and returns bytes as READ response data; requester DMA-writes D.
- If signaled, local CQE follows placement; the remote app granted access earlier.
- Operation semantics:
  - SEND = message push.
  - WRITE = addressed push.
  - READ = addressed pull.

points.title: RDMA Control Path vs. Data Path
points.body_markdown:
- **Setup / resource changes**: create queues (QP / CQ), use registered memory, endpoint info (one-sided: addr + key), configure communication; create, update, and release resources over their lifetime.
- **Repeated data path**: post work + doorbell → NIC fetch and execute → eligible completion → poll / notification.
- Submitting work and polling completions are part of the data path.

points.title: Inside the RDMA Transport Engine
points.body_markdown:
- RX and TX pipelines share indexed transport state.
- **RX**: parse headers → QP / PSN lookup (QPN-indexed tables: PSN, MSN, connection state) → opcode order check → placement DMA → payload merge → ACK / event output.
- **TX**: QP command arbitration → state / PSN update → header generation → ICRC / MAC.
- Also: timer / timeout events, recovery, ordering, rate control, PFC at MAC / link.
- Payload uses a wide streaming path; metadata / events use a narrow path with ordered state updates.

points.title: Go-Back-N vs. Selective Retransmission (IRN)
points.body_markdown:
- **Go-Back-N**: receiver gets 0, 1, hole at 2, then 3, 4; receiver **discards 3 and 4**; NACK says expected PSN = 2; sender retransmits 2, 3, 4 (3 packets sent again).
- **Selective retransmission (IRN)**: receiver **retains 3 and 4**; NACK says expected = 2, received = 3 / 4; sender retransmits only 2 (1 packet + receipt state).
- Selective recovery saves retransmissions but tracks more state.

points.title: Reliability Hardware: State, Timers, and Replay
points.body_markdown:
- Flow: packet / ACK / NACK → QP lookup / read state → event arbitration (timer expiry) → update state / select retransmission → TX-ready event → locate payload / DMA or replay → TX.
- State kept:
  - Outstanding range: first / last PSN.
  - Receipt bitmap: received / missing.
  - Retry / timer state: expiry + attempts.
  - Payload locator: WQE + byte offset.
- Replay implementation choices:
  - Re-read host memory (extra PCIe access).
  - On-card replay buffer (extra card storage).

points.title: Out-of-Order Placement and Message Completion
points.body_markdown:
- One SEND message uses receive WQE #7 into destination buffer B.
- Packets arrive as 0, 1, hole, 3, 4; the message-relative bitmap snapshot shows receipt 1 1 0 1 1 with message end 0 0 0 0 1.
- The CQE is **held while receipt contains a hole**.
- Receive retry P2 fills the hole; receipt = 11111; all required data placement is complete.
- Then advance the message completion frontier and publish receive CQE #7.
- The last packet can arrive before the message is complete.

points.title: Ordering Across Operations and Queue Pairs
points.body_markdown:
- **Same RC QP** (RC, host memory, normal ordered MR, pre-posted RECV): QP 7 WRITE(data) then QP 7 SEND(ready) → successful ready CQE means data can be used.
  - Within one QP, progress gates notification: prior work incomplete → hold ready CQE; prior work complete → release ready CQE.
- **Different QPs**: QP A WRITE(data), QP B SEND(ready) — independent connections; the ready CQE may arrive while data is incomplete.

points.title: DCQCN: From ECN Marks to Rate Feedback
points.body_markdown:
- Switch marks data; receiver reports; sender adjusts rate.
- Sender RNIC: rate control.
- Egress queue: ECN marking.
- Receiver RNIC: CNP generation → CNP to the affected QP.
- CNP reduces rate; timers and byte counters guide rate recovery.
- Roles: CNP = congestion; ACK/NACK = delivery, recovery.

points.title: Congestion Control in the RNIC
points.body_markdown:
- Components: CNP parser, timer, byte counter, per-flow rate update, scheduler / pacer.
- Eligibility interval ≈ packet bits / rate.
- On congestion feedback: Rc ← Rc (1 − α / 2).
- Per-flow state:
  - Current rate Rc: rate enforced now.
  - Target rate Rt: recovery target.
  - Congestion estimate α: smoothed feedback.
  - Timer / counter: recovery trigger.
- Lower rate → wider packet spacing.

points.title: PFC: Protecting the Next-Hop Buffer
points.body_markdown:
- Components: occupancy counter → XOFF / XON comparison → PFC frame generator → upstream MAC → priority TX gate.
- PFC pauses a priority on one link.
- Pause duration and XOFF / XON hysteresis govern pause and resume.

points.title: PFC Headroom and Backpressure
points.body_markdown:
- Headroom example: 100 Gb/s × 2 μs = 25 KB of reaction data (the 2 μs is an assumed reaction-data term).
- Headroom also covers wire and committed data.
- Flow A + Flow B share one priority; PFC pauses the priority → **both flows stall**; pause can spread.

points.title: InfiniBand and RoCEv2 Packet Formats
points.body_markdown:
- Common: RDMA operations / QP / reliable transport.
- **Native InfiniBand**: LRH | GRH (optional) | BTH | Operation header | Payload | ICRC | VCRC.
- **RoCEv2 over Ethernet**: Ethernet | IPv4 / IPv6 | UDP | BTH | Operation header | Payload | ICRC | FCS.
- RoCEv2 uses IP routing and UDP encapsulation; the RC transport supplies reliability and ordering.

points.title: InfiniBand vs. Ethernet: Fabric Responsibilities
points.body_markdown:
- **InfiniBand**: per-VL credit — sender needs enough credits; next-hop VL buffer; credit update back to sender.
- **Ethernet**: per-priority pause — sender priority TX gate; next-hop priority buffer; PFC pause / duration back to sender.

| Dimension | Native InfiniBand | RoCEv2 over Ethernet |
|---|---|---|
| Forwarding | LID in subnet; GRH across subnets | Ethernet + IP; routing and ECMP |
| Link flow control | Per-VL credits | Per-priority PFC (lossless setup) |
| Congestion | IB congestion signaling | IP ECN + CNP (DCQCN example) |
| Management | Subnet Manager | Ethernet / IP control |

points.title: Kernel Bypass + Selective Offload vs. RDMA: Design Trade-offs
points.body_markdown:
- Trade-off framing: software flexibility vs. a more uniform hardware transport path; workload examples overlap; end-to-end performance depends on the deployment.

| | Kernel bypass + selective offload | RDMA |
|---|---|---|
| Interface | Sockets through a stack / runtime | Verbs + registered buffers |
| Protocol control | Software-defined CC, recovery, policies | Transport mechanisms executed by the RNIC |
| Offload boundary | Choose functions for each stack / workload | Transport + direct data placement |
| Workload fit | Diverse cloud services; per-service stacks | Storage, databases, AI; structured communication |
| Trade-off | Software freedom; CPU / runtime cost remains | Less protocol freedom; low host cost and a more uniform fast path |

points.title: AI communication has structure: training groups and phases repeat across iterations
points.body_markdown:
Training groups and communication phases repeat across iterations. Different parallelism types map to different network domains:
- **Tensor parallel**: local shards exchanged via collective exchange; needs fast local links for frequent exchanges.
- **Data parallel**: gradient AllReduce across replicas.
- **Pipeline parallel**: activations forward / gradients backward between stages.
- **Expert all-to-all**: adds patterns that need broader connectivity.

The opportunity is to co-design topology and collective communication: map repeated groups to matching paths, and match traffic to domain bandwidth.

points.title: AI traffic arrives in bursts and heavy flows
points.body_markdown: A communication phase can raise demand across many GPUs. A few heavy flows make hash-based balancing harder. High, stable throughput needs burst capacity and balanced paths. Production training measurements show bursts reaching NIC capacity (Figure 2: NIC egress traffic pattern) and few concurrent connections per host (Figure 3).

points.title: Scale-out network landscape: designs differ in fabric, organization, and path control
points.body_markdown:
Fabric, topology, routing, and runtime choose different boundaries across designs:

| Design | Fabric | Organization | Path control and coordination |
|---|---|---|---|
| NVIDIA InfiniBand | IB | Rail-optimized fat-tree | Adaptive routing; collective / rail mapping |
| NVIDIA Spectrum-X | Ethernet RoCE | Clos / multiple planes | Per-packet adaptive routing; SuperNIC handles out-of-order data |
| Alibaba HPN | Ethernet RoCE | Rail segments; dual planes | Library selects disjoint connections; schedules outstanding WQE bytes |
| Meta | Ethernet RoCE | Clos AI zones | Topology-aware placement; ECMP / centralized traffic engineering |
| Tencent Astral | Ethernet RoCE | Rail aggregation domains | Per-flow ECMP; telemetry and runtime coordination |

points.title: Scale-out network design has not converged; HPN is used as a case study
points.body_markdown: Scale-out network design has yet to converge, so the lecture turns to Alibaba HPN as a case study to explore key design choices and trade-offs. The landscape table (repeated on this page) shows designs choosing different boundaries for fabric, topology, routing, and runtime.

points.title: HPN server–network interface: 8 GPUs, 8 backend NICs, 1 frontend NIC per server
points.body_markdown: Each server has 8 GPUs, 8 backend NICs, and 1 frontend NIC. Backend bandwidth is 8 × (2 × 200 Gb/s) = 3.2 Tb/s per server. Each backend NIC reaches two independent ToRs.

points.title: Rails and segments: same-index GPU/NIC pairs share a ToR pair
points.body_markdown: A **rail** is the same-index GPU / NIC pairs across hosts sharing a ToR pair (e.g., Rail 1 = GPU 1 / NIC 1 across hosts, via ToR 1 + ToR 2; Rail 8 via ToR 15 + ToR 16). One **segment** = 128 active hosts × 8 GPUs = 1,024 GPUs. Eight rails cover the same 128 hosts, plus the associated ToR pairs.

points.title: Structured communication on rails: one switching tier per rail
points.body_markdown:
Example: 512 GPUs = 64 hosts × 8 GPUs, with TP=8, DP=64.
- TP peers use the fast intra-host interconnect.
- DP group 1 is GPU 1 on all 64 hosts; other indices form other groups.
- Same-index DP traffic stays within its rail's ToR pair (rail-optimized network under dual-ToR), versus two switching tiers in a traditional DCN.

Per ToR: 128 active 200G downlinks. Downlinks used per host: DCN 8 per ToR (16 hosts/pair), HPN 1 per rail ToR (128 hosts/pair).

points.title: Independent dual-ToR connectivity: two NIC ports with shared QP contexts
points.body_markdown: Two NIC ports share QP contexts. A failed NIC–ToR link redirects traffic through the other port, and active RDMA QPs can survive the access-path change. Independent ToRs remove the direct switch-state synchronization dependency. In stacked dual-ToR, a malfunction of ToR1's data plane would eventually trigger the offline of ToR2; in non-stacked dual-ToR, the two ToRs run independently.

points.title: Pods and forwarding planes: separate paths and switch resources per plane
points.body_markdown:
A **plane** is a separate set of forwarding paths and switch resources. Key figures:
- Core switches per plane: 60 × 8 × 400G = 192 Tb/s; 8 uplinks per Aggregation switch.
- Per segment / plane: 8 × 60 × 400G = 192 Tb/s; 8 ToRs per plane; 1,024 active GPUs.
- 15 segments × 1,024 = 15,360 active GPUs per Pod.
- Per Aggregation switch: 120 × 400G down + 8 × 400G up = 51.2 Tb/s; 120 downlinks = 15 segments × 8 ToRs; 48 Tb/s : 3.2 Tb/s = 15:1.
- GPU injection: 1,024 × 200G = 204.8 Tb/s per segment / plane; ToR active down:up = 1.067:1.

points.title: Dual planes reduce hash polarization
points.body_markdown: NIC port 0 stays in plane 1; port 1 stays in plane 2. After the source ToR selects an uplink / aggregation switch, the remaining path inside the Pod is fixed. Fewer hash stages reduce reconvergence during concurrent elephant flows (dual-plane vs. typical Clos, Figure 12).

points.title: Burst waves and path collisions
points.body_markdown: A communication phase launches heavy transfers from several host pairs (A, B, C, D). Hash collisions can concentrate traffic on one path while others sit idle; disjoint connections give the library alternatives for each new message. The burst still occurs — path selection reduces spatial concentration.

points.title: The collective library selects paths and schedules by outstanding bytes
points.body_markdown:
The library's procedure:
1. Simulate switch hashes.
2. Choose disjoint source-port tuples.
3. Establish RDMA connections.
4. For each work item, choose the smallest outstanding-byte count (a slow-draining connection keeps more unfinished bytes).

Accounting: post WQE adds bytes; CQE subtracts completed bytes. Example: with connections A=8 MB, B=2 MB, C=5 MB outstanding, a 2 MB post selects B (→4 MB); when a 1 MB WQE completes, B drops to 3 MB.

points.title: Putting HPN together: one cross-segment transfer path
points.body_markdown: A cross-segment transfer traverses: (1) host / NIC, (2) source ToR, (3) selected Agg, (4) remote ToR, (5) remote NIC. On access failure, the same NIC uses its other port and independent plane. A segment contains 1,024 active GPUs and 64 backup GPUs; dual-plane is shown as two dotted parallelograms; a Pod contains 15K GPUs (Figure 7).

points.title: HPN evidence and design trade-offs
points.body_markdown:
- 2,300+ H800 GPUs, proprietary LLM: HPN throughput +14.9% vs DCN; +256 GPUs, LLaMa7B.
- One link fails: dual-ToR loses 6.25%.
- Tier 2 retains any-to-any connectivity for MoE and cross-rail traffic.
- More port capacity in a Pod comes with less cross-Pod bandwidth.

points.title: Beyond 10K GPUs: communication locality and placement
points.body_markdown: Example: one ring round with 256 MB sent on each edge. A spread group across high-bandwidth domains A and B incurs 2 edges crossing domains = 2 × 256 MB = 512 MB of cross-domain traffic. A local group with the same ring and data volume incurs 0 cross-domain bytes but needs 4 free GPU slots in A. Same 1,024 MB exchanged; placement changes the cross-domain load. Choose a domain with enough GPU slots and local bandwidth.

points.title: Beyond 10K GPUs: diagnosing a slow collective
points.body_markdown:
Example: Rank 3 enters a four-rank AllReduce late; ranks 0–2 wait or make partial progress. A long collective interval can include waiting for a late rank. Evidence to correlate (collective/rank, NIC/QP, ToR/Agg path, port counters) and likely causes:

| Evidence | Likely cause | Next action |
|---|---|---|
| Rank 3 enters late; queues / errors normal | Input / compute / launch skew | Fix input, compute, or launch timing |
| Ranks enter together; one path queues more | Path congestion / load imbalance | Remap path or adjust send timing |
| Link / CRC errors plus retry events | Link / device fault | Fail over / repair; coordinate runtime recovery |

Re-measure collective time and useful training throughput after the fix.

points.title: Beyond 10K GPUs: adapting sequence partitions
points.body_markdown:
One 16K-token sequence with capacity of 8K tokens per GPU:
- **Fixed four-GPU partition**: 16K / 4 = 4K tokens per GPU; 4 GPUs exchange KV for this sequence.
- **Two GPUs for this sequence**: 16K / 2 = 8K tokens per GPU; 2 GPUs exchange KV; remaining GPUs handle another sequence.

The same attention still covers all 16K tokens. Choose the participants before choosing network paths. Each selected GPU handles more tokens (4K to 8K), and global gradient synchronization is still required.

points.title: Requirements for 100K-GPU networks
points.body_markdown:
100K GPUs require usable bandwidth for the communication groups that run. Place work; choose paths; control when and how much to send.

| Requirement | Mechanisms already seen |
|---|---|
| Capacity and locality | High-bandwidth domains; topology-aware rank / group placement |
| Path balance and bursts | Planes and disjoint paths; library scheduling, pacing, bounded in-flight data |
| Fault isolation and recovery | Independent access paths; fast failover with transport / runtime coordination |
| Observability and runtime | Correlate rank, QP, path, and port; validate recovery and reduce communication demand |

points.title: The accelerator memory wall: bandwidth and capacity limits
points.body_markdown:
Two walls motivate scale-up networks:

- **Bandwidth wall:** compute outpaces HBM bandwidth, so low arithmetic intensity (AI) limits the attainable FLOPs.
- **Capacity wall:** larger weights and context states increase the memory footprint.

points.title: Aggregating HBM resources across devices
points.body_markdown:
Scale-up aggregation works along two axes:

- **Capacity across HBM stacks:** expert-parallel (EP) / context-parallel (CP) partition weights and context states across devices.
- **Aggregate HBM bandwidth:** distribute memory traffic across stacks and exchange tokens and states over the interconnect.

Frequent dispatch, combine, and state exchange require a fast scale-up network.

The slide's table relates EP degree to AI and GPU utilization:

| EP degree | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 | 192 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AI (FLOP/byte) | 109.8 | 180.9 | 267.6 | 352.0 | 417.9 | 445.7 |
| GPU utilization | 18.8% | 31.0% | 45.9% | 60.3% | 66.2% | 66.2% |

points.title: NVIDIA: rack-scale NVLink domain (GB200 NVL72)
points.body_markdown:
- 72 GPUs share one rack-scale NVLink domain.
- Path: rack and copper backplane, GPU → NVSwitch → GPU.
- Composition: 18 compute trays × 4 GPUs = 72 GPUs; 9 switch trays × 2 ASICs = 18 NVSwitches.
- 1.8 TB/s bidirectional aggregate per GPU.
- IB / Ethernet connects separate NVLink domains.

points.title: Google: ICI cubes and optical reconfiguration
points.body_markdown:
- ICI links form a reconfigurable torus; DCN connects separate slices.
- Each chip has six logical ICI neighbors.
- OCS reconnects cube boundaries into larger slices.
- A large domain is not a single-hop full mesh.
- Slice examples: a 64-chip cube; one cube → two-cube slice; 4x4x4 slice; 4x8x4 slice.

points.title: Huawei: multi-rack UB domain (CloudMatrix384)
points.body_markdown:
- CloudMatrix384 forms one multi-rack UB scale-up domain.
- 384 NPU packages + 192 CPUs; 48 servers span multiple racks.
- UB uses two switching levels; RoCE scale-out is a separate network.
- UB path: NPU → L1 → L2 → L1 → NPU.

points.title: Meta: Ethernet scale-up with integrated NICs (MTIA300)
points.body_markdown:
- MTIA300 pairs Ethernet switching with integrated network chiplets.
- Tahan scale-up switch; one rack = 16 accelerator packages.
- Rack scale-up / DSF scale-out.
- Compute + network chiplets.
- Path: MTIA 1 → rack SU switch → MTIA 2.

points.title: Alibaba: modular ALink supernodes
points.body_markdown:
- The 2025 cabinet disclosure contains two AL64 scale-up domains.
- One AL64 is a single-stage ALink domain (upper AL64 / lower AL64).
- Path: GPU node → ALink switch → GPU node.

points.title: Design requirements for a scale-up domain
points.body_markdown:
A scale-up domain needs bandwidth, reliable paths, and correct completion. Three design questions:

- **Endpoint:** how many bytes can each device inject?
- **Fabric:** which paths will carry those bytes?
- **Software:** when may the receiver consume them?

EtherNode project goals: ≥128 accelerators; ≥200 GB/s per GPU (unidirectional); collective abstraction.

Serialization example for a 16 MB transfer:

| Rate | Time |
|---|---|
| 50 GB/s | 320 µs |
| 400 GB/s | 40 µs |

Beyond serialization, cost also comes from fixed overhead, queueing, and synchronization.

points.title: EtherNode's three design layers
points.body_markdown:
One GPU-to-GPU transfer crosses three layers:

- **Endpoint:** turn requests into reliable transfers on each path.
- **Fabric:** provide parallel, single-hop paths across the domain.
- **Middleware:** manage buffers and QPs; plan and execute collectives.

points.title: Endpoint layer: from GPU requests to Ethernet
points.body_markdown:
- GPU software manages transactions; packet engines deliver each path.
- Payload path: HBM ↔ packet engines ↔ Ethernet.
- Bandwidth: 16 × 200 Gb/s = 3.2 Tb/s = 400 GB/s, unidirectional.

points.title: Endpoint layer: optical I/O and physical reach
points.body_markdown:
Three reach options:

- **Full copper:** short reach; dense rack cabling; lower optics cost.
- **Copper + optics:** longer reach; additional switch tier; more complex paths.
- **Full optical:** across racks in one tier; higher optics cost / power; NPO or pluggable LPO.

EtherNode chooses optical reach to preserve a flat fabric.

points.title: Fabric layer: sixteen single-hop planes
points.body_markdown:
- Each GPU port connects to a plane switch (GPU A / port 1 → Plane 1 switch → GPU B / port 1).
- Scale: 4 GPUs/tray × 8 trays/rack × 16 racks = 512 GPUs.
- Per plane: 512 × 200G endpoint-facing ports; no aggregation uplinks inside the domain.

points.title: Fabric layer: parallel paths and transaction completion
points.body_markdown:
Illustrative write: a 64 KiB write split over four of the sixteen planes.

- Per-QP ordered paths: QP 0 / offset 0 KiB, QP 1 / offset 16 KiB, QP 2 / offset 32 KiB, QP 3 / offset 48 KiB.
- Disjoint regions: S0 = 0–16 KiB, S1 = 16–32 KiB, S2 = 32–48 KiB, S3 = 48–64 KiB.
- Completion: when all four segments arrive (1111), wait for preceding TIDs, then commit TID 7.
- TIDs are per communication pair; the example assumes earlier transactions have committed.

Segment arrival and receipt bitmap:

| Arrives | Receipt: S0 S1 S2 S3 |
|---|---|
| S2 | 0 0 1 0 |
| S0 | 1 0 1 0 |
| S3 | 1 0 1 1 |
| S1 | 1 1 1 1 |

points.title: Middleware layer: buffers and QP resources
points.body_markdown:
- The Network Abstraction Layer (NAL) manages buffers, mappings, and QPs.
- GPU / rank channels → NAL buffer + QP pool → leased QP / path bundles.
- Static full-path provisioning would need 32 local GPUs × 511 peers × 16 paths = 261,632 QP contexts, but only 65,536 QPs are available per rack.
- Therefore: allocate paths on demand; reclaim only after outstanding work drains.
- Unified buffer management is a software abstraction, not cache-coherent shared HBM.

points.title: Middleware layer: executing a collective
points.body_markdown:
An all-to-all phase becomes a plan of one-sided transactions:

- Logical channels are carried over switch planes.
- Resolve ranks, regions, lengths.
- Bind SMs / channels / QPs (update SM–channel–QP mapping).
- Run GPU communication kernels.
- Track received segments; commit in order → phase complete.
- A CPU daemon manages resources and refreshes mappings off the transfer path.

The slide's all-to-all table (rows/columns A–D, e.g., A→B = 64 KiB) illustrates the per-pair transfer plan.

points.title: EtherNode: summary of design choices
points.body_markdown:
EtherNode scales accelerator and memory domains over commodity Ethernet; a scale-up network combines high-bandwidth connectivity with explicit transfer semantics and resource management.

| Design constraint | Design choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Limited physical reach | Full optical I/O | Extend connectivity across racks while preserving a single-tier fabric |
| High bandwidth under a tight I/O-die budget | Multi-plane, single-hop fabric with fixed per-QP paths | Aggregate bandwidth while reducing packet-reordering buffer requirements |
| Cross-path ordering and finite connection resources | Software transaction module and shared resource pools | Coordinate completion and ordering; allocate QPs and buffers on demand |

Trade-offs: optical reach adds cost and power; software carries cross-path semantics and resource management.

documents.markdown:
This lecture document provides a comprehensive overview of the Transformer model family, tracing its evolution from foundational language model concepts to modern Large Language Models (LLMs). It details the progression from word embeddings and recurrent neural networks to the introduction of attention mechanisms and self-attention as core architectural components. The text explains the specific building blocks of the Transformer, including multi-head attention, positional embeddings, and residual connections, while distinguishing between encoder, decoder, and encoder-decoder variants. Additionally, the document covers the scaling laws and historical milestones of LLMs, such as the GPT series, and discusses practical applications and training costs.

## Rapid growth of LLMs and their real-world applications

The lecture frames LLM progress as a timeline: Transformer (2017), BERT (2018), T5 (2019), GPT-3 (2020), ChatGPT (2022), GPT-4 and Mixtral (2023), Llama 3 and DeepSeek (2024), and Gemini-3, Opus, and GPT-5 (2025). LLMs and their associated bots like ChatGPT are developed across many organizations (Amazon, Chinese Google, Meta/Facebook, Microsoft, OpenAI, and others).

LLMs are shown to power real-world applications including question answering, coding, computer use, and personal assistants. Example QA task: given a passage about Marco Polo's travels, the model answers "How did some suspect that Polo learned about China instead of by actually visiting it?" with "through contact with Persian traders."

## LLMs excel across general and advanced benchmarks

LLMs perform strongly on semantic similarity and classification benchmarks (GPT-1 results table):

| Method | CoLA (mc) | SST2 (acc) | MRPC (F1) | STSB (pc) | QQP (F1) | GLUE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single-task BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn | 35.0 | 90.2 | 80.2 | 55.5 | 66.1 | 64.8 |
| Multi-task BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn | 18.9 | 91.6 | 83.5 | 72.8 | 63.3 | 68.9 |
| Finetuned Transformer LM (ours) | 45.4 | 91.3 | 82.3 | 82.0 | 70.3 | 72.8 |

On question answering and commonsense reasoning (GPT-1):

| Method | Story Cloze | RACE-m | RACE-h | RACE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dynamic Fusion Net (9x) | - | 55.6 | 49.4 | 51.2 |
| BiAttention MRU (9x) | - | 60.2 | 50.3 | 53.3 |
| Finetuned Transformer LM (ours) | 86.5 | 62.9 | 57.4 | 59.0 |

Advanced math and competitive programming results are reported as Codeforces Elo / percentile, and the improved OL model ranked 49th at IOI 2024.

## Definition of a language model

A language model is a probabilistic model of a sequence of words. Formally, it computes the joint probability:

$$P(w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t)})$$

This value expresses how likely a given sequence of words is to appear in real-world language use. Example sequences: "The cat sits on the mat.", "The dog runs in the park.", "I like machine learning."

## Chain rule decomposition of sentence probability

The probability of a sentence can be decomposed into a product of next-word (conditional) probabilities:

$$P(w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t)}) = P(w^{(1)}) \times P(w^{(2)} \mid w^{(1)}) \times \cdots \times P(w^{(t)} \mid w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t-1)})$$

Concrete example for "The dog runs in the park.":

$$P(\text{The dog runs in the park.}) = P(\text{The}) \cdot P(\text{dog} \mid \text{The}) \cdot P(\text{runs} \mid \text{The dog}) \cdot P(\text{in} \mid \text{The dog runs}) \cdot P(\text{the} \mid \text{The dog runs in}) \cdot P(\text{park} \mid \text{The dog runs in the})$$

## Next-word prediction as the universal task framing

Given previous words, the model predicts the probability of the next word:

$$P(w^{(t)} \mid w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t-1)})$$

Generation proceeds by selecting or sampling one word, appending it to the context, and repeating. Almost all tasks can be framed as next-word prediction:

- Translation: "Hello in Chinese is" → "你好"
- Coding: "def add(a, b): return" → a + b
- QA: "The first man on the moon was" → Neil
- Sentiment: "I hated this movie. Sentiment:" → Negative

## How a language model works in practice

Input tokens (e.g., "The / Capital / Of / France / is") are fed to a neural network, which outputs a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary. Internally, tokens are represented as vectors (e.g., 8-dimensional vectors with positive and negative entries).

## Intuition for word representations

Two guiding properties for word representations:
- Different words should have different representations.
- Related words should have similar representations.

## One-hot representation and its limitation

Each word is assigned a unique sparse vector over the vocabulary. With vocabulary [cat, dog, car, apple, run]:

- cat => [1,0,0,0,0]
- dog => [0,1,0,0,0]
- car => [0,0,1,0,0]
- apple => [0,0,0,1,0]
- run => [0,0,0,0,1]

Issue: all words are equally (dis)similar — e.g., the dot products for (cat, dog) and (cat, car) are both zero.

## Context as a signal of word meaning

Nearby words reveal what a word means. Examples of target words and their typical contexts:
- cherry — pie, dessert
- strawberry — rhubarb, pie
- digital — computer, devices

The question posed: which nearby words tell you what "banking" means, and which two target words occur in similar contexts?

## Word-word co-occurrence matrix

A co-occurrence matrix counts context words within a window (4 words to the left + 4 words to the right). Example counts:

| Target | computer | data | result | pie | sugar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cherry | 2 | 8 | 9 | 442 | 25 |
| strawberry | 0 | 0 | 1 | 60 | 19 |
| digital | 1670 | 1683 | 85 | 5 | 4 |
| information | 3325 | 3982 | 378 | 5 | 13 |

Cosine similarity computed using three columns (pie, data, computer) gives cos(digital, information) ≈ 0.996.

## From co-occurrence counts to short dense vectors

Two coordinates can still separate fruit terms from computing terms. GloVe also uses corpus counts: it learns vectors that fit log co-occurrence counts.

Four context counts per word:

| Target | computer | data | pie | sugar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cherry | 2 | 8 | 442 | 25 |
| strawberry | 0 | 0 | 60 | 19 |
| digital | 1,670 | 1,683 | 5 | 4 |
| information | 3,325 | 3,982 | 5 | 13 |

Two SVD coordinates:

| Target | Axis 1 | Axis 2 |
|---|---|---|
| cherry | 8.0 | 442.7 |
| strawberry | 0.1 | 61.0 |
| digital | 2,365.0 | 0.7 |
| information | 5,187.1 | -1.0 |

Axis 1 mainly tracks computer and data; Axis 2 mainly tracks pie.

## Word2Vec training examples: Skip-gram vs. CBOW

With "banking" at the center:
- Skip-gram: banking → turning, into, crises, as (four separate targets)
- CBOW: turning, into, crises, as → banking (one target)

## Negative sampling and embedding updates

An observed pair trains its score upward; sampled noise pairs train their scores downward. Example: negative sampling with observed pair (banking, crises), target = 1, learning rate = 0.2. The question posed is how one observed pair changes the two vectors.

## Nearest neighbors by cosine similarity

Neighbors of Sweden ranked by cosine similarity:

| Word | Cosine |
|---|---|
| norway | 0.760124 |
| denmark | 0.715460 |
| finland | 0.620022 |
| switzerland | 0.588132 |
| belgium | 0.585835 |
| netherlands | 0.574631 |
| iceland | 0.562368 |
| estonia | 0.547621 |
| slovenia | 0.531408 |

The neighbor making the smallest angle with the Sweden vector ranks first (0.760 → 41°; 0.586 → 54°). The ranking uses the full embedding vectors, normalized to unit length.

## Token embeddings in a language model

The model fetches an input vector for a token by multiplying its one-hot vector by the embedding table E. Example: training prefix "The Broadway play" with token IDs 0, 1, 2; the one-hot for ID 2 is [0, 0, 1, 0] × E.

Embedding table E (toy vocabulary):

| ID | Token | Input vector |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | The | [0.3, 0.1, 0.5] |
| 1 | Broadway | [0.1, 0.8, 0.2] |
| 2 | play | [0.6, -0.2, 0.4] |
| 3 | opened | [0.5, -0.1, 0.3] |

Observed next token: opened. The next-token loss updates the model and the input rows used for this prefix.

## One token, two meanings

The same token ("play") may not retrieve the same neighbor in different sentences. The question posed: which words in each sentence tell the model which sense of "play" is intended?

## What the neural network learns

From word embeddings to neural networks, the network learns to:
- Capture the meaning of the previous sequence
- Estimate probabilities for possible next tokens

## Requirements of a good sequence representation

A good sequence representation should capture:
- Relevance/importance between tokens (e.g., in "The capital of France is", some tokens are highly relevant)
- Information from all previous tokens
- Positional meaning: "dog bites man" ≠ "man bites dog"

## Recap of fully connected networks

For input $X = [x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d]$ and weights $W = [w_1; w_2; \ldots; w_d]$:

$$Y = \sigma(WX + b)$$

where $\sigma$ is a nonlinear function such as ReLU or GeLU. Worked example:

$$\begin{bmatrix}0.40 & 0.35 & 0.01\\ 0.25 & 0.30 & 0.35\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.6025\\ 0.6019\\ 0.6038\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0.7\\ 0.7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1.1577\\ 1.2425\end{bmatrix}$$

## Bag-of-words representation via one-hot vectors

A vocabulary table maps each word to a one-hot vector. For the vocabulary `[cat, chase, dog, run, car]`:

- `cat` => `[1,0,0,0,0]`
- `chase` => `[0,1,0,0,0]`
- `dog` => `[0,0,1,0,0]`

A sentence/document is represented by the **counts** of words in the vocabulary. For example, "cat chase dog" => `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`.

The vector is written as:

$$ \mathbf{x}=[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{k}] $$

where $x_{1}$ is how many times the word "love" appears in document $d$.

## Naïve fully connected language model

The model uses bag-of-words representation (sum of one-hot vectors, e.g. $c_1+c_2+c_3+c_4$) as input:

- Hidden layer: $h=f(W_{1}x+b)$
- Output distribution: $\hat{y}=softmax(W_{2}h)$

## Problem: bag-of-words loses word order

Bag-of-Words only counts word occurrences, so different sentences may have the same vector:

- "cat chase dog" => `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`
- "dog chase cat" => `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`

Same words, same BoW vector, but different meanings. The fully connected network predicts from a bag of words, not from an ordered sequence representation.

## Recurrent neural network hidden state update

The same cell updates the hidden state at every word:

$$ \mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{t}}=\tanh(\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{t}}+\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{h}}\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{t}-1}+\mathrm{b}) $$

where $\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{t}}$ is the current word vector.

## RNN language models process words in sequence

The same RNN cell processes each word in turn. The model predicts the next word conditioned on the preceding words, e.g.:

$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{(4)} = P(\boldsymbol{x}^{(5)}|\mathrm{the~students~opened~their}) $$

## Last hidden state summarizes the entire prefix

In an RNN language model, the last hidden state summarizes the entire prefix. For the prefix "the students opened their", the prefix is summarized by $h_{4}$, which is used to predict the next word.

## Sequence-to-sequence generation

In seq2seq generation, every decoder step receives the same source summary produced by the encoder (e.g., a Chinese source encoded, an English prefix decoded).

## Limitations of recurrent language models

- **Learning bottleneck: information decay.** All previous tokens are compressed into $h_{t}$; information from $x_{i}$ must pass through many updates to affect $h_{t}$.
- **System inefficiency.** Sequential computation: $h_{t}$ depends on $h_{t-1}$. Training/serving large models becomes cost-prohibitive due to time constraints.

## Attention intuition: query and key vectors

- A **key vector** represents the type of information present at a step (keys come from saved states).
- A **query vector** represents what we are looking for at this step.

Intuition: a key might encode "the subject of the sentence," and a query might ask for "the subject of the sentence." In practice, what keys and queries mean and how they interact are learned; they do not need to be defined manually.

## Scoring: comparing a query with every key

The query is compared with every key to get one score per position (e.g., over the words "Students", "open", "their", "books").

## Attention is a weighted average

The query at "books" reads three earlier states. Softmax turns the three scores into weights that add up to one, producing a context vector:

$$ \mathrm{c}=\alpha_{1}\mathrm{h}_{1}+\alpha_{2}\mathrm{h}_{2}+\alpha_{3}\mathrm{h}_{3} $$

where $h_{1}$, $h_{2}$, $h_{3}$ are the saved states for the three earlier words and $\alpha_i$ are the attention weights.

## Dot-product attention walkthrough

- **Scores:** one dot product per key.
- **Weights:** one softmax across all three scores.

## Attention as a soft, weighted lookup table

In attention, the query softly matches each key, producing a weight between 0 and 1; the keys' values are multiplied by the weights and summed. In a lookup table, a table of keys maps to values, and the query matches one of the keys, returning its value.

## Sequence-to-sequence with attention

The first decoder state queries the saved source states (encoder Chinese source, decoder English prefix). After "Anna left," the decoder reads the same source states again.

## Do we still need recurrence?

- **Reading a state:** the decoder can read any saved state.
- **Building a state:** the fourth update still needs the third.

Question raised: could each position build its own representation directly from the inputs?

## Building context without recurrence

Once the inputs are available, both outputs can be computed together in a layer — layer outputs for the Chinese prefix input vectors can be computed in parallel, without recurrence.

## What makes this self-attention

The query at 北京 reads keys and values from the same Chinese prefix — i.e., queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence.

## Step 1: transform each input into query, key, and value vectors

For each input $x_i$:

$$ \mathbf{q}_i = x_i \mathbf{W}^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_q}, \quad \mathbf{W}^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_q} $$

$$ \mathbf{k}_i = x_i \mathbf{W}^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}, \quad \mathbf{W}^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_k} $$

$$ \mathbf{v}_i = x_i \mathbf{W}^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\nu}, \quad \mathbf{W}^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_\nu} $$

Example with inputs "Thinking" ($x_1$) and "Machines" ($x_2$), producing queries $q_1, q_2$, keys $k_1, k_2$, values $v_1, v_2$.

## Step 2: turn one query's scores into attention weights

Use the query at "Thinking" to score both keys (both words are visible):

| | Thinking | Machines |
|---|---|---|
| Score | $q_1 \cdot k_1 = 112$ | $q_1 \cdot k_2 = 96$ |
| Divide by 8 ($\sqrt{d_k}$) | 14 | 12 |
| Softmax | 0.88 | 0.12 |

The keys have 64 features; dividing both scores by $\sqrt{64} = 8$ helps keep softmax from saturating. Result: `softmax([14, 12]) ≈ [0.88, 0.12]`.

## Step 3: mix value vectors using the query's weights

$$ \mathbf{o}_{\mathrm{Thinking}}\approx0.88\,v_{\mathrm{Thinking}}+0.12\,v_{\mathrm{Machines}} $$

Take 0.88 of the first value vector and 0.12 of the second, and add them coordinate by coordinate. "Machines" gets its own row of weights.

## Matrix form of attention and causal masking

$$ Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK^{T}/\sqrt{d_{k}}+M)V $$

- Each row compares one query with every key; apply softmax across that row.
- **Causal self-attention:** $M$ adds 0 to allowed scores and $-\infty$ to future scores before softmax.
- For "Thinking," masking "Machines" changes the weights from [0.88, 0.12] to [1, 0].
- Doubling the sequence length gives four times as many cells in the full score grid.

## Multi-head attention

$$ Head=Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V $$

$$ Multi-head Attention(Q,K,V)=concat(head_{1},head_{2},...,head_{h})W^{O} $$

Why it works:

- Different heads learn different attention patterns.
- Heads can capture multiple relations simultaneously, e.g., local context, long-range dependencies, and syntactic/semantic links.
- Concatenation aggregates diverse information into a richer token representation.

With $d = 512$ and $h = 8$ heads, each key has $d_{k} = 64$ features; scale each head's scores by dividing by $\sqrt{64} = 8$. Each head has its own Q, K and V projections.

## Barriers and solutions for self-attention as a building block

- **Masking:** give future positions zero attention weight so a prediction can use only its prefix.
- **Position information:** add position representations to the inputs so attention can use word order.
- **Feed-forward network:** transform each position's attention output with the same nonlinear feed-forward network.

## Causal masking and parallel computation

- Each position sees its prefix. During training, input tokens are already available; compute all positions within a layer, and the mask controls information access.
- The mask (added before softmax) is lower-triangular: allowed positions get 0, future positions get $-\infty$; masked positions receive zero weight.
- **Autoregressive generation:** select a token, append it, and repeat.

## Self-attention needs position information

The query at "bites" can see all three words, but the embeddings carry only word identity. Example weights: dog 0.50, bites 0.20, man 0.30. The weighted output at "bites" is:

$$ 0.50\,v_{dog}+0.20\,v_{bites}+0.30\,v_{man} $$

Each word keeps its key, value and weight, so both rows give the same sum — word order is not distinguished without position information.

## Positional embeddings

Sinusoidal positional representations concatenate sinusoidal functions with varying periods:

$$ \widetilde{x}_{i}=x_{i}+p_{i} $$

$$ \pmb{p}_{i}=\left(\begin{matrix}{\sin(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\{\cos(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\{\vdots}\\{\sin(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\{\cos(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\end{matrix}\right) $$

where $i$ is the index in the sequence.

## Adding nonlinearities after self-attention

- Self-attention has no elementwise nonlinear activation on its outputs; stacking attention layers keeps re-averaging value vectors.
- Add a feed-forward network after self-attention; its activation function, such as ReLU, introduces elementwise nonlinearity:

$$ m_{i}\;=\;W_{2}\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{1}\,o_{i}\;+\;b_{1})\;+\;b_{2} $$

where $o_i$ is the attention output at position $i$. Softmax sets attention weights; ReLU adds a nonlinear transformation of the output features. Each layer shares its FFN weights across token positions.

## Residual connections and layer normalization

- **Residual connection:** the sublayer learns an update, while the input retains a direct path (additive input path). Residuals give gradients a direct path.
- **Layer normalization:** operates on one token, across its features; it centers and rescales features, stabilizing each token's feature scale.

## Transformer block equations: attention sublayer and MLP/FFN sublayer

The Transformer block combines Multi-Head Attention and an MLP/FFN, each wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization.

**Attention sublayer:**
$$ \mathrm{Z}=LN(X+MHA(XW_{q},XW_{k},XW_{v})) $$

**MLP / FFN sublayer:**
$$ H=LN(Z+ReLU(ZW_{1})W_{2}) $$

- The attention sublayer computes queries, keys, and values by multiplying the input $X$ with $W_q$, $W_k$, $W_v$.
- The MLP uses a ReLU activation between two linear transformations ($W_1$, then $W_2$).
- Both sublayers use the pattern: residual add, then layer normalization ($LN$).

## Transformer Decoder block composition

The Transformer Decoder is a stack of Transformer Decoder Blocks. Each block consists of:

1. Self-attention
2. Add & Norm
3. Feed-Forward
4. Add & Norm

## From decoder states to next-token probabilities

The decoder produces contextual states $h_t$ with $d$ features. These are converted to a distribution over the vocabulary:

- **Vocabulary logits:** one score per vocabulary token, computed from $h_t$.
- **Output softmax:** converts logits into probabilities over the vocabulary.
- **Generation loop:** select a token, append it to the prefix, and repeat.

Illustrative example: prompt "The capital of France is" → contextual states from the decoder → vocabulary logits → softmax probabilities → vocabulary output.

## Transformer Encoder: bidirectional (non-causal) attention

The whole source sentence is available before translation begins, so the encoder uses no causal mask.

- Each query position can attend to **all** source positions (both left and right context).
- Example source "昨天安娜离开了北京": every query position (昨天, 安娜, 离开了, 北京) can read all four positions.
- Each query position produces a state for that position (e.g., state for 昨天, state for 安娜, ...).

## Encoder-Decoder: masked self-attention and cross-attention

For source "昨天安娜离开了北京":

- **Encoder inputs:** each position can use context on both sides.
- **Masked self-attention (decoder):** to predict "Beijing," the decoder can read the English prefix "Anna left." — i.e., only the target prefix is visible.
- **Cross-attention:** the decoder supplies the **query**; the encoder states for the Chinese input supply the **keys and values**.

## Three Transformer model families

| Architecture | Visible context | Typical output / use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encoder-only | All supplied input tokens; bidirectional context | Contextual representations; understanding tasks | BERT |
| Decoder-only | Prefix tokens; causal self-attention | Next-token probabilities; autoregressive generation | GPT |
| Encoder-decoder | Encoder: full source; Decoder: target prefix + source cross-attention | Conditional output sequence; translation / summarization | T5 |

The lecture follows the decoder-only branch into the GPT family.

## Scaling laws for next-token prediction loss

Experiment varies three quantities across training runs:

- $N$ = non-embedding parameters (768 to 1.5B)
- $D$ = dataset size in tokens (22M to 23B)
- $C$ = total non-embedding training FLOPs

Prediction loss is evaluated on held-out text. In the dataset-size fit, **doubling the data cuts test loss by about 6%**.

## Effect of context window length on reasoning

- Each bar averages three models at that window size.
- A longer window keeps earlier reasoning steps available to later steps.
- In this experiment, long-context retrieval and math accuracy both **peaked at $16\times$**.

## Scaling model size together with training data

Models are getting larger and trained on more and more data ("the blessings of scale").

| Model parameters | Training tokens |
|---|---|
| 400 million | 8.0 billion |
| 1 billion | 20.2 billion |
| 10 billion | 205.1 billion |

Rule of thumb: **10× the parameters → about 10× the training tokens.**

## GPT-1 (2018): decoder pretraining

GPT (2018) was a major success in decoder pretraining.

- Transformer decoder with **12 layers, 117M parameters**.
- **768-dimensional** hidden states; **3072-dimensional** feed-forward hidden layers.
- Byte-pair encoding with **40,000 merges**.
- Trained on **BookCorpus**: over 7,000 unique books — containing long spans of contiguous text for learning long-distance dependencies.
- Finetuned Transformer LM results on natural language inference tasks (MNLI-m, MNLI-mm, SNLI, SciTail, QNLI, RTE), e.g., MNLI-m 82.1, SNLI 89.9, SciTail 88.3, QNLI 88.1, RTE 56.0.

## GPT-2 (2019): unsupervised pretraining as text-to-text

- Unsupervised pre-training for general NLP tasks.
- Frames tasks as **text-to-text prediction**.
- Larger training corpus: **8M webpages, around 40 GB of text**.
- Larger model: **1.5B parameters**.
- Demonstrated conditional text generation (e.g., continuing a human-written prompt about unicorns in the Andes).

## GPT-3 (2020): in-context learning

Very large language models seem to perform some kind of learning **without gradient steps**, simply from examples provided within their context windows.

- The in-context examples seem to specify the task to be performed.
- The conditional distribution mimics performing the task to a certain extent.
- Example: prefix "thanks → 谢谢, hello → 你好, cat → 猫, dog →" yields the conditional generation "狗".

## GPT-4 (2023): multimodal image and text in, text out

- GPT-4 accepts **image and text in, text out**.
- Example: asked "What makes this picture funny?", it explains that the oversized monitor plug hides a tiny phone connector — the joke depends on seeing both.

## GPT-5 and GPT-6 Astra (2025–2026)

- **GPT-5 · Reasoning on demand:** ChatGPT routes a request to a fast model or a deeper reasoning model.
- **GPT-6 Astra · Computer use:** Astra inspects the screen, takes an action, and uses the result to choose its next move (e.g., OpenAI's KiCad demo placing components and routing a circuit board).

## Pre-training vs. post-training processes

- **Pre-training process:** learn general knowledge.
- **Post-training process:** behavior alignment, reasoning, tool use — updated based on the reward model's response.

## Scaling curse: training and serving costs

**Hardware example:** Llama 3 405B is trained on up to 16K H100 GPUs, each at 700W TDP with 80GB HBM3, on Meta's Grand Teton AI server platform. Each server has eight GPUs and two CPUs; the eight GPUs within a server are connected via NVLink. Training jobs are scheduled using MAST, Meta's global-scale training scheduler.

**Training GPU costs:**
- Llama 3.1 405B: **30.84M GPU-hours**
- One GPU-hour = one GPU running for one hour
- At 700 W: 0.7 kW × 1 h = 0.7 kWh

**Serving is also expensive:**
- 128K-token prefill: 3.8s
- 1M-token prefill: 77s
- on up to 128 H100 GPUs

| Model | Training Time (GPU hours) | Training Power (W) | GHG Emissions (tons CO₂eq) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Llama 3.1 8B | 1.46M | 700 | 420 |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 7.0M | 700 | 2,040 |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 30.84M | 700 | 8,930 |
| Total | 39.3M | | 11,390 |
documents.intro_markdown: This lecture document provides a comprehensive overview of the Transformer model family, tracing its evolution from foundational language model concepts to modern Large Language Models (LLMs). It details the progression from word embeddings and recurrent neural networks to the introduction of attention mechanisms and self-attention as core architectural components. The text explains the specific building blocks of the Transformer, including multi-head attention, positional embeddings, and residual connections, while distinguishing between encoder, decoder, and encoder-decoder variants. Additionally, the document covers the scaling laws and historical milestones of LLMs, such as the GPT series, and discusses practical applications and training costs.
