points.title: Rapid growth of LLMs and their real-world applications
points.body_markdown:
The lecture frames LLM progress as a timeline: Transformer (2017), BERT (2018), T5 (2019), GPT-3 (2020), ChatGPT (2022), GPT-4 and Mixtral (2023), Llama 3 and DeepSeek (2024), and Gemini-3, Opus, and GPT-5 (2025). LLMs and their associated bots like ChatGPT are developed across many organizations (Amazon, Chinese Google, Meta/Facebook, Microsoft, OpenAI, and others).

LLMs are shown to power real-world applications including question answering, coding, computer use, and personal assistants. Example QA task: given a passage about Marco Polo's travels, the model answers "How did some suspect that Polo learned about China instead of by actually visiting it?" with "through contact with Persian traders."

points.title: LLMs excel across general and advanced benchmarks
points.body_markdown:
LLMs perform strongly on semantic similarity and classification benchmarks (GPT-1 results table):

| Method | CoLA (mc) | SST2 (acc) | MRPC (F1) | STSB (pc) | QQP (F1) | GLUE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single-task BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn | 35.0 | 90.2 | 80.2 | 55.5 | 66.1 | 64.8 |
| Multi-task BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn | 18.9 | 91.6 | 83.5 | 72.8 | 63.3 | 68.9 |
| Finetuned Transformer LM (ours) | 45.4 | 91.3 | 82.3 | 82.0 | 70.3 | 72.8 |

On question answering and commonsense reasoning (GPT-1):

| Method | Story Cloze | RACE-m | RACE-h | RACE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dynamic Fusion Net (9x) | - | 55.6 | 49.4 | 51.2 |
| BiAttention MRU (9x) | - | 60.2 | 50.3 | 53.3 |
| Finetuned Transformer LM (ours) | 86.5 | 62.9 | 57.4 | 59.0 |

Advanced math and competitive programming results are reported as Codeforces Elo / percentile, and the improved OL model ranked 49th at IOI 2024.

points.title: Definition of a language model
points.body_markdown:
A language model is a probabilistic model of a sequence of words. Formally, it computes the joint probability:

$$P(w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t)})$$

This value expresses how likely a given sequence of words is to appear in real-world language use. Example sequences: "The cat sits on the mat.", "The dog runs in the park.", "I like machine learning."

points.title: Chain rule decomposition of sentence probability
points.body_markdown:
The probability of a sentence can be decomposed into a product of next-word (conditional) probabilities:

$$P(w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t)}) = P(w^{(1)}) \times P(w^{(2)} \mid w^{(1)}) \times \cdots \times P(w^{(t)} \mid w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t-1)})$$

Concrete example for "The dog runs in the park.":

$$P(\text{The dog runs in the park.}) = P(\text{The}) \cdot P(\text{dog} \mid \text{The}) \cdot P(\text{runs} \mid \text{The dog}) \cdot P(\text{in} \mid \text{The dog runs}) \cdot P(\text{the} \mid \text{The dog runs in}) \cdot P(\text{park} \mid \text{The dog runs in the})$$

points.title: Next-word prediction as the universal task framing
points.body_markdown:
Given previous words, the model predicts the probability of the next word:

$$P(w^{(t)} \mid w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t-1)})$$

Generation proceeds by selecting or sampling one word, appending it to the context, and repeating. Almost all tasks can be framed as next-word prediction:

- Translation: "Hello in Chinese is" → "你好"
- Coding: "def add(a, b): return" → a + b
- QA: "The first man on the moon was" → Neil
- Sentiment: "I hated this movie. Sentiment:" → Negative

points.title: How a language model works in practice
points.body_markdown: Input tokens (e.g., "The / Capital / Of / France / is") are fed to a neural network, which outputs a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary. Internally, tokens are represented as vectors (e.g., 8-dimensional vectors with positive and negative entries).

points.title: Intuition for word representations
points.body_markdown:
Two guiding properties for word representations:
- Different words should have different representations.
- Related words should have similar representations.

points.title: One-hot representation and its limitation
points.body_markdown:
Each word is assigned a unique sparse vector over the vocabulary. With vocabulary [cat, dog, car, apple, run]:

- cat => [1,0,0,0,0]
- dog => [0,1,0,0,0]
- car => [0,0,1,0,0]
- apple => [0,0,0,1,0]
- run => [0,0,0,0,1]

Issue: all words are equally (dis)similar — e.g., the dot products for (cat, dog) and (cat, car) are both zero.

points.title: Context as a signal of word meaning
points.body_markdown:
Nearby words reveal what a word means. Examples of target words and their typical contexts:
- cherry — pie, dessert
- strawberry — rhubarb, pie
- digital — computer, devices

The question posed: which nearby words tell you what "banking" means, and which two target words occur in similar contexts?

points.title: Word-word co-occurrence matrix
points.body_markdown:
A co-occurrence matrix counts context words within a window (4 words to the left + 4 words to the right). Example counts:

| Target | computer | data | result | pie | sugar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cherry | 2 | 8 | 9 | 442 | 25 |
| strawberry | 0 | 0 | 1 | 60 | 19 |
| digital | 1670 | 1683 | 85 | 5 | 4 |
| information | 3325 | 3982 | 378 | 5 | 13 |

Cosine similarity computed using three columns (pie, data, computer) gives cos(digital, information) ≈ 0.996.

points.title: From co-occurrence counts to short dense vectors
points.body_markdown:
Two coordinates can still separate fruit terms from computing terms. GloVe also uses corpus counts: it learns vectors that fit log co-occurrence counts.

Four context counts per word:

| Target | computer | data | pie | sugar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cherry | 2 | 8 | 442 | 25 |
| strawberry | 0 | 0 | 60 | 19 |
| digital | 1,670 | 1,683 | 5 | 4 |
| information | 3,325 | 3,982 | 5 | 13 |

Two SVD coordinates:

| Target | Axis 1 | Axis 2 |
|---|---|---|
| cherry | 8.0 | 442.7 |
| strawberry | 0.1 | 61.0 |
| digital | 2,365.0 | 0.7 |
| information | 5,187.1 | -1.0 |

Axis 1 mainly tracks computer and data; Axis 2 mainly tracks pie.

points.title: Word2Vec training examples: Skip-gram vs. CBOW
points.body_markdown:
With "banking" at the center:
- Skip-gram: banking → turning, into, crises, as (four separate targets)
- CBOW: turning, into, crises, as → banking (one target)

points.title: Negative sampling and embedding updates
points.body_markdown: An observed pair trains its score upward; sampled noise pairs train their scores downward. Example: negative sampling with observed pair (banking, crises), target = 1, learning rate = 0.2. The question posed is how one observed pair changes the two vectors.

points.title: Nearest neighbors by cosine similarity
points.body_markdown:
Neighbors of Sweden ranked by cosine similarity:

| Word | Cosine |
|---|---|
| norway | 0.760124 |
| denmark | 0.715460 |
| finland | 0.620022 |
| switzerland | 0.588132 |
| belgium | 0.585835 |
| netherlands | 0.574631 |
| iceland | 0.562368 |
| estonia | 0.547621 |
| slovenia | 0.531408 |

The neighbor making the smallest angle with the Sweden vector ranks first (0.760 → 41°; 0.586 → 54°). The ranking uses the full embedding vectors, normalized to unit length.

points.title: Token embeddings in a language model
points.body_markdown:
The model fetches an input vector for a token by multiplying its one-hot vector by the embedding table E. Example: training prefix "The Broadway play" with token IDs 0, 1, 2; the one-hot for ID 2 is [0, 0, 1, 0] × E.

Embedding table E (toy vocabulary):

| ID | Token | Input vector |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | The | [0.3, 0.1, 0.5] |
| 1 | Broadway | [0.1, 0.8, 0.2] |
| 2 | play | [0.6, -0.2, 0.4] |
| 3 | opened | [0.5, -0.1, 0.3] |

Observed next token: opened. The next-token loss updates the model and the input rows used for this prefix.

points.title: One token, two meanings
points.body_markdown: The same token ("play") may not retrieve the same neighbor in different sentences. The question posed: which words in each sentence tell the model which sense of "play" is intended?

points.title: What the neural network learns
points.body_markdown:
From word embeddings to neural networks, the network learns to:
- Capture the meaning of the previous sequence
- Estimate probabilities for possible next tokens

points.title: Requirements of a good sequence representation
points.body_markdown:
A good sequence representation should capture:
- Relevance/importance between tokens (e.g., in "The capital of France is", some tokens are highly relevant)
- Information from all previous tokens
- Positional meaning: "dog bites man" ≠ "man bites dog"

points.title: Recap of fully connected networks
points.body_markdown:
For input $X = [x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d]$ and weights $W = [w_1; w_2; \ldots; w_d]$:

$$Y = \sigma(WX + b)$$

where $\sigma$ is a nonlinear function such as ReLU or GeLU. Worked example:

$$\begin{bmatrix}0.40 & 0.35 & 0.01\\ 0.25 & 0.30 & 0.35\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.6025\\ 0.6019\\ 0.6038\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0.7\\ 0.7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1.1577\\ 1.2425\end{bmatrix}$$

points.title: Bag-of-words representation via one-hot vectors
points.body_markdown:
A vocabulary table maps each word to a one-hot vector. For the vocabulary `[cat, chase, dog, run, car]`:

- `cat` => `[1,0,0,0,0]`
- `chase` => `[0,1,0,0,0]`
- `dog` => `[0,0,1,0,0]`

A sentence/document is represented by the **counts** of words in the vocabulary. For example, "cat chase dog" => `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`.

The vector is written as:

$$ \mathbf{x}=[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{k}] $$

where $x_{1}$ is how many times the word "love" appears in document $d$.

points.title: Naïve fully connected language model
points.body_markdown:
The model uses bag-of-words representation (sum of one-hot vectors, e.g. $c_1+c_2+c_3+c_4$) as input:

- Hidden layer: $h=f(W_{1}x+b)$
- Output distribution: $\hat{y}=softmax(W_{2}h)$

points.title: Problem: bag-of-words loses word order
points.body_markdown:
Bag-of-Words only counts word occurrences, so different sentences may have the same vector:

- "cat chase dog" => `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`
- "dog chase cat" => `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`

Same words, same BoW vector, but different meanings. The fully connected network predicts from a bag of words, not from an ordered sequence representation.

points.title: Recurrent neural network hidden state update
points.body_markdown:
The same cell updates the hidden state at every word:

$$ \mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{t}}=\tanh(\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{x}}\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{t}}+\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{h}}\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{t}-1}+\mathrm{b}) $$

where $\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{t}}$ is the current word vector.

points.title: RNN language models process words in sequence
points.body_markdown:
The same RNN cell processes each word in turn. The model predicts the next word conditioned on the preceding words, e.g.:

$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{y}}^{(4)} = P(\boldsymbol{x}^{(5)}|\mathrm{the~students~opened~their}) $$

points.title: Last hidden state summarizes the entire prefix
points.body_markdown: In an RNN language model, the last hidden state summarizes the entire prefix. For the prefix "the students opened their", the prefix is summarized by $h_{4}$, which is used to predict the next word.

points.title: Sequence-to-sequence generation
points.body_markdown: In seq2seq generation, every decoder step receives the same source summary produced by the encoder (e.g., a Chinese source encoded, an English prefix decoded).

points.title: Limitations of recurrent language models
points.body_markdown:
- **Learning bottleneck: information decay.** All previous tokens are compressed into $h_{t}$; information from $x_{i}$ must pass through many updates to affect $h_{t}$.
- **System inefficiency.** Sequential computation: $h_{t}$ depends on $h_{t-1}$. Training/serving large models becomes cost-prohibitive due to time constraints.

points.title: Attention intuition: query and key vectors
points.body_markdown:
- A **key vector** represents the type of information present at a step (keys come from saved states).
- A **query vector** represents what we are looking for at this step.

Intuition: a key might encode "the subject of the sentence," and a query might ask for "the subject of the sentence." In practice, what keys and queries mean and how they interact are learned; they do not need to be defined manually.

points.title: Scoring: comparing a query with every key
points.body_markdown: The query is compared with every key to get one score per position (e.g., over the words "Students", "open", "their", "books").

points.title: Attention is a weighted average
points.body_markdown:
The query at "books" reads three earlier states. Softmax turns the three scores into weights that add up to one, producing a context vector:

$$ \mathrm{c}=\alpha_{1}\mathrm{h}_{1}+\alpha_{2}\mathrm{h}_{2}+\alpha_{3}\mathrm{h}_{3} $$

where $h_{1}$, $h_{2}$, $h_{3}$ are the saved states for the three earlier words and $\alpha_i$ are the attention weights.

points.title: Dot-product attention walkthrough
points.body_markdown:
- **Scores:** one dot product per key.
- **Weights:** one softmax across all three scores.

points.title: Attention as a soft, weighted lookup table
points.body_markdown: In attention, the query softly matches each key, producing a weight between 0 and 1; the keys' values are multiplied by the weights and summed. In a lookup table, a table of keys maps to values, and the query matches one of the keys, returning its value.

points.title: Sequence-to-sequence with attention
points.body_markdown: The first decoder state queries the saved source states (encoder Chinese source, decoder English prefix). After "Anna left," the decoder reads the same source states again.

points.title: Do we still need recurrence?
points.body_markdown:
- **Reading a state:** the decoder can read any saved state.
- **Building a state:** the fourth update still needs the third.

Question raised: could each position build its own representation directly from the inputs?

points.title: Building context without recurrence
points.body_markdown: Once the inputs are available, both outputs can be computed together in a layer — layer outputs for the Chinese prefix input vectors can be computed in parallel, without recurrence.

points.title: What makes this self-attention
points.body_markdown: The query at 北京 reads keys and values from the same Chinese prefix — i.e., queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence.

points.title: Step 1: transform each input into query, key, and value vectors
points.body_markdown:
For each input $x_i$:

$$ \mathbf{q}_i = x_i \mathbf{W}^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_q}, \quad \mathbf{W}^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_q} $$

$$ \mathbf{k}_i = x_i \mathbf{W}^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}, \quad \mathbf{W}^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_k} $$

$$ \mathbf{v}_i = x_i \mathbf{W}^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\nu}, \quad \mathbf{W}^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_\nu} $$

Example with inputs "Thinking" ($x_1$) and "Machines" ($x_2$), producing queries $q_1, q_2$, keys $k_1, k_2$, values $v_1, v_2$.

points.title: Step 2: turn one query's scores into attention weights
points.body_markdown:
Use the query at "Thinking" to score both keys (both words are visible):

| | Thinking | Machines |
|---|---|---|
| Score | $q_1 \cdot k_1 = 112$ | $q_1 \cdot k_2 = 96$ |
| Divide by 8 ($\sqrt{d_k}$) | 14 | 12 |
| Softmax | 0.88 | 0.12 |

The keys have 64 features; dividing both scores by $\sqrt{64} = 8$ helps keep softmax from saturating. Result: `softmax([14, 12]) ≈ [0.88, 0.12]`.

points.title: Step 3: mix value vectors using the query's weights
points.body_markdown:
$$ \mathbf{o}_{\mathrm{Thinking}}\approx0.88\,v_{\mathrm{Thinking}}+0.12\,v_{\mathrm{Machines}} $$

Take 0.88 of the first value vector and 0.12 of the second, and add them coordinate by coordinate. "Machines" gets its own row of weights.

points.title: Matrix form of attention and causal masking
points.body_markdown:
$$ Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK^{T}/\sqrt{d_{k}}+M)V $$

- Each row compares one query with every key; apply softmax across that row.
- **Causal self-attention:** $M$ adds 0 to allowed scores and $-\infty$ to future scores before softmax.
- For "Thinking," masking "Machines" changes the weights from [0.88, 0.12] to [1, 0].
- Doubling the sequence length gives four times as many cells in the full score grid.

points.title: Multi-head attention
points.body_markdown:
$$ Head=Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V $$

$$ Multi-head Attention(Q,K,V)=concat(head_{1},head_{2},...,head_{h})W^{O} $$

Why it works:

- Different heads learn different attention patterns.
- Heads can capture multiple relations simultaneously, e.g., local context, long-range dependencies, and syntactic/semantic links.
- Concatenation aggregates diverse information into a richer token representation.

With $d = 512$ and $h = 8$ heads, each key has $d_{k} = 64$ features; scale each head's scores by dividing by $\sqrt{64} = 8$. Each head has its own Q, K and V projections.

points.title: Barriers and solutions for self-attention as a building block
points.body_markdown:
- **Masking:** give future positions zero attention weight so a prediction can use only its prefix.
- **Position information:** add position representations to the inputs so attention can use word order.
- **Feed-forward network:** transform each position's attention output with the same nonlinear feed-forward network.

points.title: Causal masking and parallel computation
points.body_markdown:
- Each position sees its prefix. During training, input tokens are already available; compute all positions within a layer, and the mask controls information access.
- The mask (added before softmax) is lower-triangular: allowed positions get 0, future positions get $-\infty$; masked positions receive zero weight.
- **Autoregressive generation:** select a token, append it, and repeat.

points.title: Self-attention needs position information
points.body_markdown:
The query at "bites" can see all three words, but the embeddings carry only word identity. Example weights: dog 0.50, bites 0.20, man 0.30. The weighted output at "bites" is:

$$ 0.50\,v_{dog}+0.20\,v_{bites}+0.30\,v_{man} $$

Each word keeps its key, value and weight, so both rows give the same sum — word order is not distinguished without position information.

points.title: Positional embeddings
points.body_markdown:
Sinusoidal positional representations concatenate sinusoidal functions with varying periods:

$$ \widetilde{x}_{i}=x_{i}+p_{i} $$

$$ \pmb{p}_{i}=\left(\begin{matrix}{\sin(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\{\cos(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\{\vdots}\\{\sin(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\{\cos(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\end{matrix}\right) $$

where $i$ is the index in the sequence.

points.title: Adding nonlinearities after self-attention
points.body_markdown:
- Self-attention has no elementwise nonlinear activation on its outputs; stacking attention layers keeps re-averaging value vectors.
- Add a feed-forward network after self-attention; its activation function, such as ReLU, introduces elementwise nonlinearity:

$$ m_{i}\;=\;W_{2}\operatorname{ReLU}(W_{1}\,o_{i}\;+\;b_{1})\;+\;b_{2} $$

where $o_i$ is the attention output at position $i$. Softmax sets attention weights; ReLU adds a nonlinear transformation of the output features. Each layer shares its FFN weights across token positions.

points.title: Residual connections and layer normalization
points.body_markdown:
- **Residual connection:** the sublayer learns an update, while the input retains a direct path (additive input path). Residuals give gradients a direct path.
- **Layer normalization:** operates on one token, across its features; it centers and rescales features, stabilizing each token's feature scale.

points.title: Transformer block equations: attention sublayer and MLP/FFN sublayer
points.body_markdown:
The Transformer block combines Multi-Head Attention and an MLP/FFN, each wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization.

**Attention sublayer:**
$$ \mathrm{Z}=LN(X+MHA(XW_{q},XW_{k},XW_{v})) $$

**MLP / FFN sublayer:**
$$ H=LN(Z+ReLU(ZW_{1})W_{2}) $$

- The attention sublayer computes queries, keys, and values by multiplying the input $X$ with $W_q$, $W_k$, $W_v$.
- The MLP uses a ReLU activation between two linear transformations ($W_1$, then $W_2$).
- Both sublayers use the pattern: residual add, then layer normalization ($LN$).

points.title: Transformer Decoder block composition
points.body_markdown:
The Transformer Decoder is a stack of Transformer Decoder Blocks. Each block consists of:

1. Self-attention
2. Add & Norm
3. Feed-Forward
4. Add & Norm

points.title: From decoder states to next-token probabilities
points.body_markdown:
The decoder produces contextual states $h_t$ with $d$ features. These are converted to a distribution over the vocabulary:

- **Vocabulary logits:** one score per vocabulary token, computed from $h_t$.
- **Output softmax:** converts logits into probabilities over the vocabulary.
- **Generation loop:** select a token, append it to the prefix, and repeat.

Illustrative example: prompt "The capital of France is" → contextual states from the decoder → vocabulary logits → softmax probabilities → vocabulary output.

points.title: Transformer Encoder: bidirectional (non-causal) attention
points.body_markdown:
The whole source sentence is available before translation begins, so the encoder uses no causal mask.

- Each query position can attend to **all** source positions (both left and right context).
- Example source "昨天安娜离开了北京": every query position (昨天, 安娜, 离开了, 北京) can read all four positions.
- Each query position produces a state for that position (e.g., state for 昨天, state for 安娜, ...).

points.title: Encoder-Decoder: masked self-attention and cross-attention
points.body_markdown:
For source "昨天安娜离开了北京":

- **Encoder inputs:** each position can use context on both sides.
- **Masked self-attention (decoder):** to predict "Beijing," the decoder can read the English prefix "Anna left." — i.e., only the target prefix is visible.
- **Cross-attention:** the decoder supplies the **query**; the encoder states for the Chinese input supply the **keys and values**.

points.title: Three Transformer model families
points.body_markdown:
| Architecture | Visible context | Typical output / use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Encoder-only | All supplied input tokens; bidirectional context | Contextual representations; understanding tasks | BERT |
| Decoder-only | Prefix tokens; causal self-attention | Next-token probabilities; autoregressive generation | GPT |
| Encoder-decoder | Encoder: full source; Decoder: target prefix + source cross-attention | Conditional output sequence; translation / summarization | T5 |

The lecture follows the decoder-only branch into the GPT family.

points.title: Scaling laws for next-token prediction loss
points.body_markdown:
Experiment varies three quantities across training runs:

- $N$ = non-embedding parameters (768 to 1.5B)
- $D$ = dataset size in tokens (22M to 23B)
- $C$ = total non-embedding training FLOPs

Prediction loss is evaluated on held-out text. In the dataset-size fit, **doubling the data cuts test loss by about 6%**.

points.title: Effect of context window length on reasoning
points.body_markdown:
- Each bar averages three models at that window size.
- A longer window keeps earlier reasoning steps available to later steps.
- In this experiment, long-context retrieval and math accuracy both **peaked at $16\times$**.

points.title: Scaling model size together with training data
points.body_markdown:
Models are getting larger and trained on more and more data ("the blessings of scale").

| Model parameters | Training tokens |
|---|---|
| 400 million | 8.0 billion |
| 1 billion | 20.2 billion |
| 10 billion | 205.1 billion |

Rule of thumb: **10× the parameters → about 10× the training tokens.**

points.title: GPT-1 (2018): decoder pretraining
points.body_markdown:
GPT (2018) was a major success in decoder pretraining.

- Transformer decoder with **12 layers, 117M parameters**.
- **768-dimensional** hidden states; **3072-dimensional** feed-forward hidden layers.
- Byte-pair encoding with **40,000 merges**.
- Trained on **BookCorpus**: over 7,000 unique books — containing long spans of contiguous text for learning long-distance dependencies.
- Finetuned Transformer LM results on natural language inference tasks (MNLI-m, MNLI-mm, SNLI, SciTail, QNLI, RTE), e.g., MNLI-m 82.1, SNLI 89.9, SciTail 88.3, QNLI 88.1, RTE 56.0.

points.title: GPT-2 (2019): unsupervised pretraining as text-to-text
points.body_markdown:
- Unsupervised pre-training for general NLP tasks.
- Frames tasks as **text-to-text prediction**.
- Larger training corpus: **8M webpages, around 40 GB of text**.
- Larger model: **1.5B parameters**.
- Demonstrated conditional text generation (e.g., continuing a human-written prompt about unicorns in the Andes).

points.title: GPT-3 (2020): in-context learning
points.body_markdown:
Very large language models seem to perform some kind of learning **without gradient steps**, simply from examples provided within their context windows.

- The in-context examples seem to specify the task to be performed.
- The conditional distribution mimics performing the task to a certain extent.
- Example: prefix "thanks → 谢谢, hello → 你好, cat → 猫, dog →" yields the conditional generation "狗".

points.title: GPT-4 (2023): multimodal image and text in, text out
points.body_markdown:
- GPT-4 accepts **image and text in, text out**.
- Example: asked "What makes this picture funny?", it explains that the oversized monitor plug hides a tiny phone connector — the joke depends on seeing both.

points.title: GPT-5 and GPT-6 Astra (2025–2026)
points.body_markdown:
- **GPT-5 · Reasoning on demand:** ChatGPT routes a request to a fast model or a deeper reasoning model.
- **GPT-6 Astra · Computer use:** Astra inspects the screen, takes an action, and uses the result to choose its next move (e.g., OpenAI's KiCad demo placing components and routing a circuit board).

points.title: Pre-training vs. post-training processes
points.body_markdown:
- **Pre-training process:** learn general knowledge.
- **Post-training process:** behavior alignment, reasoning, tool use — updated based on the reward model's response.

points.title: Scaling curse: training and serving costs
points.body_markdown:
**Hardware example:** Llama 3 405B is trained on up to 16K H100 GPUs, each at 700W TDP with 80GB HBM3, on Meta's Grand Teton AI server platform. Each server has eight GPUs and two CPUs; the eight GPUs within a server are connected via NVLink. Training jobs are scheduled using MAST, Meta's global-scale training scheduler.

**Training GPU costs:**
- Llama 3.1 405B: **30.84M GPU-hours**
- One GPU-hour = one GPU running for one hour
- At 700 W: 0.7 kW × 1 h = 0.7 kWh

**Serving is also expensive:**
- 128K-token prefill: 3.8s
- 1M-token prefill: 77s
- on up to 128 H100 GPUs

| Model | Training Time (GPU hours) | Training Power (W) | GHG Emissions (tons CO₂eq) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Llama 3.1 8B | 1.46M | 700 | 420 |
| Llama 3.1 70B | 7.0M | 700 | 2,040 |
| Llama 3.1 405B | 30.84M | 700 | 8,930 |
| Total | 39.3M | | 11,390 |

documents.markdown:
This lecture from Advanced AI Computing and Systems covers the fundamental principles of LLM training, including next-token prediction, cross-entropy loss, and optimization techniques such as gradient descent and Adam. It details distributed training strategies like data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism to address compute and memory constraints on modern GPUs. The document also explores LLM inference fundamentals, distinguishing between compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode stages using the roofline model. Finally, it examines serving systems, focusing on scheduling methods like continuous batching and memory management techniques such as PagedAttention for efficient KV cache utilization.

## Next-token prediction supplies the training target for every position

A training step uses a batch of text to update the model weights. The training text supplies the target for every prediction: given the input tokens, the model produces a vocabulary distribution, and the next token in the text is the target.

## The training objective maximizes the likelihood of the training corpus

A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of tokens. Training maximizes the likelihood of the training corpus over the model parameters:

$$\arg\max_{\theta}\prod_{x\in D_{train}}P_{\theta}(x)$$

## Cross-entropy loss is negative log-likelihood over next-token predictions

The likelihood objective is equivalent to minimizing the average negative log-likelihood:

$$\arg\max_{\theta}\prod_{x\in D_{train}}P_{\theta}(x)=\arg\min_{\theta}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in D_{train}}\sum_{i=1}^{t}-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i})$$

The cross-entropy loss for a single prediction is

$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i})$$

Lower is better. Example: for "The capital of France", a model giving "is" probability 0.9 has $L_{CE}\approx -\log(0.9)\approx 0.1$, while a model giving "is" probability 0.4 has $L_{CE}\approx -\log(0.4)\approx 0.9$.

## Population risk versus empirical risk

- **Population risk $R(\theta)$**: the expected loss per token on new text drawn from the target distribution — how much loss to expect when predicting the next token in new text.
- **Empirical risk**: an estimate of that loss using the text in the training corpus:

$$\hat{R}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{i}(\theta)$$

where $N$ counts the target tokens in the training corpus.

## Gradient descent updates parameters along the negative gradient

Calculate the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, $\frac{\partial L(\theta)}{\partial\theta}$, then take a small step along the negative gradient:

$$\theta^{new}\leftarrow\theta^{old}-\eta\frac{\partial L(\theta)}{\partial\theta}$$

$\eta$ is the learning rate.

## Why gradient descent works

- The gradient gives the local slope of a smooth loss surface.
- At a point with nonzero gradient, a sufficiently small step along the negative gradient lowers the loss.
- Near a stationary point, the gradient becomes small.

## The learning rate sets the size of each update

- A small learning rate can require many updates to reduce the loss.
- A large step can overshoot the low point and increase the loss.

## Batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent differ in how many examples they use

| Variant | Examples used | Properties |
|---|---|---|
| Batch gradient descent | all $N$ examples | stable but expensive |
| Stochastic gradient descent | one example | cheap but noisy |
| Mini-batch gradient descent | $B$ examples | more stable than SGD, much cheaper than GD |

$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{N}\sum\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) \quad\text{(batch)}$$
$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) \quad\text{(stochastic)}$$
$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{B}\sum\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) \quad\text{(mini-batch)}$$

## SGD with momentum adds part of the previous step to the current step

Plain SGD: $\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}-\eta g_{t}$

SGD + Momentum:
$$d_{t}=\rho d_{t-1}-\eta g_{t}$$
$$\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}+d_{t}$$

$g_{t}$ is the mini-batch gradient, $\eta$ is the learning rate, and $\rho$ is the fraction of the last step retained. Momentum carries part of the previous step into the current update.

## Adam uses first and second moment estimates to set direction and step scale

Each weight has a mini-batch gradient $g_{t}$.

First moment (the signed average sets the direction):
$$m_{t}=\beta_{1}m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1})g_{t}, \qquad \widehat{m}_{t}=m_{t}/(1-\beta_{1}^{t})$$

Second moment (the mean square sets the scale of the step):
$$v_{t}=\beta_{2}v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{2})g_{t}^{2}, \qquad \hat{v}_{t}=v_{t}/(1-\beta_{2}^{t})$$

Update each weight:
$$\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}-\eta\frac{\widehat{m}_{t}}{\sqrt{\widehat{v}_{t}}+\varepsilon}$$

The hats correct for the bias from starting both averages at zero; a small $\varepsilon$ keeps the denominator positive.

## Basic calculus rules for derivatives

The derivative measures how sensitive the output is to a small change in the input:

$$f^{\prime}(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$$

- Power rule: $f(x)=x^{r}\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)=rx^{r-1}$
- Exponential: $\frac{d}{dx}e^{x}=e^{x}$
- Sum rule: $(\alpha f+\beta g)^{\prime}=\alpha f^{\prime}+\beta g^{\prime}$ ($\alpha,\beta$ real constants)
- Product rule: $(fg)^{\prime}=f^{\prime}g+fg^{\prime}$
- Chain rule: $f(x)=h(g(x))\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)=h^{\prime}(g(x))\cdot g^{\prime}(x)$

## Gradients and Jacobians for multivariate functions

For a differentiable scalar-valued function $f:\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$, the gradient collects one partial derivative per input:

$$\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x})=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}(\boldsymbol{x})\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}(\boldsymbol{x})\end{bmatrix}$$

For a vector-valued function with $m$ outputs and $n$ inputs, the Jacobian has $m$ rows and $n$ columns:

$$\left(\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{f}}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}\right)_{ij}=\frac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}$$

Local Jacobians:
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b})=\boldsymbol{W}, \qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{b}}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b})=\boldsymbol{I}$$
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{u}}\left(\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{h}\right)=\boldsymbol{h}^{\mathrm{T}}$$

## The chain rule computes gradients of composite functions

Neural networks are compositions of functions.

- One-variable composition: multiply derivatives. For $z=3y$, $y=x^{2}$: $\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{dz}{dy}\frac{dy}{dx}=(3)(2x)=6x$. Each derivative measures how one step responds to its input.
- Multiple variables at once: multiply Jacobians. For $\boldsymbol{h}=f(\boldsymbol{z})$, $\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}$: $\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$. The outer function's Jacobian is the left factor in the product.

## Chain rule through a linear layer and element-wise activation

For $\boldsymbol{s}=\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{h}$, $\boldsymbol{h}=f(\boldsymbol{z})$, $\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $\boldsymbol{x}$ the input:

$$\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial s}{\partial h}\frac{\partial h}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=u^{T}\,\mathrm{diag}\left(f^{\prime}(z)\right)W$$

where $f$ is an element-wise activation.

## Backpropagation applies the chain rule in reverse order on a computational graph

For the graph $\boldsymbol{s}=\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{h}$, $\boldsymbol{h}=f(\boldsymbol{z})$, $\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}$, backpropagation applies the chain rule in reverse order; the gradient flow passes through the graph (e.g., $\partial s/\partial z$, $\partial s/\partial b$).

## Backpropagation through an activation function

Chain rule: downstream gradient = upstream gradient × local gradient.

## Linear layer gradients for weights and inputs

For a mini-batch, the linear layer computes $Y=XW$. The optimizer uses the weight gradient; the input gradient flows to the preceding layer.

- Weight gradient $(H_{1}\times H_{2})$: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^{T}\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}$
- Input gradient $(B\times H_{1})$: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}W^{T}$

## Automatic differentiation in PyTorch records the computation graph during the forward pass

Models are built as modules (building blocks), e.g. a `Net2(nn.Module)` with `MyLinear(4, 3)` and `MyLinear(3, 1)` layers and a ReLU in between; calling the model on a sample input produces an output tensor carrying `grad_fn`. Autograd records the computation graph during the forward pass, and `z.backward()` then computes gradients (e.g., `z.grad`, weight gradients, `x.grad`); `requires_grad` and `retain_grad()` control which tensors' gradients are tracked and kept.

## One PyTorch training step: forward pass, backward pass, optimizer step

- Forward pass → batch loss: `inputs, targets = ids[:, :-1], ids[:, 1:]`; `logits = model(inputs)`; `loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.transpose(1, 2), targets, ignore_index=pad_id)`
- Backward pass → weight gradients: `loss.backward()`
- Optimizer step → updated weights: `optimizer.step()`, then `optimizer.zero_grad()`

Training loss guides the update; validation loss is evaluated on held-out text with fixed weights.

## Dense-model training FLOP estimate: \(C \approx 6ND\)

For a dense model with \(N\) parameters and \(D\) training tokens, the total training compute is estimated as:

\[
C \approx 6ND
\]

This comes from one forward and two backward products per linear layer.

Worked example from the slides: a 7B model trained on 140B tokens:

\[
6 \times (7 \times 10^9) \times (140 \times 10^9) = 5.88 \times 10^{21}\ \text{FLOPs}
\]

### Related estimates in the slides

- Achieved compute on an H100: \(0.40 \times 989.5 = 395.8\ \text{TFLOP/s}\), i.e. 40% MFU of the H100 SXM dense BF16 peak.
- Estimated training time: \(t \approx \frac{5.88 \times 10^{21}}{395.8 \times 10^{12}}\ \text{s} \approx 172\ \text{days}\).
- Scaling table (assuming 20 training tokens per parameter and enough GPU memory for one training step):

| Parameters | Training tokens (\(D = 20N\)) | Time on one H100 at 40% MFU |
|---|---|---|
| 70B | 1.4T | ≈ 47 years |
| 1T | 20T | ≈ 9,600 years |

## Training memory: model states dominate on one H100

With FP32 weights, gradients, and Adam moments, model states take **16 bytes per parameter**.

- The 7B model needs **112 GB for model states alone**.
- One H100 has only **80 GB**.
- The estimate assumes one sequence per batch for both models.

## Why distribute training: memory and time

Two motivations appear in the slides:

- **Memory:** the 7B model states need 112 GB, but one H100 has 80 GB — the training step does not fit on a single GPU.
- **Time:** even if the 7B training step fit on one H100, 140B tokens would take ~172 days at 40% MFU.

The slides illustrate two splitting strategies:

- **Split the weight matrix by column** (each GPU holds part of \(W\)).
- **Split the batch by sequence** (each GPU computes gradients on its own data; gradients are combined before updating \(W\)).

In the column-split illustration, both GPUs receive the same input \(X\) and each computes its own columns of \(Y\).

## Data parallelism: definition and cost

- Each replica trains on a different part of the same mini-batch.
- Each GPU needs to store a **copy of the entire model**.

## Computation and communication in data parallelism

- The global batch costs \(C\) FLOPs and is split evenly: **≈ \(C/K\) FLOPs per GPU** across \(K\) replicas.
- Each GPU produces **local gradients of \(N\) elements**.
- An **AllReduce** (sum) combines the local gradients into the global mean gradient.

The global mean gradient uses an **equal-token mean**, weighting each GPU's contribution by its valid-token count:

\[
\overline{g}_t = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i_1=1}^{B_1}\nabla f(w_t;\xi_{i_1}) + \cdots + \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i_K=1}^{B_K}\nabla f(w_t;\xi_{i_K})
\]

where \(B_k\) is the valid-token count on GPU \(k\) and \(B\) is the total.

## Column-parallel linear layer

- The weight matrix \(A\) is split by column into \(A_1, A_2, A_3\) on different GPUs.
- The **input is replicated** on every GPU.
- Each GPU computes its own output shard: \(Y_1 = X A_1\), \(Y_2 = X A_2\), \(Y_3 = X A_3\).
- Result: **replicated input, separate output features**.

## Row-parallel linear layer

- The weight matrix \(B\) is split by row into \(B_1, B_2, B_3\).
- The **input is split** into local shards (\(Y_1, Y_2, Y_3\)).
- Each GPU computes a **partial sum**: \(Z_1 = Y_1 B_1\), \(Z_2 = Y_2 B_2\), \(Z_3 = Y_3 B_3\).
- An **AllReduce** combines the partial sums: \(Z = Z_1 + Z_2 + Z_3\).
- Result: **local input shards, partial sums of one output**.

## Tensor parallelism in MLP and attention

- **MLP:** keep intermediate features partitioned — a 4D-wide intermediate gives 2D features per GPU.
- **Multi-head attention:** each GPU computes a group of heads — e.g. 16 heads ÷ 2 tensor-parallel GPUs = 8 heads per GPU.

## Communication cost of tensor parallelism

Classic tensor parallelism uses **four AllReduce operations per transformer block per training step**:

- 2 AllReduce in forward + backward for one sub-layer,
- 2 AllReduce in forward + backward for the other sub-layer.

## Pipeline parallelism: stages and boundaries

- Each pipeline stage owns a **consecutive group of layers**.
- At the boundary, the two GPUs exchange **activations and their gradients** using **point-to-point sends**.

## Naïve pipeline implementation

A single batch moves through the stages **one at a time**, so only one stage is active at any moment (the rest idle).

## GPipe: micro-batches and idle fraction

- GPipe splits a batch into **micro-batches** that flow through the pipeline, overlapping forward and backward work across stages.
- For balanced stages, the **idle fraction** is:

\[
\frac{p-1}{p+m-1}
\]

where \(p\) is the number of stages and \(m\) the number of micro-batches.

- Example: four stages and four micro-batches → \(\frac{3}{7}\) of stage time is idle.
- With **uneven stage times, the slowest stage sets the pace**.

## GPipe throughput results

GPipe throughput on TPUs at a fixed number of partitions (normalized):

| TPU | AmoebaNet \(K=2\) | AmoebaNet \(K=4\) | AmoebaNet \(K=8\) | Transformer \(K=2\) | Transformer \(K=4\) | Transformer \(K=8\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(M=1\) | 1 | 1.13 | 1.38 | 1 | 1.07 | 1.3 |
| \(M=4\) | 1.07 | 1.26 | 1.72 | 1.7 | 3.2 | 4.8 |
| \(M=32\) | 1.21 | 1.84 | 3.48 | 1.8 | 3.4 | 6.3 |

For the Transformer with \(K=8\) partitions, normalized throughput goes **1.3 → 4.8 → 6.3** as \(M\) increases.

## 3D parallelism layout: a 16-GPU case study

- DP = 2, TP = 2, PP = 4 use **16 GPUs** in the layout.
- Example communication partners for GPU 0: **GPU 1 for TP, GPU 4 for PP, GPU 2 for DP**.
- Each cube represents a GPU; each color represents the node it belongs to.

## Decoder-only next-token prediction

- The **final prompt position** supplies a distribution over the next token:

\[
p(\text{next token} \mid \text{prefix}) = \text{softmax}(h_{\text{last}} W_{\text{out}})
\]

- The next token is **selected from the vocabulary distribution**.
- Example: "The capital of" → "France".

## Autoregressive inference loop

- Each output token becomes the input to the next step.
- The process runs as **Prefill** followed by **Decode** steps:
  - Prefill: "The capital of" → selects "France".
  - Decode 1: "The capital of France" → selects "is".
  - Decode 2: "The capital of France is" → selects "Paris".
- Generation stops at an **end-of-sequence token or the output limit**.

## Prefill processes all prompt positions together

- Prefill processes **all prompt positions together within each layer**.
- The three prompt positions advance together; the state at "of" supplies the first prediction.

## KV cache: keys and values saved per position

- Each KV head stores a **key and a value for every processed position**.
- Keys and values computed during prefill are **saved** and reused in later decode steps.
- Example: "of" sees positions 1–3 in both calls; its stored key and value stay valid in every block.
- The table shows, per block, \(V_1\)–\(V_3\) saved during prefill and \(V_4\) added at the first decode step, with corresponding \(K\) vectors (key coordinates illustrative; each \(V\) denotes a full value vector).

## Decode: attending to the cached prefix and itself

- Every new token attends to the **cached prefix and to itself**.
- Each decode step **adds one new K/V pair** (the outlined position) and reads the existing ones:
  - Step 1: \(Q_4\) ("France") — add 1, read 4.
  - Step 2: \(Q_5\) ("is") — add 1, read 5.
- Illustrative keys at "is": Block 1 \(K_5 = [-0.6, 0.0, 0.9]\); Block N \(K_5 = [0.1, -2.1, 0.5]\).

## Model weights vs. per-request KV cache

- **Model weights are shared across requests** — all requests use the same parameters.
- **KV cache is private per request** and grows as more positions are processed.
- Example memory breakdown for a 13B LLM on A100-40GB: parameters 26GB (65%), KV cache 13GB (33%), plus others.

## Estimating KV cache memory

Model configuration used: \(L = 80\) layers, \(H_{KV} = 8\) KV heads, \(d_h = 128\), \(b = 2\) bytes/element.

KV cache per token:

\[
2 L H_{KV} d_h b = 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2\text{B} = 327{,}680\text{B} = 320\ \text{KiB}
\]

Scaling:

- One request at 8,192 tokens: \(8{,}192 \times 320\ \text{KiB} = 2.5\ \text{GiB}\).
- 32 concurrent requests: \(32 \times 2.5\ \text{GiB} = 80\ \text{GiB}\).
- Model weights and temporary buffers need **additional** memory.

## KV memory grows with sequence length and batch size

KV memory grows with **both** sequence length and batch size (shown as two separate plots: (a) sequence length, (b) batch size).

## Time to first token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL)

- **TTFT:** arrival to the first token delivered, **including queueing**.
- **ITL:** elapsed time between two consecutive outputs from the same request.
- Illustration: top row first token at tick 6, next at tick 8; bottom row has one gap lasting 4 ticks.

## Roofline model: compute and memory bounds

Compute and memory bandwidth each set a limit on performance:

\[
t_{\text{compute}} \geq \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak compute rate (FLOP/s)}}
\]

\[
t_{\text{memory}} \geq \frac{\text{Bytes transferred}}{\text{Peak bandwidth (bytes/s)}}
\]

At the **bend** of the roofline, the compute and memory time bounds are equal.

## Prefill is compute-bound

- Prefill computes attention for **all prompt positions together**.
- It is **compute-bound** (axes: sequence length, model dimension).
- Once throughput levels off, **batching more prompt tokens brings little further gain**.

## Decode is memory-bound

- The decode stage is **memory-bound**.
- Each step **reads cached K and V from GPU HBM** (memory hierarchy with bandwidth and memory size).

## Request lifecycle and the scheduler queue

An arriving request waits for a scheduler before it can use the GPU. The queue separates arrival from execution, and each engine step determines which requests make progress.

## Static batching keeps slots until all requests finish

A static batch keeps its slots until every request finishes. After a request ends (emits END), its slot stays empty while the remaining requests keep generating — the unused slot is not reused.

## Continuous batching lets waiting requests take finished slots

A waiting request can take the place of a finished one. One row = one batch slot; a new S label marks the start of another request. In the example, after END, S5 takes S3's slot, S6 takes S1's, and S7 takes S4's.

## Continuous batching step-by-step: prefill and decode interleaving

New requests can join while earlier requests are still active. With room for four active requests, iteration 1 prefills S1–S4, and later iterations alternate decode and prefill steps:

- Iteration 2 (Decode): S1, S2, S4 decode; S3 emits END.
- Iteration 3 (Prefill): S5 prefills into S3's slot; S1, S2, S4 wait.
- Iteration 4 (Decode): S1, S2, S5 decode; S4 emits END.
- Iteration 5 (Prefill): S6 prefills into S1's slot, S7 into S4's slot; S2, S5 wait.

Active requests keep their KV while waiting to decode. S5 processes "Birds can" in iteration 3 and uses its first output, "fly," as input in iteration 4.

## Chunked prefill and scheduling policies

Chunked prefill runs part of a long prompt alongside ongoing decode. The timeline compares four schedulers:

| Scheduler | Behavior shown |
|---|---|
| vLLM (Prefill Prioritized) | Decodes for A, B stalled while C, D prefill |
| Orca (Decode Prioritized) | Prefills for C, D stalled while A, B decode |
| FasterTransformer | Prefills for C, D stalled until A and B exit |
| Sarathi-Serve (Stall-free) | No stalls; prefill split into chunks (C_p1, C_p2, D_p1, D_p2) interleaved with decodes |

The timeline also contrasts TBT (time between tokens) without prefill interference versus TBT with prefill interference.

## Prefill can slow down decodes in the same batch

One prefill can slow down the decodes in the same batch. The slide illustrates this with input length 128 versus input length 1024.

## Fixed max sequence length allocation wastes memory

The prompt size is known at admission, but the final response length is uncertain. Reserving the maximum length occupies space even before the tokens exist, causing low utilization due to internal fragmentation (wasted space within each request's reservation).

## Sources of reduced usable KV capacity

Unused reservations and scattered gaps reduce usable KV capacity. Three sources are identified:

- Future reservation
- Unused space inside an allocation
- Free gaps between allocations

## Token blocks: logical vs. physical blocks

A token block is a fixed-size contiguous chunk of memory that can store token states from left to right. A logical block is a fixed number of consecutive token positions in a sequence. A physical block is a contiguous GPU allocation; the next block can be elsewhere. Example: with block size = 4, block 4 holds "Artificial Intelligence is the".

## PagedAttention memory management with block tables

PagedAttention manages KV memory via a block table mapping logical KV blocks to physical KV blocks, allocated on demand. For request A (prompt "Alan Turing is a computer scientist", completion "and mathematician renowned"):

| Logical block | Physical block number | # filled |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 7 | 4 |
| 1 | 1 | 4 |
| 2 | 5 | 1 |
| 3 | – | – |

Physical block 7 holds "Alan Turing is a"; block 1 holds "computer scientist and mathematician"; block 5 holds "renowned".

## Prefix sharing across requests

Both block tables can point to the same physical prefix block. Requests A and B share the prompt prefix "Alan Turing is a":

| Logical block | Request A | Request B |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 7 | 7 |
| 1 | 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 5 | – |

Physical block 6 holds B's continuation "pioneer of computer science". Sharing saves KV memory and avoids repeated prefill.

## Finding and reusing a cached prefix

For a new prompt (e.g., "Alan Turing is a pioneer of computer science whose work"), the system reuses the longest cached prefix and prefills only the rest.

## Throughput under greedy decoding

Throughput is related to the average number of batched requests, measured with OPT-13B on 1×A100 40G using a ShareGPT trace.
documents.intro_markdown: This lecture from Advanced AI Computing and Systems covers the fundamental principles of LLM training, including next-token prediction, cross-entropy loss, and optimization techniques such as gradient descent and Adam. It details distributed training strategies like data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism to address compute and memory constraints on modern GPUs. The document also explores LLM inference fundamentals, distinguishing between compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode stages using the roofline model. Finally, it examines serving systems, focusing on scheduling methods like continuous batching and memory management techniques such as PagedAttention for efficient KV cache utilization.

points.title: Next-token prediction supplies the training target for every position
points.body_markdown: A training step uses a batch of text to update the model weights. The training text supplies the target for every prediction: given the input tokens, the model produces a vocabulary distribution, and the next token in the text is the target.

points.title: The training objective maximizes the likelihood of the training corpus
points.body_markdown:
A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of tokens. Training maximizes the likelihood of the training corpus over the model parameters:

$$\arg\max_{\theta}\prod_{x\in D_{train}}P_{\theta}(x)$$

points.title: Cross-entropy loss is negative log-likelihood over next-token predictions
points.body_markdown:
The likelihood objective is equivalent to minimizing the average negative log-likelihood:

$$\arg\max_{\theta}\prod_{x\in D_{train}}P_{\theta}(x)=\arg\min_{\theta}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in D_{train}}\sum_{i=1}^{t}-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i})$$

The cross-entropy loss for a single prediction is

$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i})$$

Lower is better. Example: for "The capital of France", a model giving "is" probability 0.9 has $L_{CE}\approx -\log(0.9)\approx 0.1$, while a model giving "is" probability 0.4 has $L_{CE}\approx -\log(0.4)\approx 0.9$.

points.title: Population risk versus empirical risk
points.body_markdown:
- **Population risk $R(\theta)$**: the expected loss per token on new text drawn from the target distribution — how much loss to expect when predicting the next token in new text.
- **Empirical risk**: an estimate of that loss using the text in the training corpus:

$$\hat{R}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{i}(\theta)$$

where $N$ counts the target tokens in the training corpus.

points.title: Gradient descent updates parameters along the negative gradient
points.body_markdown:
Calculate the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, $\frac{\partial L(\theta)}{\partial\theta}$, then take a small step along the negative gradient:

$$\theta^{new}\leftarrow\theta^{old}-\eta\frac{\partial L(\theta)}{\partial\theta}$$

$\eta$ is the learning rate.

points.title: Why gradient descent works
points.body_markdown:
- The gradient gives the local slope of a smooth loss surface.
- At a point with nonzero gradient, a sufficiently small step along the negative gradient lowers the loss.
- Near a stationary point, the gradient becomes small.

points.title: The learning rate sets the size of each update
points.body_markdown:
- A small learning rate can require many updates to reduce the loss.
- A large step can overshoot the low point and increase the loss.

points.title: Batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent differ in how many examples they use
points.body_markdown:
| Variant | Examples used | Properties |
|---|---|---|
| Batch gradient descent | all $N$ examples | stable but expensive |
| Stochastic gradient descent | one example | cheap but noisy |
| Mini-batch gradient descent | $B$ examples | more stable than SGD, much cheaper than GD |

$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{N}\sum\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) \quad\text{(batch)}$$
$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) \quad\text{(stochastic)}$$
$$L_{CE}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{B}\sum\log p_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{<i}) \quad\text{(mini-batch)}$$

points.title: SGD with momentum adds part of the previous step to the current step
points.body_markdown:
Plain SGD: $\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}-\eta g_{t}$

SGD + Momentum:
$$d_{t}=\rho d_{t-1}-\eta g_{t}$$
$$\theta_{t}=\theta_{t-1}+d_{t}$$

$g_{t}$ is the mini-batch gradient, $\eta$ is the learning rate, and $\rho$ is the fraction of the last step retained. Momentum carries part of the previous step into the current update.
