where $f$ is an element-wise activation.

points.title: Backpropagation applies the chain rule in reverse order on a computational graph
points.body_markdown: For the graph $\boldsymbol{s}=\boldsymbol{u}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{h}$, $\boldsymbol{h}=f(\boldsymbol{z})$, $\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}$, backpropagation applies the chain rule in reverse order; the gradient flow passes through the graph (e.g., $\partial s/\partial z$, $\partial s/\partial b$).

points.title: Backpropagation through an activation function
points.body_markdown: Chain rule: downstream gradient = upstream gradient × local gradient.

points.title: Linear layer gradients for weights and inputs
points.body_markdown:
For a mini-batch, the linear layer computes $Y=XW$. The optimizer uses the weight gradient; the input gradient flows to the preceding layer.

- Weight gradient $(H_{1}\times H_{2})$: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=X^{T}\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}$
- Input gradient $(B\times H_{1})$: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial X}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}W^{T}$

points.title: Automatic differentiation in PyTorch records the computation graph during the forward pass
points.body_markdown: Models are built as modules (building blocks), e.g. a `Net2(nn.Module)` with `MyLinear(4, 3)` and `MyLinear(3, 1)` layers and a ReLU in between; calling the model on a sample input produces an output tensor carrying `grad_fn`. Autograd records the computation graph during the forward pass, and `z.backward()` then computes gradients (e.g., `z.grad`, weight gradients, `x.grad`); `requires_grad` and `retain_grad()` control which tensors' gradients are tracked and kept.

points.title: One PyTorch training step: forward pass, backward pass, optimizer step
points.body_markdown:
- Forward pass → batch loss: `inputs, targets = ids[:, :-1], ids[:, 1:]`; `logits = model(inputs)`; `loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.transpose(1, 2), targets, ignore_index=pad_id)`
- Backward pass → weight gradients: `loss.backward()`
- Optimizer step → updated weights: `optimizer.step()`, then `optimizer.zero_grad()`

Training loss guides the update; validation loss is evaluated on held-out text with fixed weights.

points.title: Dense-model training FLOP estimate: \(C \approx 6ND\)
points.body_markdown:
For a dense model with \(N\) parameters and \(D\) training tokens, the total training compute is estimated as:

\[
C \approx 6ND
\]

This comes from one forward and two backward products per linear layer.

Worked example from the slides: a 7B model trained on 140B tokens:

\[
6 \times (7 \times 10^9) \times (140 \times 10^9) = 5.88 \times 10^{21}\ \text{FLOPs}
\]

### Related estimates in the slides

- Achieved compute on an H100: \(0.40 \times 989.5 = 395.8\ \text{TFLOP/s}\), i.e. 40% MFU of the H100 SXM dense BF16 peak.
- Estimated training time: \(t \approx \frac{5.88 \times 10^{21}}{395.8 \times 10^{12}}\ \text{s} \approx 172\ \text{days}\).
- Scaling table (assuming 20 training tokens per parameter and enough GPU memory for one training step):

| Parameters | Training tokens (\(D = 20N\)) | Time on one H100 at 40% MFU |
|---|---|---|
| 70B | 1.4T | ≈ 47 years |
| 1T | 20T | ≈ 9,600 years |

points.title: Training memory: model states dominate on one H100
points.body_markdown:
With FP32 weights, gradients, and Adam moments, model states take **16 bytes per parameter**.

- The 7B model needs **112 GB for model states alone**.
- One H100 has only **80 GB**.
- The estimate assumes one sequence per batch for both models.

points.title: Why distribute training: memory and time
points.body_markdown:
Two motivations appear in the slides:

- **Memory:** the 7B model states need 112 GB, but one H100 has 80 GB — the training step does not fit on a single GPU.
- **Time:** even if the 7B training step fit on one H100, 140B tokens would take ~172 days at 40% MFU.

The slides illustrate two splitting strategies:

- **Split the weight matrix by column** (each GPU holds part of \(W\)).
- **Split the batch by sequence** (each GPU computes gradients on its own data; gradients are combined before updating \(W\)).

In the column-split illustration, both GPUs receive the same input \(X\) and each computes its own columns of \(Y\).

points.title: Data parallelism: definition and cost
points.body_markdown:
- Each replica trains on a different part of the same mini-batch.
- Each GPU needs to store a **copy of the entire model**.

points.title: Computation and communication in data parallelism
points.body_markdown:
- The global batch costs \(C\) FLOPs and is split evenly: **≈ \(C/K\) FLOPs per GPU** across \(K\) replicas.
- Each GPU produces **local gradients of \(N\) elements**.
- An **AllReduce** (sum) combines the local gradients into the global mean gradient.

The global mean gradient uses an **equal-token mean**, weighting each GPU's contribution by its valid-token count:

\[
\overline{g}_t = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i_1=1}^{B_1}\nabla f(w_t;\xi_{i_1}) + \cdots + \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i_K=1}^{B_K}\nabla f(w_t;\xi_{i_K})
\]

where \(B_k\) is the valid-token count on GPU \(k\) and \(B\) is the total.

points.title: Column-parallel linear layer
points.body_markdown:
- The weight matrix \(A\) is split by column into \(A_1, A_2, A_3\) on different GPUs.
- The **input is replicated** on every GPU.
- Each GPU computes its own output shard: \(Y_1 = X A_1\), \(Y_2 = X A_2\), \(Y_3 = X A_3\).
- Result: **replicated input, separate output features**.

points.title: Row-parallel linear layer
points.body_markdown:
- The weight matrix \(B\) is split by row into \(B_1, B_2, B_3\).
- The **input is split** into local shards (\(Y_1, Y_2, Y_3\)).
- Each GPU computes a **partial sum**: \(Z_1 = Y_1 B_1\), \(Z_2 = Y_2 B_2\), \(Z_3 = Y_3 B_3\).
- An **AllReduce** combines the partial sums: \(Z = Z_1 + Z_2 + Z_3\).
- Result: **local input shards, partial sums of one output**.

points.title: Tensor parallelism in MLP and attention
points.body_markdown:
- **MLP:** keep intermediate features partitioned — a 4D-wide intermediate gives 2D features per GPU.
- **Multi-head attention:** each GPU computes a group of heads — e.g. 16 heads ÷ 2 tensor-parallel GPUs = 8 heads per GPU.

points.title: Communication cost of tensor parallelism
points.body_markdown:
Classic tensor parallelism uses **four AllReduce operations per transformer block per training step**:

- 2 AllReduce in forward + backward for one sub-layer,
- 2 AllReduce in forward + backward for the other sub-layer.

points.title: Pipeline parallelism: stages and boundaries
points.body_markdown:
- Each pipeline stage owns a **consecutive group of layers**.
- At the boundary, the two GPUs exchange **activations and their gradients** using **point-to-point sends**.

points.title: Naïve pipeline implementation
points.body_markdown: A single batch moves through the stages **one at a time**, so only one stage is active at any moment (the rest idle).

points.title: GPipe: micro-batches and idle fraction
points.body_markdown:
- GPipe splits a batch into **micro-batches** that flow through the pipeline, overlapping forward and backward work across stages.
- For balanced stages, the **idle fraction** is:

\[
\frac{p-1}{p+m-1}
\]

where \(p\) is the number of stages and \(m\) the number of micro-batches.

- Example: four stages and four micro-batches → \(\frac{3}{7}\) of stage time is idle.
- With **uneven stage times, the slowest stage sets the pace**.

points.title: GPipe throughput results
points.body_markdown:
GPipe throughput on TPUs at a fixed number of partitions (normalized):

| TPU | AmoebaNet \(K=2\) | AmoebaNet \(K=4\) | AmoebaNet \(K=8\) | Transformer \(K=2\) | Transformer \(K=4\) | Transformer \(K=8\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(M=1\) | 1 | 1.13 | 1.38 | 1 | 1.07 | 1.3 |
| \(M=4\) | 1.07 | 1.26 | 1.72 | 1.7 | 3.2 | 4.8 |
| \(M=32\) | 1.21 | 1.84 | 3.48 | 1.8 | 3.4 | 6.3 |

For the Transformer with \(K=8\) partitions, normalized throughput goes **1.3 → 4.8 → 6.3** as \(M\) increases.

points.title: 3D parallelism layout: a 16-GPU case study
points.body_markdown:
- DP = 2, TP = 2, PP = 4 use **16 GPUs** in the layout.
- Example communication partners for GPU 0: **GPU 1 for TP, GPU 4 for PP, GPU 2 for DP**.
- Each cube represents a GPU; each color represents the node it belongs to.

points.title: Decoder-only next-token prediction
points.body_markdown:
- The **final prompt position** supplies a distribution over the next token:

\[
p(\text{next token} \mid \text{prefix}) = \text{softmax}(h_{\text{last}} W_{\text{out}})
\]

- The next token is **selected from the vocabulary distribution**.
- Example: "The capital of" → "France".

points.title: Autoregressive inference loop
points.body_markdown:
- Each output token becomes the input to the next step.
- The process runs as **Prefill** followed by **Decode** steps:
  - Prefill: "The capital of" → selects "France".
  - Decode 1: "The capital of France" → selects "is".
  - Decode 2: "The capital of France is" → selects "Paris".
- Generation stops at an **end-of-sequence token or the output limit**.

points.title: Prefill processes all prompt positions together
points.body_markdown:
- Prefill processes **all prompt positions together within each layer**.
- The three prompt positions advance together; the state at "of" supplies the first prediction.

points.title: KV cache: keys and values saved per position
points.body_markdown:
- Each KV head stores a **key and a value for every processed position**.
- Keys and values computed during prefill are **saved** and reused in later decode steps.
- Example: "of" sees positions 1–3 in both calls; its stored key and value stay valid in every block.
- The table shows, per block, \(V_1\)–\(V_3\) saved during prefill and \(V_4\) added at the first decode step, with corresponding \(K\) vectors (key coordinates illustrative; each \(V\) denotes a full value vector).

points.title: Decode: attending to the cached prefix and itself
points.body_markdown:
- Every new token attends to the **cached prefix and to itself**.
- Each decode step **adds one new K/V pair** (the outlined position) and reads the existing ones:
  - Step 1: \(Q_4\) ("France") — add 1, read 4.
  - Step 2: \(Q_5\) ("is") — add 1, read 5.
- Illustrative keys at "is": Block 1 \(K_5 = [-0.6, 0.0, 0.9]\); Block N \(K_5 = [0.1, -2.1, 0.5]\).

points.title: Model weights vs. per-request KV cache
points.body_markdown:
- **Model weights are shared across requests** — all requests use the same parameters.
- **KV cache is private per request** and grows as more positions are processed.
- Example memory breakdown for a 13B LLM on A100-40GB: parameters 26GB (65%), KV cache 13GB (33%), plus others.

points.title: Estimating KV cache memory
points.body_markdown:
Model configuration used: \(L = 80\) layers, \(H_{KV} = 8\) KV heads, \(d_h = 128\), \(b = 2\) bytes/element.

KV cache per token:

\[
2 L H_{KV} d_h b = 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2\text{B} = 327{,}680\text{B} = 320\ \text{KiB}
\]

Scaling:

- One request at 8,192 tokens: \(8{,}192 \times 320\ \text{KiB} = 2.5\ \text{GiB}\).
- 32 concurrent requests: \(32 \times 2.5\ \text{GiB} = 80\ \text{GiB}\).
- Model weights and temporary buffers need **additional** memory.

points.title: KV memory grows with sequence length and batch size
points.body_markdown: KV memory grows with **both** sequence length and batch size (shown as two separate plots: (a) sequence length, (b) batch size).

points.title: Time to first token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL)
points.body_markdown:
- **TTFT:** arrival to the first token delivered, **including queueing**.
- **ITL:** elapsed time between two consecutive outputs from the same request.
- Illustration: top row first token at tick 6, next at tick 8; bottom row has one gap lasting 4 ticks.

points.title: Roofline model: compute and memory bounds
points.body_markdown:
Compute and memory bandwidth each set a limit on performance:

\[
t_{\text{compute}} \geq \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak compute rate (FLOP/s)}}
\]

\[
t_{\text{memory}} \geq \frac{\text{Bytes transferred}}{\text{Peak bandwidth (bytes/s)}}
\]

At the **bend** of the roofline, the compute and memory time bounds are equal.

points.title: Prefill is compute-bound
points.body_markdown:
- Prefill computes attention for **all prompt positions together**.
- It is **compute-bound** (axes: sequence length, model dimension).
- Once throughput levels off, **batching more prompt tokens brings little further gain**.

points.title: Decode is memory-bound
points.body_markdown:
- The decode stage is **memory-bound**.
- Each step **reads cached K and V from GPU HBM** (memory hierarchy with bandwidth and memory size).

points.title: Request lifecycle and the scheduler queue
points.body_markdown: An arriving request waits for a scheduler before it can use the GPU. The queue separates arrival from execution, and each engine step determines which requests make progress.

points.title: Static batching keeps slots until all requests finish
points.body_markdown: A static batch keeps its slots until every request finishes. After a request ends (emits END), its slot stays empty while the remaining requests keep generating — the unused slot is not reused.

points.title: Continuous batching lets waiting requests take finished slots
points.body_markdown: A waiting request can take the place of a finished one. One row = one batch slot; a new S label marks the start of another request. In the example, after END, S5 takes S3's slot, S6 takes S1's, and S7 takes S4's.

points.title: Continuous batching step-by-step: prefill and decode interleaving
points.body_markdown:
New requests can join while earlier requests are still active. With room for four active requests, iteration 1 prefills S1–S4, and later iterations alternate decode and prefill steps:

- Iteration 2 (Decode): S1, S2, S4 decode; S3 emits END.
- Iteration 3 (Prefill): S5 prefills into S3's slot; S1, S2, S4 wait.
- Iteration 4 (Decode): S1, S2, S5 decode; S4 emits END.
- Iteration 5 (Prefill): S6 prefills into S1's slot, S7 into S4's slot; S2, S5 wait.

Active requests keep their KV while waiting to decode. S5 processes "Birds can" in iteration 3 and uses its first output, "fly," as input in iteration 4.

points.title: Chunked prefill and scheduling policies
points.body_markdown:
Chunked prefill runs part of a long prompt alongside ongoing decode. The timeline compares four schedulers:

| Scheduler | Behavior shown |
|---|---|
| vLLM (Prefill Prioritized) | Decodes for A, B stalled while C, D prefill |
| Orca (Decode Prioritized) | Prefills for C, D stalled while A, B decode |
| FasterTransformer | Prefills for C, D stalled until A and B exit |
| Sarathi-Serve (Stall-free) | No stalls; prefill split into chunks (C_p1, C_p2, D_p1, D_p2) interleaved with decodes |

The timeline also contrasts TBT (time between tokens) without prefill interference versus TBT with prefill interference.

points.title: Prefill can slow down decodes in the same batch
points.body_markdown: One prefill can slow down the decodes in the same batch. The slide illustrates this with input length 128 versus input length 1024.

points.title: Fixed max sequence length allocation wastes memory
points.body_markdown: The prompt size is known at admission, but the final response length is uncertain. Reserving the maximum length occupies space even before the tokens exist, causing low utilization due to internal fragmentation (wasted space within each request's reservation).

points.title: Sources of reduced usable KV capacity
points.body_markdown:
Unused reservations and scattered gaps reduce usable KV capacity. Three sources are identified:

- Future reservation
- Unused space inside an allocation
- Free gaps between allocations

points.title: Token blocks: logical vs. physical blocks
points.body_markdown: A token block is a fixed-size contiguous chunk of memory that can store token states from left to right. A logical block is a fixed number of consecutive token positions in a sequence. A physical block is a contiguous GPU allocation; the next block can be elsewhere. Example: with block size = 4, block 4 holds "Artificial Intelligence is the".

points.title: PagedAttention memory management with block tables
points.body_markdown:
PagedAttention manages KV memory via a block table mapping logical KV blocks to physical KV blocks, allocated on demand. For request A (prompt "Alan Turing is a computer scientist", completion "and mathematician renowned"):

| Logical block | Physical block number | # filled |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 7 | 4 |
| 1 | 1 | 4 |
| 2 | 5 | 1 |
| 3 | – | – |

Physical block 7 holds "Alan Turing is a"; block 1 holds "computer scientist and mathematician"; block 5 holds "renowned".

points.title: Prefix sharing across requests
points.body_markdown:
Both block tables can point to the same physical prefix block. Requests A and B share the prompt prefix "Alan Turing is a":

| Logical block | Request A | Request B |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 7 | 7 |
| 1 | 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 5 | – |

Physical block 6 holds B's continuation "pioneer of computer science". Sharing saves KV memory and avoids repeated prefill.

points.title: Finding and reusing a cached prefix
points.body_markdown: For a new prompt (e.g., "Alan Turing is a pioneer of computer science whose work"), the system reuses the longest cached prefix and prefills only the rest.

points.title: Throughput under greedy decoding
points.body_markdown: Throughput is related to the average number of batched requests, measured with OPT-13B on 1×A100 40G using a ShareGPT trace.

documents.markdown:
This lecture explores the evolution of memory systems, focusing on the 'memory wall' that limits modern CPU and GPU performance. It details the CPU memory hierarchy, including cache levels, locality principles, and the technical differences between SRAM and DRAM. The document also examines GPU memory architectures, covering CUDA memory spaces, coalescing, and the transition from GDDR to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Finally, it addresses state-of-the-art technologies such as CXL for memory expansion and the capacity challenges faced by LLM inference.

## Von Neumann architecture separates memory from the processing unit

The Von Neumann architecture consists of an Arithmetic/Logic Unit and memory, with a fetch-and-execute workflow:
- Fetch instructions and data from memory
- Execute instructions on the ALU
- Write back computation results to memory

The processing unit executes instructions orders of magnitude faster than memory access, which creates the bottleneck known as the memory wall.

## Main memory is a critical component across all computing systems

Main memory matters in servers, mobile, embedded, desktop, and sensor systems. The storage hierarchy roles are:
- **Storage (SSD/HDD):** retains programs and data across runs.
- **Main memory:** holds the portions available for active execution.
- **Caches:** keep copies close to the execution units, reducing transfers from main memory.

## FPGA systems use on-chip SRAM to buffer data near logic

An FPGA configures logic blocks and their connections into a circuit for a particular task. On-chip SRAM, such as block RAM, buffers inputs and intermediate results near the processing logic.

## Discrete GPUs use their own device DRAM

A discrete GPU uses its own device DRAM: GDDR chips or HBM stacks. Results can stay in device memory for the next computation, or return to CPU memory when needed.

## The processor–DRAM performance gap grows about 50% per year

The processor–DRAM memory gap (latency) widens over time; the 50% gap describes the historical period in the graph. Faster processors alone do not guarantee faster applications.

## Scaling laws push AI workloads into the memory-bound region

Scaling laws of LLM workloads involve increased amounts of parameters and data, and increased chain-of-thought length and search depth, leading to larger model size and context state. Under post-Dennard scaling of AI accelerators, Tensor Core throughput has been growing much faster than HBM capacity, widening the memory wall across generations. The arithmetic intensity shifts toward memory-bound as model size and context length increase, and the memory-bound region keeps growing across GPU generations.

## Memory capacity per core is expected to drop

PU core number doubles every ~2 years, while DRAM DIMM capacity doubles every ~3 years. Memory capacity per core is expected to drop by 30% every two years, so much data may load from low-speed disk.

## Bandwidth and latency trends worsen, making memory the system bottleneck

Trends of bandwidth and latency are worsening. In modern computing systems, memory performance is typically the bottleneck of entire systems.

## Modern memory systems use registers and caches to reduce dependence on main memory

Registers and caches reduce how often execution depends on slower main memory. Data reuse near the processor reduces traffic across the memory hierarchy.

## Cache hierarchies have become deeper and larger

Private caches keep frequently used data near each core, and a shared cache supports reuse across the processor. Examples across systems:
- **AMD Barcelona (2007):** deeper and larger cache hierarchy. 
- **Apple M1 (2020):** the die dedicates substantial area to on-chip storage, keeping data near the CPU and GPU execution resources. 
- **AMD Ryzen 5000 (2020):** 8 cores; L1 32KB per core, L2 512KB per core, L3 32MB shared. A shared last-level cache can retain data used by several cores before a request reaches DRAM. 
- **IBM POWER10 (2020):** 15–16 cores; L2 2MB per core, L3 120MB shared. Cache capacity helps reduce traffic to main memory, while access time still depends on the location of the data. 
- **NVIDIA Ampere (GA102, 2020):** L1 128KB per SM, L2 6MB shared; the A100 accelerator shares the same architecture but includes more SMs and L2 caches. Many SMs share the device-wide L2 cache; a larger accelerator needs more capacity and data supply. 
- **AMD Zen 3:** an additional 64MB L3 cache die stacked on top of the processor die, increasing L3 from 32MB to 96MB total for 8-core processors. 
- **Apple M1 Ultra System (2022):** places multiple storage levels around its compute resources, balancing capacity, access time, and reuse.

## Memory hierarchy exploits locality by matching data frequency to memory speed

For frequent data, use fast but expensive and small memory (e.g., cache); for not frequent data, use slow but cheap and large memory (e.g., main memory, disk). The working set changes over time; the hierarchy is useful when a small, active subset receives most accesses.

## Temporal and spatial locality make caches useful

Programs touch a small working set at a time within the address space.
- **Temporal locality:** a piece of data is quickly reused in the future (e.g., loops).
- **Spatial locality:** the neighbors of the current data access tend to be accessed in the future (e.g., array), captured by one cache line fill. 

Capturing localities with high-speed caches addresses the memory wall.

## Locality example: loop reuse and sequential array access

In the loop `C[i] = A[i] * B[i] + D`:
- `D` is reused every iteration → temporal locality.
- `A`, `B`, `C` are used in sequence → spatial locality; fetch once, cache a line.

## Cache hits and misses are measured by rate and penalty

- **Hit:** the requested memory block is found in the current cache level, with a valid tag match. Hit rate = hits / total accesses.
- **Cache read/write:** find the data in cache, then perform read/write.
- **Miss:** the requested memory block is not present in the current cache level, so it must be retrieved from the next lower level. Miss rate = 1 − hit rate.
- **Miss penalty:** the additional time required to service a miss.

## Average Memory Access Time (AMAT)

Access time is the latency for the memory to handle one access; transfer time is the latency to transfer a data block to a higher level:
- Miss penalty = access time + data size / bandwidth
- AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty

A cache helps when common hits remain fast and sufficiently few accesses pay the miss penalty.

## AMAT example with a single cache level

With cache hit = 1 cycle, miss rate = 10% = 0.1, and miss penalty = 300 cycles:
- AMAT = 1 + 0.1 × 300 = 31 cycles

## Multi-level caches reduce the miss penalty

AMAT with multiple levels:
AMAT = T_hit(L1) + Miss%(L1) × (T_hit(L2) + Miss%(L2) × (T_hit(L3) + Miss%(L3) × T(memory)))

The resulting AMAT is 2.115 (compared to 31 with no multi-levels), a 14.7× speedup.

## Code optimization via blocking/tiling improves locality

Column-wise traversal (`for j … for i … sum += A[i][j]`) has poor locality. Blocking/tiling gives better locality:
```
for (ii = 0; ii < N; ii += B)
    for (jj = 0; jj < N; jj += B)
        compute_tile(A[ii:ii+B][jj:jj+B])
```

## End-to-end load/store path: address resolution → TLB → cache hierarchy → DRAM

A TLB miss requires address translation work. A cache miss determines whether the data must come from a lower level. Only a miss through the cache hierarchy sends the data request to the memory controller and DRAM.

## SRAM operation: write and read via bit lines and sense amps

- **Write:** drive bit lines (bit=1, bitbar=0), then select row.
- **Read:** precharge bit and bitbar to Vdd, select row, cell pulls one line down, sense amp on column detects the difference between bit and bitbar.

## SRAM vs. DRAM characteristics and usage

- **SRAM:** stores data via a stable transistor circuit; requires low power to retain a bit (423mV for 45nm); requires 6 transistors/bit — expensive. Usage: caches, register files.
- **DRAM:** stores data via tiny capacitors (bit represented as charged/discharged); one transistor/bit — cheap; must be re-written after being read; must also be periodically refreshed, with each row refreshed simultaneously. Address lines are multiplexed: upper half of address = row access strobe (RAS), lower half = column access strobe (CAS). Usage: DDR / GDDR / HBM.

## DRAM Read and Write Operations

- **Read:** precharge the bit line to Vdd, select the row, and let the cell and bit line share charges. This produces a very small voltage change on the bit line, which the sense amplifier detects (it can detect changes of ~10–100k electrons).
- **Write:** drive the bit lines and select the row; the value is restored.
- Rows are selected via wordlines (Wordline0 … Wordline1023).

## DRAM Refresh and Its Cost

- DRAM storage is leaky, so it needs periodic refresh across rows.
- Refreshing means reading and writing the same data back; the row is un-accessible while being refreshed.
- Worked example: 4K rows, 100 ns read cycle, each row refreshed within 64 ms.
  - 4096 × 100 ns = 410 μs to refresh once
  - 410 μs / 64 ms = 0.64% unavailability
- Refresh is bursty.

## Why DRAM Is Slow

- **Weak storage signal:** bits are tiny capacitor charges, giving only a small voltage difference on long bitlines.
- **Sensing takes time:** the sense amplifier must detect and amplify a very small voltage change into a full 0/1 value.
- **Destructive read:** reading disturbs the stored charge, so data must be restored after every row activation.
- **Large dense arrays:** DRAM prioritizes capacity and cost per bit, so rows/bitlines are long and have higher RC delay.
- Stated solution: multi-bank, multi-rank DRAM.

## Multi-Bank DRAM

- Banks are independent storage arrays; work in one bank can overlap preparation in another.
- The shared data bus still limits how much data the channel can return at once.

## Ranks and DIMMs

- A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width.
- Multiple ranks share the channel; the controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.

## Memory Controller Functions

- Buffers cache lines in both directions (cache line read buffer, cache line write buffer).
- Schedules requests at two levels: bank and channel.
- Interfaces with the cache data bus and the SDRAM command/address bus.

## Channel Organization and Peak Bandwidth

- One memory-controller port drives one channel.
- Command, address, and clock signals select the destination.
- All ranks share the data bus; only the selected rank may drive it.
- **Peak Bandwidth = Transfer Rate × Bus Width / 8**

## Bandwidth Scaling Across Channels and DDR Generations

- Independent channels add bandwidth when requests use them concurrently; bank scheduling improves bus utilization.
- DDR5 splits 64 data bits into two 32-bit subchannels; this split alone does not double total data width.
- DDR generations mainly scale bandwidth; DRAM core latency improves much more slowly.

## DDR1 to DDR5 Comparison

- Headline trends: pin rate 16×, peak ×64 bandwidth 16×, voltage 2.5 V → 1.1 V; at selected upper rates the same aggregate ×64 width rises from 3.2 to 51.2 GB/s.

| Generation | Data Rate | Prefetch / Burst | Bank Parallelism | DIMM Data Path | VDD | Peak BW (×64) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DDR | 200–400 MT/s | 2n / BL2-8 | 4 banks | 1 × 64-bit | 2.5 V | 3.2 GB/s |
| DDR2 | 400–1066 MT/s | 4n / BL4-8 | 4–8 banks | 1 × 64-bit | 1.8 V | 8.5 GB/s |
| DDR3 | 800–2133 MT/s | 8n / BL8 | 8 banks | 1 × 64-bit | 1.5 V | 17.1 GB/s |
| DDR4 | 1600–3200 MT/s | 8n / BL8 | 16 banks / 4 BG | 1 × 64-bit | 1.2 V | 25.6 GB/s |
| DDR5 | 3200–6400 MT/s | 16n / BL16 | Up to 32 banks / 8 BG | 2 × 32-bit | 1.1 V | 51.2 GB/s |

- The interface evolves faster than the DRAM cell: bandwidth rises through faster I/O and more parallelism.

## GPU Memory Hierarchy Levels

Larger capacity comes with longer access time:
- **Registers:** allocated per thread, hardware managed.
- **Shared Memory + L1 Cache:** per SM, explicit scratchpad plus hardware cache.
- **L2 Cache:** device-wide, shared by all SMs.
- **Device Memory (GDDR / HBM):** off-chip physical memory serving the global address space.

## Path of a GPU Memory Access

- GDDR/HBM is off-chip; data returns along the same path.
- SM-local resources have low latency but limited capacity.
- A request reaches device-wide L2 through the on-chip interconnect; an L2 miss continues to a memory controller.
- All SMs share L2 and the DRAM partitions, implemented with GDDR devices or HBM channels.

## Scope and Lifetime in CUDA Memories

- **Scope** identifies which threads can access data; **lifetime** identifies how long the data exists.
- `__syncthreads()` coordinates threads within one block; it does not synchronize different blocks.

## CUDA Memory Spaces and Their Physical Resources

- Local memory is thread-private in scope but usually resides in device DRAM and passes through L1/L2.
- Register and shared-memory allocations limit how many blocks and warps can reside on an SM.

| Memory Space | Physical Location | Cached? | Scope | Lifetime | Access | Relative Latency | Performance Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Registers | On-chip register file | — | Thread | Thread | R/W | Lowest | Usage can limit occupancy |
| Local | Device DRAM | L1 / L2 | Thread | Thread | R/W | High | Spills and large private arrays |
| Shared | On-chip per SM | — | Block | Block | R/W | Low | Capacity can limit occupancy |
| Global | Device DRAM | L1 / L2 | Grid / host | Allocation | R/W | High | Coalescing determines traffic |
| Constant | Device DRAM | Constant cache | Grid | Allocation | Read-only | Low on hit | Best for warp-uniform reads |
| Texture | Device DRAM | Texture cache | Grid | Allocation | Read / surface write | Low on hit | Optimized for spatial locality |

- Key distinction: local is private in scope but usually off-chip in physical location.

## Warp Memory Instructions and Transaction Granularity

- One warp memory instruction (e.g., `LDG R0, [base + tid × 4]`) is executed by 32 threads, generating up to 32 addresses.
- 32 addresses are not automatically 32 DRAM operations; the address pattern determines how many cache sectors/transactions are needed.
- The coalescer groups addresses by cache-sector or transaction granularity before DRAM access.
- Transaction count depends on alignment, address spacing, access width, and GPU architecture.

## Coalescing Patterns

- **Aligned + contiguous:** minimum transactions (1–few).
- **Misaligned:** crosses an extra boundary (few + 1).
- **Strided:** touches many segments (many).
- Coalescing is evaluated per warp instruction and depends on access width, alignment, cache-sector size, and architecture.

## Data Layout and Useful Bandwidth

- **Useful bandwidth = Physical bandwidth × Requested bytes / Transferred bytes**
- Row-major matrix: a warp walking across a row uses contiguous addresses (coalesced); walking down a column uses strided addresses.
- Same arithmetic with different layout → different memory traffic; row-wise and column-wise traversal can transfer different byte counts.

## Shared Memory as an Explicit On-Chip Stage

- Software explicitly chooses the data to stage in shared memory and when threads must synchronize.
- One off-chip load can support repeated on-chip reuse, reducing DRAM traffic and increasing arithmetic intensity.
- Shared memory is an explicitly addressed scratchpad; it does not automatically cache arbitrary global-memory accesses.

## Shared Memory Bank Conflicts

- Typical mapping for 32-bit words: **bank = (address / 4) mod 32**
- Typical GPUs use 32 banks (figures may show 8 for readability); same-address reads can use broadcast.
- Different addresses in the same bank require multiple service rounds.
- Bank conflicts differ from global-memory coalescing.

## GDDR vs. Socketed DDR DIMMs

- **DDR DIMM:** socketed, multiple ranks, replaceable modules, longer routed channel.
- **GDDR:** soldered devices, short point-to-point links.
- Short, fixed point-to-point routes permit higher per-pin data rates, with less expandability than socketed DIMMs.

## GDDR Aggregate Bandwidth

- Aggregate bandwidth is the sum across independent memory-controller channels.
- More channels, wider buses, and faster signaling also raise pin count, routing complexity, and I/O power.
- Aggregate bandwidth rises along three independent axes.

## GDDR5 to GDDR7 Signaling

- GDDR6X uses PAM4 as a vendor extension; GDDR7 uses PAM3 and further divides the channels.
- GDDR6X is a vendor extension, not the next JEDEC generation.
- Rates shown are representative; actual rates depend on product and speed bin.

## GDDR vs. HBM Design Trade-offs

- **Bandwidth = Per-pin data rate × Interface width**
- **GDDR — narrower + faster:** 256–384-bit board bus, multiple GDDR devices each typically ×32, 20–32 Gb/s per pin, PCB point-to-point links; signal integrity and I/O power dominate.
- **HBM — ultra-wide + moderate-rate:** 1024 bits per stack (2048 bits for HBM4), thousands of short package wires, lower signaling rate per wire; bandwidth/package and bandwidth/watt dominate.
- HBM1–HBM3 use a 1024-bit interface per stack; HBM4 expands to 2048 bits.
- Dense, short wiring improves bandwidth and energy per bit, while requiring advanced packaging.

## HBM Stack Structure

- Memory stack in one package: TSVs carry signals and power through the stack; micro-bumps connect adjacent dies.
- More stacked dies increase capacity; wide channel organization increases bandwidth.

## 2.5D Packaging for HBM

- HBM commonly sits beside the XPU on an interposer, forming a 2.5D package.
- Dense connections improve bandwidth and energy per bit, with costs in assembly, yield, cooling, and power delivery.

## HBM scaling levers: signaling, stack height, and interface width

HBM generations (HBM1 to HBM4) scale bandwidth through three main levers:
- Faster signaling
- Greater stack height
- The wider HBM4 interface

Constraints on stack count and height come from package space, thermal limits, and yield. Per-stack bandwidth figures are representative; JEDEC limits and shipping products vary by vendor and speed bin.

## DDR, GDDR, and HBM optimize different design constraints

Each memory technology targets a different balance:
- **DDR** favors capacity, expandability, and cost per GB.
- **GDDR** balances pin bandwidth and board cost.
- **HBM** favors bandwidth per package and per watt.

The choice depends on the workload and system constraints.

| Design Dimension | DDR | GDDR | HBM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary target | CPU main memory | Graphics / edge AI | Datacenter AI / HPC |
| Topology | Shared channel + DIMMs | Point-to-point soldered devices | Stacked DRAM beside XPU |
| Interface strategy | Moderate width and rate | High per-pin rate | Ultra-wide interface |
| Packaging | Socketed module + PCB | BGA devices on PCB | TSV stack + interposer |
| Capacity scaling | More / denser DIMMs | More or denser devices | More stacks and taller stacks |
| Bandwidth / energy | Moderate / moderate | High / higher I/O power | Highest / best bandwidth per watt |
| Cost | Lowest system cost per GB | Middle | Highest packaging cost |
| Typical products | Servers and PCs | Gaming GPUs, edge accelerators | H100/B200-class GPUs, AI ASICs |

Summary: DDR optimizes capacity and expandability; GDDR optimizes pin bandwidth and cost; HBM optimizes bandwidth/package and bandwidth/watt.

## A banked LLC is logically shared but physically distributed

- A physical-address hash selects a home LLC slice for each line.
- Reads/writes to remote slices would slow down memory access speed.

## Shared LLC behavior: cold reads and private copies

- Only the first cold read must reach DRAM; a second reader can obtain the line from the LLC or the current owner.
- The second reader creates another private copy of the same cache line.
- This is a simplified inclusive teaching model; modern LLCs may also be non-inclusive.

## Coherence requirements: write propagation and write serialization

- **Write propagation:** other processors must eventually observe the write.
- **Write serialization:** all processors must agree on one order for writes to the same location.

The stale-copy problem illustrated: both cores read X = 0; Core 0 writes X = 1; Core 1 reads its stale copy and gets 0. Core 1 is not notified, so the system contains two observable values for one memory location — incorrect.

## Coherence protocols: MESI permissions vs. snooping/directory transport

- Snooping broadcasts coherence requests; a directory tracks owners and sharers to target the messages.
- MESI describes permissions (a permission/state machine).
- Snooping and directory designs determine how coherence messages reach the caches — i.e., how coherence messages are transported.

## The LLM inference capacity wall: KV-cache size limits batch size

Case study of DeepSeek with a GB200 GPU:
- Available HBM capacity for KV-cache: ~150 GB.
- At 1M context length, maximum sessions per GPU: DeepSeek v3.2 ≈ 4; DeepSeek v4pro ≈ 32 — the GPU is much underutilized.

Approximate KV-cache size per session:

| Context Length | DeepSeek v3.2 | DeepSeek v4 (w CSA/HCA/SWA) |
|---|---|---|
| 128K | ~5.72 GiB | ~0.62 GiB |
| 256K | ~11.44 GiB | ~1.21 GiB |
| 1M | ~45.75 GiB | ~4.83 GiB |
| 2M | ~91.50 GiB | ~9.65 GiB |

**Capacity wall:** HBM can only hold limited KV-caches, resulting in low batch size and low computation utilization.

## CXL provides unified memory across host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM

- The host address map provides unified memory across host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM.
- Software sees host-memory ranges.
- Hardware translates load/store instructions into CXL remote memory accesses.

## CXL switches enable expansion, pooling, and sharing

- **Expansion** adds capacity to one host.
- **Pooling** assigns portions of memory devices to different hosts.
- CXL 3.0 coherent sharing differs from merely allowing several hosts to map the same memory region.
- CXL changes capacity from a fixed motherboard resource into a composable system resource.

## LPDDR extends addressable capacity, not HBM itself

- Hopper retains local HBM; Grace connects LPDDR5X through the coherent NVLink-C2C CPU-GPU link.
- LPDDR extends the capacity the accelerator can address; it does not enlarge HBM itself.

## Tiered memory management decides what stays in HBM

- Keep hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM.
- Place large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier.
- Promotion helps only when future reuse saves more than the transfer and bookkeeping cost.
- Migration is useful only when future reuse repays transfer cost.
- Granularity, prediction accuracy, and placement overhead determine the result.
documents.intro_markdown: This lecture explores the evolution of memory systems, focusing on the 'memory wall' that limits modern CPU and GPU performance. It details the CPU memory hierarchy, including cache levels, locality principles, and the technical differences between SRAM and DRAM. The document also examines GPU memory architectures, covering CUDA memory spaces, coalescing, and the transition from GDDR to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Finally, it addresses state-of-the-art technologies such as CXL for memory expansion and the capacity challenges faced by LLM inference.

points.title: Von Neumann architecture separates memory from the processing unit
points.body_markdown:
The Von Neumann architecture consists of an Arithmetic/Logic Unit and memory, with a fetch-and-execute workflow:
- Fetch instructions and data from memory
- Execute instructions on the ALU
- Write back computation results to memory

The processing unit executes instructions orders of magnitude faster than memory access, which creates the bottleneck known as the memory wall.

points.title: Main memory is a critical component across all computing systems
points.body_markdown:
Main memory matters in servers, mobile, embedded, desktop, and sensor systems. The storage hierarchy roles are:
- **Storage (SSD/HDD):** retains programs and data across runs.
- **Main memory:** holds the portions available for active execution.
- **Caches:** keep copies close to the execution units, reducing transfers from main memory.

points.title: FPGA systems use on-chip SRAM to buffer data near logic
points.body_markdown: An FPGA configures logic blocks and their connections into a circuit for a particular task. On-chip SRAM, such as block RAM, buffers inputs and intermediate results near the processing logic.

points.title: Discrete GPUs use their own device DRAM
points.body_markdown: A discrete GPU uses its own device DRAM: GDDR chips or HBM stacks. Results can stay in device memory for the next computation, or return to CPU memory when needed.

points.title: The processor–DRAM performance gap grows about 50% per year
points.body_markdown: The processor–DRAM memory gap (latency) widens over time; the 50% gap describes the historical period in the graph. Faster processors alone do not guarantee faster applications.

points.title: Scaling laws push AI workloads into the memory-bound region
points.body_markdown: Scaling laws of LLM workloads involve increased amounts of parameters and data, and increased chain-of-thought length and search depth, leading to larger model size and context state. Under post-Dennard scaling of AI accelerators, Tensor Core throughput has been growing much faster than HBM capacity, widening the memory wall across generations. The arithmetic intensity shifts toward memory-bound as model size and context length increase, and the memory-bound region keeps growing across GPU generations.

points.title: Memory capacity per core is expected to drop
points.body_markdown: PU core number doubles every ~2 years, while DRAM DIMM capacity doubles every ~3 years. Memory capacity per core is expected to drop by 30% every two years, so much data may load from low-speed disk.

points.title: Bandwidth and latency trends worsen, making memory the system bottleneck
points.body_markdown: Trends of bandwidth and latency are worsening. In modern computing systems, memory performance is typically the bottleneck of entire systems.

points.title: Modern memory systems use registers and caches to reduce dependence on main memory
points.body_markdown: Registers and caches reduce how often execution depends on slower main memory. Data reuse near the processor reduces traffic across the memory hierarchy.

points.title: Cache hierarchies have become deeper and larger
points.body_markdown:
Private caches keep frequently used data near each core, and a shared cache supports reuse across the processor. Examples across systems:
- **AMD Barcelona (2007):** deeper and larger cache hierarchy. 
- **Apple M1 (2020):** the die dedicates substantial area to on-chip storage, keeping data near the CPU and GPU execution resources. 
- **AMD Ryzen 5000 (2020):** 8 cores; L1 32KB per core, L2 512KB per core, L3 32MB shared. A shared last-level cache can retain data used by several cores before a request reaches DRAM. 
- **IBM POWER10 (2020):** 15–16 cores; L2 2MB per core, L3 120MB shared. Cache capacity helps reduce traffic to main memory, while access time still depends on the location of the data. 
- **NVIDIA Ampere (GA102, 2020):** L1 128KB per SM, L2 6MB shared; the A100 accelerator shares the same architecture but includes more SMs and L2 caches. Many SMs share the device-wide L2 cache; a larger accelerator needs more capacity and data supply. 
- **AMD Zen 3:** an additional 64MB L3 cache die stacked on top of the processor die, increasing L3 from 32MB to 96MB total for 8-core processors. 
- **Apple M1 Ultra System (2022):** places multiple storage levels around its compute resources, balancing capacity, access time, and reuse.

points.title: Memory hierarchy exploits locality by matching data frequency to memory speed
points.body_markdown: For frequent data, use fast but expensive and small memory (e.g., cache); for not frequent data, use slow but cheap and large memory (e.g., main memory, disk). The working set changes over time; the hierarchy is useful when a small, active subset receives most accesses.

points.title: Temporal and spatial locality make caches useful
points.body_markdown:
Programs touch a small working set at a time within the address space.
- **Temporal locality:** a piece of data is quickly reused in the future (e.g., loops).
- **Spatial locality:** the neighbors of the current data access tend to be accessed in the future (e.g., array), captured by one cache line fill. 

Capturing localities with high-speed caches addresses the memory wall.

points.title: Locality example: loop reuse and sequential array access
points.body_markdown:
In the loop `C[i] = A[i] * B[i] + D`:
- `D` is reused every iteration → temporal locality.
- `A`, `B`, `C` are used in sequence → spatial locality; fetch once, cache a line.

points.title: Cache hits and misses are measured by rate and penalty
points.body_markdown:
- **Hit:** the requested memory block is found in the current cache level, with a valid tag match. Hit rate = hits / total accesses.
- **Cache read/write:** find the data in cache, then perform read/write.
- **Miss:** the requested memory block is not present in the current cache level, so it must be retrieved from the next lower level. Miss rate = 1 − hit rate.
- **Miss penalty:** the additional time required to service a miss.

points.title: Average Memory Access Time (AMAT)
points.body_markdown:
Access time is the latency for the memory to handle one access; transfer time is the latency to transfer a data block to a higher level:
- Miss penalty = access time + data size / bandwidth
- AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty

A cache helps when common hits remain fast and sufficiently few accesses pay the miss penalty.

points.title: AMAT example with a single cache level
points.body_markdown:
With cache hit = 1 cycle, miss rate = 10% = 0.1, and miss penalty = 300 cycles:
- AMAT = 1 + 0.1 × 300 = 31 cycles

points.title: Multi-level caches reduce the miss penalty
points.body_markdown:
AMAT with multiple levels:
AMAT = T_hit(L1) + Miss%(L1) × (T_hit(L2) + Miss%(L2) × (T_hit(L3) + Miss%(L3) × T(memory)))

The resulting AMAT is 2.115 (compared to 31 with no multi-levels), a 14.7× speedup.

points.title: Code optimization via blocking/tiling improves locality
End-to-end load/store path: address resolution → TLB → cache hierarchy → DRAM
points.body_markdown: A TLB miss requires address translation work. A cache miss determines whether the data must come from a lower level. Only a miss through the cache hierarchy sends the data request to the memory controller and DRAM.

points.title: SRAM operation: write and read via bit lines and sense amps
points.body_markdown:
- **Write:** drive bit lines (bit=1, bitbar=0), then select row.
- **Read:** precharge bit and bitbar to Vdd, select row, cell pulls one line down, sense amp on column detects the difference between bit and bitbar.

points.title: SRAM vs. DRAM characteristics and usage
points.body_markdown:
- **SRAM:** stores data via a stable transistor circuit; requires low power to retain a bit (423mV for 45nm); requires 6 transistors/bit — expensive. Usage: caches, register files.
- **DRAM:** stores data via tiny capacitors (bit represented as charged/discharged); one transistor/bit — cheap; must be re-written after being read; must also be periodically refreshed, with each row refreshed simultaneously. Address lines are multiplexed: upper half of address = row access strobe (RAS), lower half = column access strobe (CAS). Usage: DDR / GDDR / HBM.

points.title: DRAM Read and Write Operations
points.body_markdown:
- **Read:** precharge the bit line to Vdd, select the row, and let the cell and bit line share charges. This produces a very small voltage change on the bit line, which the sense amplifier detects (it can detect changes of ~10–100k electrons).
- **Write:** drive the bit lines and select the row; the value is restored.
- Rows are selected via wordlines (Wordline0 … Wordline1023).

points.title: DRAM Refresh and Its Cost
points.body_markdown:
- DRAM storage is leaky, so it needs periodic refresh across rows.
- Refreshing means reading and writing the same data back; the row is un-accessible while being refreshed.
- Worked example: 4K rows, 100 ns read cycle, each row refreshed within 64 ms.
  - 4096 × 100 ns = 410 μs to refresh once
  - 410 μs / 64 ms = 0.64% unavailability
- Refresh is bursty.

points.title: Why DRAM Is Slow
points.body_markdown:
- **Weak storage signal:** bits are tiny capacitor charges, giving only a small voltage difference on long bitlines.
- **Sensing takes time:** the sense amplifier must detect and amplify a very small voltage change into a full 0/1 value.
- **Destructive read:** reading disturbs the stored charge, so data must be restored after every row activation.
- **Large dense arrays:** DRAM prioritizes capacity and cost per bit, so rows/bitlines are long and have higher RC delay.
- Stated solution: multi-bank, multi-rank DRAM.

points.title: Multi-Bank DRAM
points.body_markdown:
- Banks are independent storage arrays; work in one bank can overlap preparation in another.
- The shared data bus still limits how much data the channel can return at once.

points.title: Ranks and DIMMs
points.body_markdown:
- A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width.
- Multiple ranks share the channel; the controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.

points.title: Memory Controller Functions
points.body_markdown:
- Buffers cache lines in both directions (cache line read buffer, cache line write buffer).
- Schedules requests at two levels: bank and channel.
- Interfaces with the cache data bus and the SDRAM command/address bus.

points.title: Channel Organization and Peak Bandwidth
points.body_markdown:
- One memory-controller port drives one channel.
- Command, address, and clock signals select the destination.
- All ranks share the data bus; only the selected rank may drive it.
- **Peak Bandwidth = Transfer Rate × Bus Width / 8**

points.title: Bandwidth Scaling Across Channels and DDR Generations
points.body_markdown:
- Independent channels add bandwidth when requests use them concurrently; bank scheduling improves bus utilization.
- DDR5 splits 64 data bits into two 32-bit subchannels; this split alone does not double total data width.
- DDR generations mainly scale bandwidth; DRAM core latency improves much more slowly.

points.body_markdown:
HBM generations (HBM1 to HBM4) scale bandwidth through three main levers:
- Faster signaling
- Greater stack height
- The wider HBM4 interface

Constraints on stack count and height come from package space, thermal limits, and yield. Per-stack bandwidth figures are representative; JEDEC limits and shipping products vary by vendor and speed bin.

points.title: DDR, GDDR, and HBM optimize different design constraints
points.body_markdown:
Each memory technology targets a different balance:
- **DDR** favors capacity, expandability, and cost per GB.
- **GDDR** balances pin bandwidth and board cost.
- **HBM** favors bandwidth per package and per watt.

The choice depends on the workload and system constraints.

| Design Dimension | DDR | GDDR | HBM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary target | CPU main memory | Graphics / edge AI | Datacenter AI / HPC |
| Topology | Shared channel + DIMMs | Point-to-point soldered devices | Stacked DRAM beside XPU |
| Interface strategy | Moderate width and rate | High per-pin rate | Ultra-wide interface |
| Packaging | Socketed module + PCB | BGA devices on PCB | TSV stack + interposer |
| Capacity scaling | More / denser DIMMs | More or denser devices | More stacks and taller stacks |
| Bandwidth / energy | Moderate / moderate | High / higher I/O power | Highest / best bandwidth per watt |
| Cost | Lowest system cost per GB | Middle | Highest packaging cost |
| Typical products | Servers and PCs | Gaming GPUs, edge accelerators | H100/B200-class GPUs, AI ASICs |

Summary: DDR optimizes capacity and expandability; GDDR optimizes pin bandwidth and cost; HBM optimizes bandwidth/package and bandwidth/watt.

points.title: A banked LLC is logically shared but physically distributed
points.body_markdown:
- A physical-address hash selects a home LLC slice for each line.
- Reads/writes to remote slices would slow down memory access speed.

points.title: Shared LLC behavior: cold reads and private copies
points.body_markdown:
- Only the first cold read must reach DRAM; a second reader can obtain the line from the LLC or the current owner.
- The second reader creates another private copy of the same cache line.
- This is a simplified inclusive teaching model; modern LLCs may also be non-inclusive.

points.title: Coherence requirements: write propagation and write serialization
points.body_markdown:
- **Write propagation:** other processors must eventually observe the write.
- **Write serialization:** all processors must agree on one order for writes to the same location.

The stale-copy problem illustrated: both cores read X = 0; Core 0 writes X = 1; Core 1 reads its stale copy and gets 0. Core 1 is not notified, so the system contains two observable values for one memory location — incorrect.

points.title: Coherence protocols: MESI permissions vs. snooping/directory transport
points.body_markdown:
- Snooping broadcasts coherence requests; a directory tracks owners and sharers to target the messages.
- MESI describes permissions (a permission/state machine).
- Snooping and directory designs determine how coherence messages reach the caches — i.e., how coherence messages are transported.

points.title: The LLM inference capacity wall: KV-cache size limits batch size
points.body_markdown:
Case study of DeepSeek with a GB200 GPU:
- Available HBM capacity for KV-cache: ~150 GB.
- At 1M context length, maximum sessions per GPU: DeepSeek v3.2 ≈ 4; DeepSeek v4pro ≈ 32 — the GPU is much underutilized.

Approximate KV-cache size per session:

| Context Length | DeepSeek v3.2 | DeepSeek v4 (w CSA/HCA/SWA) |
|---|---|---|
| 128K | ~5.72 GiB | ~0.62 GiB |
| 256K | ~11.44 GiB | ~1.21 GiB |
| 1M | ~45.75 GiB | ~4.83 GiB |
| 2M | ~91.50 GiB | ~9.65 GiB |

**Capacity wall:** HBM can only hold limited KV-caches, resulting in low batch size and low computation utilization.

points.title: CXL provides unified memory across host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM
points.body_markdown:
- The host address map provides unified memory across host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM.
- Software sees host-memory ranges.
- Hardware translates load/store instructions into CXL remote memory accesses.

points.title: CXL switches enable expansion, pooling, and sharing
points.body_markdown:
- **Expansion** adds capacity to one host.
- **Pooling** assigns portions of memory devices to different hosts.
- CXL 3.0 coherent sharing differs from merely allowing several hosts to map the same memory region.
- CXL changes capacity from a fixed motherboard resource into a composable system resource.

points.title: LPDDR extends addressable capacity, not HBM itself
points.body_markdown:
- Hopper retains local HBM; Grace connects LPDDR5X through the coherent NVLink-C2C CPU-GPU link.
- LPDDR extends the capacity the accelerator can address; it does not enlarge HBM itself.

points.title: Tiered memory management decides what stays in HBM
points.body_markdown:
- Keep hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM.
- Place large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier.
- Promotion helps only when future reuse saves more than the transfer and bookkeeping cost.
- Migration is useful only when future reuse repays transfer cost.
- Granularity, prediction accuracy, and placement overhead determine the result.

This chapter reviews the key knowledge points from the Assignment 1 document on MPI programming for parallel GEMM. It focuses on the problem definition, the required parallelization strategy, the implementation task, and the input/output format, so you can check your understanding before starting the assignment.

## GEMM definition and the sequential algorithm

GEMM (General Matrix-Matrix Multiplication) computes $C = A \times B$ for $A \in \mathbb{R}^{M\times K}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times N}$, giving $C \in \mathbb{R}^{M\times N}$ with

$$C_{ij} = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} A_{ik} B_{kj}.$$

The sequential version (Algorithm 1) initializes $C[M][N]$ to zero, then for each $i$ and $j$ accumulates $C_{ij} = C_{ij} + A_{ik}B_{kj}$ over all $k$ from $0$ to $K-1$, and returns $C$. This sequential implementation is provided in the package for reference and result comparison.

## The 1D row-partitioning parallel strategy

The assignment parallelizes GEMM using a simple 1D row partitioning strategy:

- Matrix $A$ is divided by rows among the MPI processes.
- Every MPI process uses the **complete** matrix $B$.
- Each process computes its assigned rows of $C$ (i.e., $A_r \times B \rightarrow C_r$ for its rank $r$).
- The local result blocks are finally gathered to Process 0 and assembled as $C = [C_0; C_1; C_2; \dots]$ in correct row order.

## Row divisibility guarantee

For all provided and evaluation test cases, the number of rows $M$ is divisible by the number of MPI processes $P$:

$$M \bmod P = 0.$$

Therefore every MPI process receives the same number of rows of $A$. This holds for every tested process count $P$ (also restated on page 5).

## The three implementation steps

The task is to complete the missing code in the designated section of the `main` function in the skeleton `gemm_mpi.c`:

1. **Distribute**: Scatter the rows of matrix $A$ to the MPI processes and make matrix $B$ available to every MPI process.
2. **Compute**: Perform the local GEMM computation in each process: $local\_C = local\_A \times B$.
3. **Collect**: Gather all local result blocks to Process 0 and assemble them into the complete output matrix $C$ in the correct row order.

## Permitted MPI communication methods

A typical implementation may use `MPI_Bcast`, `MPI_Scatter`, and `MPI_Gather`. Equivalent MPI communication methods that correctly implement the required parallel computation may also be used. For MPI API details, refer to the MPI documentation introduced in the tutorial.

## Input file format

The input file begins with three integers $M$, $K$, and $N$. The following $M$ rows store matrix $A$, followed by $K$ rows storing matrix $B$.

## Worked example of input and expected output

Example input `dataset/test1.txt`:

```
2 2 2
1 2
3 4
5 6
7 8
```

This represents

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{bmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{bmatrix}.$$

The expected output (`expected/test1.txt`) is:

```
RESULT 2 2
19 22
43 50
```

i.e., $C=\begin{bmatrix}19&22\\43&50\end{bmatrix}$.

## Compiling and running the MPI program

Compile with:

```
mpicc gemm_mpi.c -O2 -o gemm_mpi
```

Run with one MPI process:

```
mpiexec -n 1 ./gemm_mpi ./dataset/test1.txt
```

Run with two MPI processes:

```
mpiexec -n 2 ./gemm_mpi ./dataset/test1.txt
```

## Compiler and library policy

- All submissions are compiled using `mpicc` with the `-O2` optimization flag during assessment.
- Only the standard C library and MPI are allowed; no additional third-party libraries.
- No additional source or header files should be submitted.

## Contents of the given package

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `gemm_mpi.c` | The MPI program skeleton — the main file to complete |
| `gemm_sequential.c` | Sequential GEMM implementation, for reference and result comparison |
| `Makefile` / `test.sh` | Scripts for compiling and running public tests locally |
| `dataset/` | Public input datasets used for testing |
| `expected/` | Expected output corresponding to the public datasets |
| `tuxiv.conf` | Configuration file used by the TACC SDK for remote testing |
| `sdk-test.sh` | Remote testing script run on TACC; activates the official course environment, compiles, and runs public tests |
| `README.md` | Guide to local testing, TACC testing, and final submission |

## What the evaluation checks

- Programs are evaluated using multiple matrix dimensions and valid MPI process counts; evaluation datasets may differ from the public test datasets.
- Evaluation focuses on **correctness and correct MPI-based parallel execution**.
- Performance and parallel speedup are **not** evaluated and no speedup measurement is included in grading.
- Grading: 10 points if the program passes the required multi-process MPI executions with correct results on all evaluation cases; 5 points if it is correct in single-process execution but fails multi-process MPI evaluation; 0 points if it fails to compile, fails to execute correctly, or produces incorrect results.

This chapter reviews the key knowledge points from Assignment 2, which assesses the implementation of scaled dot-product attention using CUDA.

## The attention computation to implement

The assignment requires implementing scaled dot-product attention for a single attention head, forward pass only. Given:
- $Q$: $M \times d$
- $K$: $N \times d$
- $V$: $N \times d$

Compute output $O$ of shape $M \times d$:
$$\mathbf{O} = \mathrm{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d})V$$

Softmax is applied independently to each row. Each output row is a weighted sum of the rows of $V$. All matrices use contiguous, row-major storage and 32-bit floating-point (FP32) values.

### Scope exclusions
No causal mask, dropout, backward pass, or multi-head attention is required.

## The three-step decomposition of attention

The computation is broken into three operations:

| Step | Operation | Output shape |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| 1 | $S = QK^T/\sqrt{d}$ | $M \times N$ |
| 2 | $P = $ row-wise softmax($S$) | $M \times N$ |
| 3 | $O = PV$ | $M \times d$ |

## The sequential reference algorithm

The CPU reference `attention_sequential.cpp` illustrates the operation using stable softmax. For each row $i$:
1. Compute scores $S[j] = \sum_t Q[i,t] \cdot K[j,t] / \sqrt{d}$ for all $j$.
2. Find the row maximum $m = \max_j S[j]$.
3. Compute exponentials $E[j] = \exp(S[j] - m)$.
4. Compute the normalizer $z = \sum_j E[j]$.
5. Compute output $O[i,t] = \sum_j (E[j]/z) \cdot V[j,t]$ for all $t$.

## Numerical stability via max subtraction

The direct expression $\exp(S[j])/\sum_k \exp(S[k])$ can overflow for large positive scores or underflow to zero for an entire row of large negative scores. Subtracting the row maximum before exponentiation preserves the mathematical result while avoiding these failures:
$$m_i = \max_j S_{ij}, \quad P_{ij} = \exp(S_{ij} - m_i)/\sum_k \exp(S_{ik} - m_i)$$

A numerically stable implementation is required for full credit; equivalent stable methods are accepted.

## The function to complete and its interface

Complete `attention_forward` in `attention.cu`. The declaration is supplied in `attention.h`:
```c
void attention_forward(
    const float* Q, const float* K, const float* V,
    float* output, int M, int N, int d);
```

### Implementation requirements
1. Compute the scaled query-key scores on the GPU.
2. Apply softmax independently to each score row on the GPU.
3. Compute the weighted sum of values and write all output elements on the GPU.
4. Release any temporary device memory allocated by your implementation.

All input and output pointers refer to device memory. The supplied runner handles file input, host/device copies, and output printing. Do not change the inputs. Use the default CUDA stream. Multiple kernels and temporary score matrices are allowed; FlashAttention and kernel fusion are not required.

## Input constraints and boundary handling

- $1 \le M, N \le 512$; $1 \le d \le 64$.
- Input values are finite FP32 numbers with absolute value at most 2048.
- Dimensions need not be multiples of a CUDA block size; the implementation must handle boundary threads correctly.

## Compiler and library policy

- Assessment uses `nvcc` with `-O2 -std=c++14` and a target appropriate to the GPU and compiler.
- Only standard C++ and CUDA runtime/device features are allowed.
- Do not use cuBLAS, cuDNN, PyTorch, or other third-party compute libraries.
- The attention computation must execute in CUDA kernels; a CPU-only solution does not receive credit.

## Numerical comparison tolerance

For each output element, the checker requires:
$$\mathrm{abs}(\mathrm{actual} - \mathrm{reference}) \le 1\text{e-}4 + 1\text{e-}3 \cdot \mathrm{abs}(\mathrm{reference})$$

NaN and infinity are rejected. The checker also validates output dimensions and element counts. Each test has a 30-second timeout to catch hangs; there is no runtime ranking.

## The given package contents

| File / directory | Purpose |
|------------------|---------|
| `attention.cu` | Student skeleton; the only source file modified and submitted |
| `attention.h` / `runner.cu` / `io.hpp` | Fixed interface, device-memory management, file I/O, CUDA error checks |
| `attention_sequential.cpp` | Stable CPU reference implementation |
| `Makefile` / `test.sh` / `tools/cuda_arch.py` | Select compiler target, compile, run public tests |
| `dataset/` / `expected/` | Public inputs and expected outputs |
| `tests.json` / `tools/check.py` | Test groups, floating-point comparison, 0/10/15 scoring |
| `tuxiv.conf` / `sdk-test.sh` | Configuration and entry script for course remote testing |
| `env/activate.sh` / `Dockerfile` | CUDA environment helper and optional container build recipe |
| `README.md` | Testing instructions and submission reminders |

## Local testing workflow

Use a Linux CUDA environment with an NVIDIA GPU, compatible driver, CUDA Toolkit, g++, make, Python 3.6+, and Bash. No third-party Python packages are required. In the extracted student-code directory:
```
source env/activate.sh
make test
```

A complete and stable implementation should end with:
```
BASIC: 7/7
STABLE: 5/5
SCORE: 15/15
ALL TESTS PASSED
```

The original skeleton deliberately returns zeros and is expected to fail. For individual runs:
```
make
./attention_cuda dataset/basic_small.txt
make cpu
./attention_seq dataset/basic_small.txt
```

The build automatically selects a compatible PTX target (e.g., `-arch=compute_80` on the tested course TACC node with CUDA 11.0). Compile on the assigned GPU node.

## TACC remote testing

The supplied configuration has been verified on course TACC. It requests one GPU in the tacc partition and uses the CUDA tools on that node. The SDK creates or reuses an empty `cuda-attention-v1` environment.

Configure your course account once:
```
tcloud config -u <username> -f <private_key_path>
tcloud init
```

In the directory containing `tuxiv.conf`, submit a testing job and inspect its result:
```
tcloud submit
tcloud ps -j JOB_ID
tcloud cat slurm_log/assignment2-sdk-JOB_ID.log
```

Submission uploads the directory and invokes `sdk-test.sh` on the allocated GPU node to compile and run all tests. Running `tcloud submit` is only a test; it does not submit the final assignment to Canvas.

## Input file format and a worked example

An input file starts with `M N d`, followed by $M$ rows of $Q$, $N$ rows of $K$, and $N$ rows of $V$. Each matrix row contains $d$ numbers.

Example: $Q = [1]$, $K = [1000; 1001; 1002]$, $V = [0; 1; 2]$. Stable softmax uses the shifted scores $[-2, -1, 0]$. The expected output is approximately:
```
RESULT 1 1
1.57521038
```

This example is included as `dataset/stable_positive.txt`. Output formatting is handled by the supplied runner; do not print debugging messages to standard output.

## Submission format

Complete and test `attention.cu`, add identification comments, and rename the file to `student_id.cu` (e.g., `20991234.cu`). Upload this single CUDA source file to Canvas before the deadline.

Do not submit a ZIP archive, executable, output file, testing log, screenshot, or additional source/header files. The supplied interface and runner will be provided during assessment.

## Grading scheme

The supplied 12 tests form the evaluation suite. Basic tests cover ordinary inputs and matrix shapes; stability tests include large positive and negative scores. Scoring is by test group, not proportional to the number of passed tests. Source code may be inspected for compliance. No performance or speedup measurement is included.

| Score | Requirements |
|-------|--------------|
| 15 points | Passes all 7 basic tests and all 5 numerical-stability tests, and complies with CUDA/library requirements |
| 10 points | Passes all 7 basic tests but fails one or more of the 5 numerical-stability tests, while complying with CUDA/library requirements |
| 0 points | Fails any basic test, fails to compile or execute in the working assessment environment, or does not comply with CUDA/library requirements |

Use a Linux CUDA environment with an NVIDIA GPU, compatible driver, CUDA Toolkit, g++, make, Python 3.6+, and Bash. No third-party Python packages are required. In the extracted student-code directory:
```
source env/activate.sh
make test
```

A complete and stable implementation should end with:
```
BASIC: 7/7
STABLE: 5/5
SCORE: 15/15
ALL TESTS PASSED
```

The original skeleton deliberately returns zeros and is expected to fail. For individual runs:
```
make
./attention_cuda dataset/basic_small.txt
make cpu
./attention_seq dataset/basic_small.txt
```

The build automatically selects a compatible PTX target (e.g., `-arch=compute_80` on the tested course TACC node with CUDA 11.0). Compile on the assigned GPU node.

points.title: TACC remote testing
points.body_markdown:
The supplied configuration has been verified on course TACC. It requests one GPU in the tacc partition and uses the CUDA tools on that node. The SDK creates or reuses an empty `cuda-attention-v1` environment.

Configure your course account once:
```
tcloud config -u <username> -f <private_key_path>
tcloud init
```

In the directory containing `tuxiv.conf`, submit a testing job and inspect its result:
```
tcloud submit
tcloud ps -j JOB_ID
tcloud cat slurm_log/assignment2-sdk-JOB_ID.log
```

Submission uploads the directory and invokes `sdk-test.sh` on the allocated GPU node to compile and run all tests. Running `tcloud submit` is only a test; it does not submit the final assignment to Canvas.

points.title: Input file format and a worked example
points.body_markdown:
An input file starts with `M N d`, followed by $M$ rows of $Q$, $N$ rows of $K$, and $N$ rows of $V$. Each matrix row contains $d$ numbers.

Example: $Q = [1]$, $K = [1000; 1001; 1002]$, $V = [0; 1; 2]$. Stable softmax uses the shifted scores $[-2, -1, 0]$. The expected output is approximately:
```
RESULT 1 1
1.57521038
```

This example is included as `dataset/stable_positive.txt`. Output formatting is handled by the supplied runner; do not print debugging messages to standard output.

points.title: Submission format
points.body_markdown:
Complete and test `attention.cu`, add identification comments, and rename the file to `student_id.cu` (e.g., `20991234.cu`). Upload this single CUDA source file to Canvas before the deadline.

Do not submit a ZIP archive, executable, output file, testing log, screenshot, or additional source/header files. The supplied interface and runner will be provided during assessment.

points.title: Grading scheme
points.body_markdown:
The supplied 12 tests form the evaluation suite. Basic tests cover ordinary inputs and matrix shapes; stability tests include large positive and negative scores. Scoring is by test group, not proportional to the number of passed tests. Source code may be inspected for compliance. No performance or speedup measurement is included.

| Score | Requirements |
|-------|--------------|
| 15 points | Passes all 7 basic tests and all 5 numerical-stability tests, and complies with CUDA/library requirements |
| 10 points | Passes all 7 basic tests but fails one or more of the 5 numerical-stability tests, while complying with CUDA/library requirements |
| 0 points | Fails any basic test, fails to compile or execute in the working assessment environment, or does not comply with CUDA/library requirements |
