5. **Wait for the GPU**: `cudaDeviceSynchronize();`
6. **Copy results GPU → CPU**: `cudaMemcpy(C, d_C, bytes, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost)`
7. **Free GPU memory**: `cudaFree(d_A); cudaFree(d_B); cudaFree(d_C);`

The example uses `const int N = 8;` and `threadsPerBlock = 4`.

points.title: Thread indexing in a 1D kernel
points.body_markdown:
In the device code `__global__ void vectorAdd(int *A, int *B, int *C, int N)`, each CUDA thread computes one output element. Each thread gets its own index:

```c
int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
```

The thread then checks whether the index is valid, reads `A[i]` and `B[i]`, and writes `C[i]` (the computation is `C[i] = A[i] + B[i]`).

points.title: Attention mask addition as a 2D matrix operation
points.body_markdown:
The operation is element-wise addition of an attention score matrix and an attention mask:

$$S'_{i,j} = S_{i,j} + M_{i,j}, \qquad S, M, S' \in (\mathbb{R} \cup \{\pm\infty\})^{L \times L}$$

where `L` is the sequence length, `S` is the attention score matrix, and `M` is the attention mask. Example with a lower-triangular mask (0 on/below the diagonal, `-∞` above):

$$\begin{bmatrix}s_{00}&s_{01}&s_{02}&s_{03}\\ s_{10}&s_{11}&s_{12}&s_{13}\\ s_{20}&s_{21}&s_{22}&s_{23}\\ s_{30}&s_{31}&s_{32}&s_{33}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0&-\infty&-\infty&-\infty\\ 0&0&-\infty&-\infty\\ 0&0&0&-\infty\\ 0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}S_{00}&-\infty&-\infty&-\infty\\S_{10}&S_{11}&-\infty&-\infty\\S_{20}&S_{21}&S_{22}&-\infty\\S_{30}&S_{31}&S_{32}&S_{33}\end{bmatrix}$$

The same operation is applied independently to every `(row, col)`.

points.title: Mapping CUDA threads to 2D data
points.body_markdown:
For 2D data, the column and row of a thread are computed from the x and y dimensions of the grid and block:

```c
col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x
row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y
```

points.title: 2D CUDA kernel for mask addition
points.body_markdown:
The kernel `__global__ void addMask(const float *S, const float *M, float *out, int rows, int cols)` performs these steps per thread:

1. Find my row: `int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;`
2. Find my column: `int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;`
3. Check whether this matrix element exists: `if (row < rows && col < cols)`
4. Convert `(row, col)` to a linear memory index: `int index = row * cols + col;`
5. Compute one output element: `out[index] = S[index] + M[index];`

The overall mapping chain is: CUDA thread → `blockIdx + threadIdx` → `(row, col)` → linear index `row * cols + col` → one output `out[index]`.

points.title: Matrix multiplication in the attention formula
points.body_markdown:
Attention is defined as:

$$Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V$$

with

$$Q=\begin{bmatrix}q_{11}&q_{12}&\cdots&q_{1d_{k}}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ q_{L1}&q_{L2}&\cdots&q_{L d_{k}}\end{bmatrix},\quad K^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}k_{11}&k_{21}&\cdots&k_{L1}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ k_{1d_{k}}&k_{2d_{k}}&\cdots&k_{L d_{k}}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times L}$$

The score matrix is `S = Q Kᵀ ∈ ℝ^{L×L}`, whose entries are:

$$S_{ij}=Q_{i,:}K_{j,:}^{T}=[q_{i1}\quad \cdots \quad q_{id_{k}}]\begin{bmatrix}k_{j1}\\ \vdots\\ k_{jd_{k}}\end{bmatrix}=\sum_{r=1}^{d_{k}}q_{ir}k_{jr}\in\mathbb{R}$$

i.e. the mapping `(i,j) ↦ S_ij = Σ_r Q_ir K_jr`. The general matrix-multiply form shown is `C ← αAB + βC`.

points.title: Standard block matrix multiplication
points.body_markdown:
Partitioning `A`, `B`, `C` into 2×2 blocks:

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\ A_{21}&A_{22}\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}B_{11}&B_{12}\\ B_{21}&B_{22}\end{bmatrix},\quad C=AB=\begin{bmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\ C_{21}&C_{22}\end{bmatrix}$$

$$C_{11} = A_{11}B_{11} + A_{12}B_{21}$$
$$C_{12} = A_{11}B_{12} + A_{12}B_{22}$$
$$C_{21} = A_{21}B_{11} + A_{22}B_{21}$$
$$C_{22} = A_{21}B_{12} + A_{22}B_{22}$$

This needs **8 block multiplications + 4 block additions**, with complexity Θ(N³). The motivation given: addition is easy (e.g. 304040 + 505040 = 809080), while multiplication is hard to do mentally (e.g. 304040 × 505040).

points.title: Strassen's algorithm
points.body_markdown:
Strassen's idea (1969) uses **seven intermediate products** (only 7 block multiplications):

$$M_{1}=(A_{11}+A_{22})(B_{11}+B_{22})$$
$$M_{2}=(A_{21}+A_{22})B_{11}$$
$$M_{3}=A_{11}(B_{12}-B_{22})$$
$$M_{4}=A_{22}(B_{21}-B_{11})$$
$$M_{5}=(A_{11}+A_{12})B_{22}$$
$$M_{6}=(A_{21}-A_{11})(B_{11}+B_{12})$$
$$M_{7}=(A_{12}-A_{22})(B_{21}+B_{22})$$

Recombine to get the blocks of `C = AB`:

$$C_{11} = M_{1}+M_{4}-M_{5}+M_{7}$$
$$C_{12} = M_{3}+M_{5}$$
$$C_{21} = M_{2}+M_{4}$$
$$C_{22} = M_{1}-M_{2}+M_{3}+M_{6}$$

It needs 7 block multiplications but more additions/subtractions, giving complexity Θ(n^{log₂7}) = Θ(n^{2.807}) — trading cheaper additions for fewer expensive multiplications.

points.title: Sparse matrices: definition and storage formats
points.body_markdown:
A sparse matrix has most entries equal to zero; only a small fraction are nonzero (e.g. 5 nonzeros out of 25 entries = 20%). A dense view stores every entry; a sparse view stores only nonzero values + positions.

**Coordinate format (COO)**: store a list of `(row, column, value)` for each nonzero. Example for the 5×5 matrix with nonzeros 4, -2, 3, 5, 1:

| values | 4 | -2 | 3 | 5 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| row index | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| col index | 3 | 5 | 1 | 4 | 2 |

**Compressed Sparse Row (CSR)**: store values and column indices, with a row pointer:

| values | 4 | -2 | 3 | 5 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| col index | 3 | 5 | 1 | 4 | 2 |
| row pointer | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |

points.title: Sparse computation: SpMV and SpMM
points.body_markdown:
Sparse matrix-vector multiplication `y = Ax` skips multiplications by zero (uses only nonzeros), reducing both storage and computation and requiring fewer memory accesses. Worked example:

$$\begin{bmatrix}4&0&4&0&3&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\ 0\\ 5\\ 0\\ 5\\ 0\end{bmatrix}$$

Dense evaluation: `4×4 + 0×0 + 4×5 + 0×0 + 3×5 + 0×0 = 51` (6 multiplications + 5 additions). Sparse evaluation: `4×4 + 4×5 + 3×5 = 51` (3 multiplications + 2 additions — faster).

Common kernels are **SpMV** (`A x`) and **SpMM** (`A B`). Performance depends on the sparsity pattern and memory access regularity.

points.title: How to think in CUDA: the four-step learning path
points.body_markdown:
A simple learning path for writing CUDA kernels:

1. **Find independent work**
2. **Map work to threads**
3. **Compute the index** — 1D: `i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`; 2D: `col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`, `row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y`
4. **Write one output**

Examples: the 1D example is `vectorAdd`; the 2D example is `addMask`. For these introductory element-wise kernels, each thread owns one output element — the key question is always the same whether the data is 1D or 2D.

documents.markdown:
This tutorial document for CSIT6000V covers the progression from basic GPU matrix multiplication to the Flash Attention algorithm. It begins by reviewing GEMM operations and detailing the implementation of shared-memory tiling to optimize data access patterns. The material then transitions to the Softmax operator, explaining the derivation of stable and online variants to handle numerical stability and parallel computation. Finally, it synthesizes these concepts to demonstrate how Flash Attention combines tiled GEMM and online softmax to achieve efficient attention computation.

## Naive CUDA GEMM: one thread per output element

The naive GEMM kernel computes `S = QK^T` with one CUDA thread per output element `S[row][col]`.

- Thread indices are derived from the block/grid: `col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`, `row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y`.
- A bounds check `if (row < L && col < L)` guards valid outputs.
- Each thread accumulates `sum` over `k` from `0` to `dk`, using `Q[row * dk + k] * K[col * dk + k]` (row `col` of `K` equals column `col` of `K^T`).
- The result is stored at `S[row * L + col]`.

The matrix product definition used is:

$$(i,j) \mapsto S_{ij} = \sum_{r=1}^{d_k} Q_{ir} K_{jr}$$

with $S_{ij} = Q_{i,:}K_{j,:}^{T} \in \mathbb{R}$.

## Matrix addition kernel and the standard CUDA program flow

The `matrixAdd` example shows the full host/device workflow for a 2-D elementwise kernel.

Kernel body:
- Compute `col` and `row` from block/thread indices.
- Bounds check `row < rows && col < cols`.
- Flatten the index: `index = row * cols + col`, then `C[index] = A[index] + B[index]`.

Host program steps:
1. Prepare data on the CPU (arrays `A`, `B`, `C`, `N = rows * cols`, `bytes = N * sizeof(int)`).
2. Allocate GPU memory with `cudaMalloc((void **)&d_A, bytes)` (and similarly for `d_B`, `d_C`).
3. Copy inputs to the GPU with `cudaMemcpy(..., cudaMemcpyHostToDevice)`.
4. Launch the kernel with a 2-D configuration: `dim3 threadsPerBlock(2, 2)` and `dim3 blocks((cols + threadsPerBlock.x - 1) / threadsPerBlock.x, (rows + threadsPerBlock.y - 1) / threadsPerBlock.y)`.
5. Wait for the GPU with `cudaDeviceSynchronize()`.
6. Copy results back with `cudaMemcpy(..., cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost)` and print.

## Naive matrix multiplication kernel

The `matrixMul` example follows the same host workflow as `matrixAdd` but adds an inner reduction loop in the kernel.

- Thread mapping and bounds check are identical to `matrixAdd`.
- Each thread computes `sum` over `k` from `0` to `cols`: `sum += A[row * cols + k] * B[k * cols + col]`.
- The result is written to `C[index]` where `index = row * cols + col`.
- The same launch configuration (`threadsPerBlock(2, 2)`, ceiling-divided block counts) and the same six host steps (prepare, allocate, copy in, launch, synchronize, copy out) are used.

## Attention as two GEMMs plus a softmax

Attention decomposes into two GEMMs and one softmax:

$$Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

- GEMM 1: $S = QK^{T}$
- Softmax: $P = softmax\left(\frac{S}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)$
- GEMM 2: $O = PV$

## Naive GEMM data path and the global-memory bottleneck

In naive GEMM, inputs live in global memory and each thread independently loads `A` and `B` from global memory.

- The same input values are repeatedly fetched by different threads.
- Computation is cheap, so global-memory traffic becomes the bottleneck.

## Shared-memory tiling reduces global loads

Tiled GEMM is presented as the alternative to naive GEMM for computing $A \times B = C$ on 4×4 matrices.

- The example uses 4×4 matrices $A$, $B$, and $C$, with output elements such as $c_{00}$ and $c_{01}$.
- The goal is to compare the number of global loads between the naive and tiled versions.

## Counting global loads in naive GEMM

For the 4×4 example, each output element requires 4 loads of `A` and 4 loads of `B`.

- $C_{00} = a_{00}b_{00} + a_{01}b_{10} + a_{02}b_{20} + a_{03}b_{30}$: 4 loads of $A$ ($a_{00}a_{01}a_{02}a_{03}$) and 4 loads of $B$ ($b_{00}b_{10}b_{20}b_{30}$).
- $C_{01} = a_{00}b_{01} + a_{01}b_{11} + a_{02}b_{21} + a_{03}b_{31}$: 4 loads of $A$ and 4 loads of $B$ ($b_{01}b_{11}b_{21}b_{31}$).
- Each output element therefore costs 8 global loads in the naive scheme.

## Naive GEMM total load count across threads

The same per-output load pattern repeats for every output element.

- $C_{00}$ and $C_{01}$ each require 4 loads of $A$ and 4 loads of $B$.
- The naive scheme's total is 8 global loads per output element, and the slide contrasts this with the tiled scheme's total.

## Naive GEMM load count for a 2×2 thread group

Extending the count to a second row of outputs:

- $C_{00} = a_{00}b_{00} + a_{01}b_{10} + a_{02}b_{20} + a_{03}b_{30}$: 4 loads of $A$ ($a_{00}a_{01}a_{02}a_{03}$) and 4 loads of $B$ ($b_{00}b_{10}b_{20}b_{30}$).
- $C_{10} = a_{10}b_{00} + a_{11}b_{10} + a_{12}b_{20} + a_{13}b_{30}$: 4 loads of $A$ ($a_{10}a_{11}a_{12}a_{13}$) and 4 loads of $B$.
- The naive and tiled totals are again compared as 8 global loads each in this slide's framing.

## Naive GEMM: 32 global loads for four outputs

For the four outputs $C_{00}$, $C_{01}$, $C_{10}$, $C_{11}$:

$$C_{00}=a_{00}b_{00}+a_{01}b_{10}+a_{02}b_{20}+a_{03}b_{30}$$
$$C_{01}=a_{00}b_{01}+a_{01}b_{11}+a_{02}b_{21}+a_{03}b_{31}$$
$$C_{10}=a_{10}b_{00}+a_{11}b_{10}+a_{12}b_{20}+a_{13}b_{30}$$
$$C_{11}=a_{10}b_{01}+a_{11}b_{11}+a_{12}b_{21}+a_{13}b_{31}$$

Per-thread load counts:

| Thread | A loads | B loads | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| T00 | 4 | 4 | 8 |
| T01 | 4 | 4 | 8 |
| T10 | 4 | 4 | 8 |
| T11 | 4 | 4 | 8 |
| Total | 16 | 16 | 32 global loads |

## Tiled GEMM: sharing tiles cuts loads from 32 to 16

Tiling exploits the fact that rows of `A` and rows of `B` can be shared across threads.

- The K dimension is split into tiles: $A_{tile1} = \begin{bmatrix}a_{00}&a_{01}\\a_{10}&a_{11}\end{bmatrix}$, $B_{tile1} = \begin{bmatrix}b_{00}&b_{01}\\b_{10}&b_{11}\end{bmatrix}$, and $A_{tile2} = \begin{bmatrix}a_{02}&a_{03}\\a_{12}&a_{13}\end{bmatrix}$, $B_{tile2} = \begin{bmatrix}b_{02}&b_{03}\\b_{12}&b_{13}\end{bmatrix}$.
- Each output accumulates partial sums per tile: $C_{00}^{(0)} = a_{00}b_{00} + a_{01}b_{10}$ from tile 1 and $C_{00}^{(1)} = a_{02}b_{20} + a_{03}b_{30}$ from tile 2, which combine into $C_{00}$.
- Load count: $4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16$ global loads, less than the 32 global loads of the naive version.

## Tiled GEMM load comparison (restated)

The same tiling example is restated with the same arithmetic and the same conclusion.

- Outputs $C_{00}$, $C_{01}$, $C_{11}$ are expanded as sums of products of $a$ and $b$ entries.
- Rows of `A` and rows of `B` can be shared across threads.
- The two tiles $A_{tile1}, B_{tile1}$ and $A_{tile2}, B_{tile2}$ split the K dimension, and partial results $C_{00}^{(0)}$, $C_{00}^{(1)}$ combine into $C_{00}$.
- Total: $4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16$ global loads < 32 global loads.

## Tiled GEMM kernel structure

The `tiledGEMM` kernel computes `C = A * B` with `TILE_SIZE 16`, one thread per output element `C[row][col]`.

Setup:
- Declare shared tiles `__shared__ float As[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];` and `__shared__ float Bs[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];`.
- Thread position in the block: `tx = threadIdx.x`, `ty = threadIdx.y`.
- Output element: `col = blockIdx.x * TILE_SIZE + tx`, `row = blockIdx.y * TILE_SIZE + ty`.
- Initialize `sum = 0.0f`.

Main loop over K tiles, `for (int t = 0; t < (N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE; t++)`:

1. Global → shared:
   - `A_col = t * TILE_SIZE + tx`; if `row < N && A_col < N`, load `As[ty][tx] = A[row * N + A_col]`, else `As[ty][tx] = 0.0f`.
   - `B_row = t * TILE_SIZE + ty`; if `B_row < N && col < N`, load `Bs[ty][tx] = B[B_row * N + col]`, else `Bs[ty][tx] = 0.0f`.
   - `__syncthreads()` to wait until the whole tile is loaded.
2. Compute from shared memory: `for (int k = 0; k < TILE_SIZE; k++) sum += As[ty][k] * Bs[k][tx];`
3. `__syncthreads()` again so all threads finish using the tile before the next tile is loaded.

Write-out:
- If `row < N && col < N`, store `C[row * N + col] = sum;`.

## Shared-memory tiling GEMM: thread and block indexing

The kernel `tiledGEMM` computes `C = A * B` with each CUDA thread producing one output element `C[row][col]`.

- `tx = threadIdx.x` and `ty = threadIdx.y` give the thread's x/y coordinate inside its thread block.
- The output element handled by the thread is located by:
  - `col = blockIdx.x * TILE_SIZE + tx`
  - `row = blockIdx.y * TILE_SIZE + ty`
- The accumulator is initialized as `float sum = 0.0f;`.

## Shared-memory tile allocation

Two shared-memory tiles are declared inside the kernel:

```c
__shared__ float As[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];
__shared__ float Bs[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];
```

- `As` holds a tile of matrix A and `Bs` holds a tile of matrix B.
- The tile size is set by `#define TILE_SIZE 16`.

## Looping over the K dimension tile by tile

The kernel moves along the K dimension one tile at a time:

```c
for (int t = 0; t < (N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE; t++)
```

- The loop bound `(N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE` is the number of tiles needed to cover N elements (ceiling division).
- Each iteration loads one A tile and one B tile, then computes the partial products for that tile.

## Loading the A tile from global to shared memory

Each thread loads one element of A into `As`:

```c
int A_col = t * TILE_SIZE + tx;
if (row < N && A_col < N)
    As[ty][tx] = A[row * N + A_col];
else
    As[ty][tx] = 0.0f;
```

- The column index within A is `t * TILE_SIZE + tx`.
- Out-of-range positions are filled with `0.0f`, so boundary tiles do not read invalid memory and contribute zero to the sum.

## Loading the B tile from global to shared memory

Each thread loads one element of B into `Bs`:

```c
int B_row = t * TILE_SIZE + ty;
if (B_row < N && col < N)
    Bs[ty][tx] = B[B_row * N + col];
else
    Bs[ty][tx] = 0.0f;
```

- The row index within B is `t * TILE_SIZE + ty`.
- As with A, out-of-range positions are set to `0.0f`.

## Synchronization after loading a tile

`__syncthreads()` is called after the A and B tiles have been loaded:

```c
// Wait until the whole tile has been loaded
__syncthreads();
```

- All threads in the block wait here until the entire A tile and B tile have been loaded into shared memory (page 19).
- This ensures no thread reads a shared-memory element before it has been written.

## Computing with data in shared memory

After the barrier, each thread accumulates over the tile:

```c
for (int k = 0; k < TILE_SIZE; k++)
{
    sum += As[ty][k] * Bs[k][tx];
}
```

- The thread multiplies one element from its row of A's tile with one element from its column of B's tile (page 20).
- The products are accumulated into `sum` across all k in the tile.

## Synchronization before loading the next tile

A second `__syncthreads()` follows the compute loop:

```c
// Make sure all threads finish using this tile
// before loading the next tile
__syncthreads();
```

- This prevents any thread from overwriting shared-memory tiles that other threads are still reading.

## Writing the final result to global memory

After the loop over all tiles, the accumulated sum is written out:

```c
if (row < N && col < N)
{
    C[row * N + col] = sum;
}
```

- The bounds check ensures only valid output elements are written.

## From max to softmax

Given scores such as `[1.2, 2.0, 3.8]`:

- MAX chooses the winning class (Class C) but gives only the winner.
- Softmax performs a non-linear normalization: it maps arbitrary real numbers to non-negative values that sum to 1, so they can be interpreted as probabilities.

$$Softmax(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\exp(x_1)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}\\ \frac{\exp(x_2)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\exp(x_n)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{V}\frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}=1$$

- Example: `softmax([1.2, 2.0, 3.8]) = [0.06, 0.13, 0.81]`.

## Overflow problem in softmax

The denominator $\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)$ may overflow.

Example with $x=(1000, 1001, 1002)$:

- $d=\exp(1000)+\exp(1001)+\exp(1002)$
- $\exp(1000)\approx 1.97\times 10^{434}$
- $\max(float64)\approx 1.8\times 10^{308}<\exp(1000)$

So the exponentials can exceed the representable range of the floating-point type.

## Stable softmax

Stable softmax subtracts $m=\max_j(x_j)$ before exponentiating:

$$x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\\vdots\\x_n\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\xrightarrow{\text{Input}}\text{Stable}\xrightarrow{\text{Output}}Y=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\exp(x_1-m)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j-m)}\\ \frac{\exp(x_2-m)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j-m)}\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\exp(x_n-m)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j-m)}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$$

- $m$ is denoted as $m=\max_j(x_j)$.
- The subtraction shifts the exponents so the largest term becomes $\exp(0)=1$, avoiding overflow.

## Translation invariance of softmax

Softmax is invariant to adding/subtracting a constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$ to every input element. With $\tilde{x}_i = x_i - c$:

$$\text{softmax}(\tilde{x})_i = \frac{\exp(x_i - c)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j - c)} = \frac{\exp(x_i)\exp(-c)}{\exp(-c)\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)} = \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)} = \text{softmax}(x)_i$$

In vector form: $\text{softmax}(\mathbf{X}) = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{X} - c\mathbf{1})$, where $\mathbf{1}$ is the all-ones vector. This property is what makes the max-subtraction trick valid.

## Choosing the shift constant $c$ to prevent overflow and underflow

- To prevent overflow, we require $\sum_j \exp(x_j - c) < \text{Float}_{max}$ and $\exp(x_j - c) < \text{Float}_{max}$, which implies $c \geq \max_j x_j - \log \text{Float}_{max}$.
- To avoid catastrophic underflow, choose $c$ such that $\max_j(x_j - c) = 0$, i.e., $c = m = \max_j(x_j)$.
- The resulting stable softmax is:

$$\text{StableSoftmax}(X) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\exp(x_1)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j - m)} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j - m)} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^n, \quad m = \max_j(x_j)$$

## Stable softmax workflow: elementwise exponentiation with max-subtraction

The workflow takes an input vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ and performs elementwise normalization $z_i = \exp(x_i - m)$. The work is distributed across threads (Thread 0 through Thread 7 shown), i.e., the elementwise exponentiation step is parallelized across threads.

## Stable softmax workflow: three-stage pipeline (MAX → SUM → normalize)

The full pipeline for the input vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}$:

1. **MAX reduction**: compute $m = \max_i x_i$.
2. **Elementwise exponentiation with max-subtraction**: compute $\exp(x_i - m)$ for each element, then **SUM reduction**: $s = \sum_i \exp(x_i - m)$.
3. **Elementwise normalization**: output $z_i / s$ to produce the softmax.

The document also shows the start of an `expKernel` with the standard thread-index pattern `int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;`.

## Naive stable softmax kernel: structure and dependencies

The naive stable softmax kernel assigns one block per softmax vector (`row = blockIdx.x`), with `input = x + row * N` and `output = y + row * N`. It uses shared variables `m` and `d` shared by all threads in the block.

- **Pass 1** (sequential, thread 0 only): find the maximum $m = \max_i x_i$.
- **Pass 2** (sequential, thread 0 only): compute the normalizer $d = \sum_j \exp(x_j - m)$.
- `__syncthreads()` waits until `m` and `d` are ready.
- **Pass 3** (parallel across threads): compute final values with a strided loop `for (int j = threadIdx.x; j < N; j += blockDim.x)`, setting `output[j] = expf(input[j] - m) / d`.

The dependency structure: $m = \max_{i \in A} x_i$ and $d = \sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j - m)$ must both be known before any output $y_i = \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j - m)}$ can be computed.

## Stable softmax requires two reductions over two scans of the input

The stable softmax pipeline needs:

1. **MAX reduction** → $m$ (first scan of the input).
2. **Compute exponentials and SUM reduction** → $s = \sum_i \exp(x_i - m)$ (second scan of the input).
3. **Normalize**: $\text{softmax}_i = \frac{\exp(x_i - m)}{s}$.

Every output needs both $m$ and $s$, so the naive approach requires two passes over the input. The document also shows the incremental forms $m_{j-1} = \max_{1 \leq i \leq j-1} x_i$ and $d_{j-1} = \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} e^{x_i - m_{j-1}}$, and the update $d_j = \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} e^{x_i - m_{j-1} + m_{j-1} - m_j} + e^{x_j - m_j}$.

## Online softmax: state variables and their meaning

Online softmax processes elements one at a time, carrying a running state. The transition takes input $m_{j-1}$, $\hat{d}_{j-1}$, $x_j$ and outputs $m_j$, $d_j$:

- $x_j$: the current input element being processed.
- $m_{j-1}$: the maximum of the first $j-1$ input elements.
- $m_j$: the maximum of the first $j$ input elements.
- $\hat{d}_{j-1}$: the previously stored normalizer for the first $j-1$ elements, computed using the **old** maximum $m_{j-1}$.
- $d_{j-1}$: the previously stored normalizer for the first $j-1$ elements, computed using the **new** maximum $m_j$.
- $d_j$: the normalizer for the first $j$ elements, computed using the new maximum $m_j$.

## Online softmax update rule

The online softmax recurrence:

$$m_j = \max(m_{j-1}, x_j)$$

$$d_j = \sum_{i=1}^{j} e^{x_i - m_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} e^{x_i - m_{j-1} + m_{j-1} - m_j} + e^{x_j - m_j} = e^{m_{j-1} - m_j}\hat{d}_{j-1} + e^{x_j - m_j}$$

Key intermediate step: rescaling the old normalizer with the new maximum, $d_{j-1} = e^{m_{j-1} - m_j}\hat{d}_{j-1}$, so that $d_j = d_{j-1} + e^{x_j - m_j}$.

This lets the maximum and normalizer be updated **together in a single pass** over the input, instead of two separate scans.

## Naive online softmax kernel

The naive online softmax kernel keeps one block per softmax vector and shared state `m`, `d`. In **Pass 1** (thread 0 only), it updates the running maximum and normalizer together in one loop:

```c
for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
    float m_new = fmaxf(m, input[j]);
    d = d * expf(m - m_new) + expf(input[j] - m_new);
    m = m_new;
}
```

After `__syncthreads()`, **Pass 2** computes the final values in parallel: `output[j] = expf(input[j] - m) / d`.

This implements $m_j = \max(m_{j-1}, x_j)$ and $d_j = \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} e^{x_i - m_{j-1} + m_{j-1} - m_j} + e^{x_j - m_j}$.

## Parallel online softmax: combining two subsets' states

For two disjoint subsets $A$ and $B$ with per-subset states:

- $m_A = \max_{i \in A} x_i$, $d_A = \sum_{i \in A} e^{x_i - m_A}$
- $m_B = \max_{i \in B} x_i$, $d_B = \sum_{i \in B} e^{x_i - m_B}$

The combined state for $A \cup B$ is $m = \max_{i \in A \cup B} x_i$ and $d = \sum_{i \in A \cup B} e^{x_i - m}$.

- $m_A$, $m_B$: maxima of sets $A$ and $B$; $m$: maximum of $A$ and $B$.
- $d_A$, $d_B$: previously stored normalizers for sets $A$ and $B$; $d$: new stored normalizer for $A \cup B$.

## Parallel online softmax: the merge (⊕) operator

The merge of two states is:

$$m = \max(m_A, m_B)$$

$$d = \sum_{i \in A \cup B} e^{x_i - m} = \sum_{i \in A} e^{x_i - m} + \sum_{i \in B} e^{x_i - m} = e^{m_A - m}\sum_{i \in A} e^{x_i - m_A} + e^{m_B - m}\sum_{i \in B} e^{x_i - m_B} = d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m}$$

Defining the associative combine operator:

$$(m_A, d_A) \oplus (m_B, d_B) = \left(m,\ d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m}\right)$$

This operator allows partial softmax states to be computed independently and then merged.

## Parallel online softmax kernel: splitting work across threads

The parallel online softmax kernel splits the vector at `mid = N / 2` and uses shared state `mA, dA, mB, dB, m, d`:

- **Thread 0** computes the online state $(m_A, d_A)$ over the first half `[0, mid)` using the same running update loop.
- **Thread 1** computes the online state $(m_B, d_B)$ over the second half `[mid, N)`.
- After `__syncthreads()`, **thread 0** merges the two states: `m = fmaxf(mA, mB); d = dA * expf(mA - m) + dB * expf(mB - m);`
- After a second `__syncthreads()`, all threads compute the final values in parallel with the strided loop: `output[j] = expf(input[j] - m) / d`.

This implements the combine operator $(m_A, d_A) \oplus (m_B, d_B) = (m,\ d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m})$ in code, with the two halves representing "one subset" and "another subset" of the input.

## Naive attention computation and its cost

Attention is defined as:

\[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
\]

The naive implementation proceeds in three materialized steps:

\[
S = QK^{T}, \quad P = \text{softmax}(S), \quad O = PV
\]

### Why naive attention is slow

- It materializes the full score matrix \(S = QK^{T}\) and the probability matrix \(P = \text{softmax}(S)\).
- This causes high HBM traffic: write \(S\), read \(S\), write \(P\), read \(P\).
- Time and memory grow quadratically with sequence length: \(O(N^2)\).

## FlashAttention idea 1: tiled GEMM

Instead of materializing the full \(N \times N\) matrix, FlashAttention computes \(QK^{T}\) and \(PV\) block by block.

- Blockwise computation of \(Q_i K_j^{T}\).
- The full score matrix is never materialized.

## FlashAttention idea 2: online softmax

Running statistics are maintained while scanning blocks, rather than computing softmax over a fully materialized score matrix.

The combination rule for two block statistics \((m_A, d_A)\) and \((m_B, d_B)\) is:

\[
(m_A, d_A) \oplus (m_B, d_B) = (m,\; d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m})
\]

## Why FlashAttention is faster

- No full attention matrix is stored in HBM.
- Much lower memory traffic.
- It computes exact attention, not an approximation.

## Scope of the teaching kernel vs. real FlashAttention-1

The explained core algorithmic idea is tiled GEMM plus online softmax:

- Avoid writing the full \(S = QK^{T}\) and \(P = \text{softmax}(S)\).
- Maintain running \(m\) and \(l\) while scanning tiles.

A small teaching kernel shows the math, not production scheduling.

### What real FlashAttention-1 adds

- One fused kernel: \(QK^{T} \rightarrow\) online softmax \(\rightarrow PV\).
- Careful SRAM/shared-memory/register tiling.
- Backward pass with recomputation to save memory.
- Causal mask, dropout, variable length, and occupancy details.

## FlashAttention evolves with GPU architecture

FlashAttention evolves with GPU architecture.
documents.intro_markdown: This tutorial document for CSIT6000V covers the progression from basic GPU matrix multiplication to the Flash Attention algorithm. It begins by reviewing GEMM operations and detailing the implementation of shared-memory tiling to optimize data access patterns. The material then transitions to the Softmax operator, explaining the derivation of stable and online variants to handle numerical stability and parallel computation. Finally, it synthesizes these concepts to demonstrate how Flash Attention combines tiled GEMM and online softmax to achieve efficient attention computation.
documents.title: Tutorial_4

points.title: Naive CUDA GEMM: one thread per output element
points.body_markdown:
The naive GEMM kernel computes `S = QK^T` with one CUDA thread per output element `S[row][col]`.

- Thread indices are derived from the block/grid: `col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`, `row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y`.
- A bounds check `if (row < L && col < L)` guards valid outputs.
- Each thread accumulates `sum` over `k` from `0` to `dk`, using `Q[row * dk + k] * K[col * dk + k]` (row `col` of `K` equals column `col` of `K^T`).
- The result is stored at `S[row * L + col]`.

The matrix product definition used is:

$$(i,j) \mapsto S_{ij} = \sum_{r=1}^{d_k} Q_{ir} K_{jr}$$

with $S_{ij} = Q_{i,:}K_{j,:}^{T} \in \mathbb{R}$.

points.title: Matrix addition kernel and the standard CUDA program flow
points.body_markdown:
The `matrixAdd` example shows the full host/device workflow for a 2-D elementwise kernel.

Kernel body:
- Compute `col` and `row` from block/thread indices.
- Bounds check `row < rows && col < cols`.
- Flatten the index: `index = row * cols + col`, then `C[index] = A[index] + B[index]`.

Host program steps:
1. Prepare data on the CPU (arrays `A`, `B`, `C`, `N = rows * cols`, `bytes = N * sizeof(int)`).
2. Allocate GPU memory with `cudaMalloc((void **)&d_A, bytes)` (and similarly for `d_B`, `d_C`).
3. Copy inputs to the GPU with `cudaMemcpy(..., cudaMemcpyHostToDevice)`.
4. Launch the kernel with a 2-D configuration: `dim3 threadsPerBlock(2, 2)` and `dim3 blocks((cols + threadsPerBlock.x - 1) / threadsPerBlock.x, (rows + threadsPerBlock.y - 1) / threadsPerBlock.y)`.
5. Wait for the GPU with `cudaDeviceSynchronize()`.
6. Copy results back with `cudaMemcpy(..., cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost)` and print.

points.title: Naive matrix multiplication kernel
points.body_markdown:
The `matrixMul` example follows the same host workflow as `matrixAdd` but adds an inner reduction loop in the kernel.

- Thread mapping and bounds check are identical to `matrixAdd`.
- Each thread computes `sum` over `k` from `0` to `cols`: `sum += A[row * cols + k] * B[k * cols + col]`.
- The result is written to `C[index]` where `index = row * cols + col`.
- The same launch configuration (`threadsPerBlock(2, 2)`, ceiling-divided block counts) and the same six host steps (prepare, allocate, copy in, launch, synchronize, copy out) are used.

points.title: Attention as two GEMMs plus a softmax
points.body_markdown:
Attention decomposes into two GEMMs and one softmax:

$$Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

- GEMM 1: $S = QK^{T}$
- Softmax: $P = softmax\left(\frac{S}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)$
- GEMM 2: $O = PV$

points.title: Naive GEMM data path and the global-memory bottleneck
points.body_markdown:
In naive GEMM, inputs live in global memory and each thread independently loads `A` and `B` from global memory.

- The same input values are repeatedly fetched by different threads.
- Computation is cheap, so global-memory traffic becomes the bottleneck.

points.title: Shared-memory tiling reduces global loads
points.body_markdown:
Tiled GEMM is presented as the alternative to naive GEMM for computing $A \times B = C$ on 4×4 matrices.

- The example uses 4×4 matrices $A$, $B$, and $C$, with output elements such as $c_{00}$ and $c_{01}$.
- The goal is to compare the number of global loads between the naive and tiled versions.

points.title: Counting global loads in naive GEMM
points.body_markdown:
For the 4×4 example, each output element requires 4 loads of `A` and 4 loads of `B`.

- $C_{00} = a_{00}b_{00} + a_{01}b_{10} + a_{02}b_{20} + a_{03}b_{30}$: 4 loads of $A$ ($a_{00}a_{01}a_{02}a_{03}$) and 4 loads of $B$ ($b_{00}b_{10}b_{20}b_{30}$).
- $C_{01} = a_{00}b_{01} + a_{01}b_{11} + a_{02}b_{21} + a_{03}b_{31}$: 4 loads of $A$ and 4 loads of $B$ ($b_{01}b_{11}b_{21}b_{31}$).
- Each output element therefore costs 8 global loads in the naive scheme.

points.title: Naive GEMM total load count across threads
points.body_markdown:
The same per-output load pattern repeats for every output element.

- $C_{00}$ and $C_{01}$ each require 4 loads of $A$ and 4 loads of $B$.
- The naive scheme's total is 8 global loads per output element, and the slide contrasts this with the tiled scheme's total.

points.title: Naive GEMM load count for a 2×2 thread group
points.body_markdown:
Extending the count to a second row of outputs:

- $C_{00} = a_{00}b_{00} + a_{01}b_{10} + a_{02}b_{20} + a_{03}b_{30}$: 4 loads of $A$ ($a_{00}a_{01}a_{02}a_{03}$) and 4 loads of $B$ ($b_{00}b_{10}b_{20}b_{30}$).
- $C_{10} = a_{10}b_{00} + a_{11}b_{10} + a_{12}b_{20} + a_{13}b_{30}$: 4 loads of $A$ ($a_{10}a_{11}a_{12}a_{13}$) and 4 loads of $B$.
- The naive and tiled totals are again compared as 8 global loads each in this slide's framing.

points.title: Naive GEMM: 32 global loads for four outputs
Tiled GEMM: sharing tiles cuts loads from 32 to 16
points.body_markdown:
Tiling exploits the fact that rows of `A` and rows of `B` can be shared across threads.

- The K dimension is split into tiles: $A_{tile1} = \begin{bmatrix}a_{00}&a_{01}\\a_{10}&a_{11}\end{bmatrix}$, $B_{tile1} = \begin{bmatrix}b_{00}&b_{01}\\b_{10}&b_{11}\end{bmatrix}$, and $A_{tile2} = \begin{bmatrix}a_{02}&a_{03}\\a_{12}&a_{13}\end{bmatrix}$, $B_{tile2} = \begin{bmatrix}b_{02}&b_{03}\\b_{12}&b_{13}\end{bmatrix}$.
- Each output accumulates partial sums per tile: $C_{00}^{(0)} = a_{00}b_{00} + a_{01}b_{10}$ from tile 1 and $C_{00}^{(1)} = a_{02}b_{20} + a_{03}b_{30}$ from tile 2, which combine into $C_{00}$.
- Load count: $4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16$ global loads, less than the 32 global loads of the naive version.

points.title: Tiled GEMM load comparison (restated)
points.body_markdown:
The same tiling example is restated with the same arithmetic and the same conclusion.

- Outputs $C_{00}$, $C_{01}$, $C_{11}$ are expanded as sums of products of $a$ and $b$ entries.
- Rows of `A` and rows of `B` can be shared across threads.
- The two tiles $A_{tile1}, B_{tile1}$ and $A_{tile2}, B_{tile2}$ split the K dimension, and partial results $C_{00}^{(0)}$, $C_{00}^{(1)}$ combine into $C_{00}$.
- Total: $4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16$ global loads < 32 global loads.

points.title: Tiled GEMM kernel structure
points.body_markdown:
The `tiledGEMM` kernel computes `C = A * B` with `TILE_SIZE 16`, one thread per output element `C[row][col]`.

Setup:
- Declare shared tiles `__shared__ float As[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];` and `__shared__ float Bs[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];`.
- Thread position in the block: `tx = threadIdx.x`, `ty = threadIdx.y`.
- Output element: `col = blockIdx.x * TILE_SIZE + tx`, `row = blockIdx.y * TILE_SIZE + ty`.
- Initialize `sum = 0.0f`.

Main loop over K tiles, `for (int t = 0; t < (N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE; t++)`:

1. Global → shared:
   - `A_col = t * TILE_SIZE + tx`; if `row < N && A_col < N`, load `As[ty][tx] = A[row * N + A_col]`, else `As[ty][tx] = 0.0f`.
   - `B_row = t * TILE_SIZE + ty`; if `B_row < N && col < N`, load `Bs[ty][tx] = B[B_row * N + col]`, else `Bs[ty][tx] = 0.0f`.
   - `__syncthreads()` to wait until the whole tile is loaded.
2. Compute from shared memory: `for (int k = 0; k < TILE_SIZE; k++) sum += As[ty][k] * Bs[k][tx];`
3. `__syncthreads()` again so all threads finish using the tile before the next tile is loaded.

Write-out:
- If `row < N && col < N`, store `C[row * N + col] = sum;`.

points.title: Shared-memory tiling GEMM: thread and block indexing
points.body_markdown:
The kernel `tiledGEMM` computes `C = A * B` with each CUDA thread producing one output element `C[row][col]`.

- `tx = threadIdx.x` and `ty = threadIdx.y` give the thread's x/y coordinate inside its thread block.
- The output element handled by the thread is located by:
  - `col = blockIdx.x * TILE_SIZE + tx`
  - `row = blockIdx.y * TILE_SIZE + ty`
- The accumulator is initialized as `float sum = 0.0f;`.

points.title: Shared-memory tile allocation
points.body_markdown:
Two shared-memory tiles are declared inside the kernel:

```c
__shared__ float As[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];
__shared__ float Bs[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];
```

- `As` holds a tile of matrix A and `Bs` holds a tile of matrix B.
- The tile size is set by `#define TILE_SIZE 16`.

points.title: Looping over the K dimension tile by tile
points.body_markdown:
The kernel moves along the K dimension one tile at a time:

```c
for (int t = 0; t < (N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE; t++)
```

- The loop bound `(N + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE` is the number of tiles needed to cover N elements (ceiling division).
- Each iteration loads one A tile and one B tile, then computes the partial products for that tile.

points.title: Loading the A tile from global to shared memory
Loading the B tile from global to shared memory
Synchronization after loading a tile
points.body_markdown:
`__syncthreads()` is called after the A and B tiles have been loaded:

```c
// Wait until the whole tile has been loaded
__syncthreads();
```

- All threads in the block wait here until the entire A tile and B tile have been loaded into shared memory (page 19).
- This ensures no thread reads a shared-memory element before it has been written.

points.title: Computing with data in shared memory
Synchronization before loading the next tile
Writing the final result to global memory
From max to softmax
points.body_markdown:
Given scores such as `[1.2, 2.0, 3.8]`:

- MAX chooses the winning class (Class C) but gives only the winner.
- Softmax performs a non-linear normalization: it maps arbitrary real numbers to non-negative values that sum to 1, so they can be interpreted as probabilities.

$$Softmax(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\exp(x_1)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}\\ \frac{\exp(x_2)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\exp(x_n)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{V}\frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)}=1$$

- Example: `softmax([1.2, 2.0, 3.8]) = [0.06, 0.13, 0.81]`.

points.title: Overflow problem in softmax
points.body_markdown:
The denominator $\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)$ may overflow.

Example with $x=(1000, 1001, 1002)$:

- $d=\exp(1000)+\exp(1001)+\exp(1002)$
- $\exp(1000)\approx 1.97\times 10^{434}$
- $\max(float64)\approx 1.8\times 10^{308}<\exp(1000)$

So the exponentials can exceed the representable range of the floating-point type.

points.title: Stable softmax
points.body_markdown:
Stable softmax subtracts $m=\max_j(x_j)$ before exponentiating:

$$x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\\vdots\\x_n\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\xrightarrow{\text{Input}}\text{Stable}\xrightarrow{\text{Output}}Y=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\exp(x_1-m)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j-m)}\\ \frac{\exp(x_2-m)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j-m)}\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\exp(x_n-m)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j-m)}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$$

- $m$ is denoted as $m=\max_j(x_j)$.
- The subtraction shifts the exponents so the largest term becomes $\exp(0)=1$, avoiding overflow.

points.title: Translation invariance of softmax
points.body_markdown:
Softmax is invariant to adding/subtracting a constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$ to every input element. With $\tilde{x}_i = x_i - c$:

$$\text{softmax}(\tilde{x})_i = \frac{\exp(x_i - c)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j - c)} = \frac{\exp(x_i)\exp(-c)}{\exp(-c)\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)} = \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j)} = \text{softmax}(x)_i$$

In vector form: $\text{softmax}(\mathbf{X}) = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{X} - c\mathbf{1})$, where $\mathbf{1}$ is the all-ones vector. This property is what makes the max-subtraction trick valid.

points.title: Choosing the shift constant $c$ to prevent overflow and underflow
points.body_markdown:
- To prevent overflow, we require $\sum_j \exp(x_j - c) < \text{Float}_{max}$ and $\exp(x_j - c) < \text{Float}_{max}$, which implies $c \geq \max_j x_j - \log \text{Float}_{max}$.
- To avoid catastrophic underflow, choose $c$ such that $\max_j(x_j - c) = 0$, i.e., $c = m = \max_j(x_j)$.
- The resulting stable softmax is:

$$\text{StableSoftmax}(X) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\exp(x_1)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j - m)} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j - m)} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^n, \quad m = \max_j(x_j)$$

points.title: Stable softmax workflow: elementwise exponentiation with max-subtraction
points.body_markdown: The workflow takes an input vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ and performs elementwise normalization $z_i = \exp(x_i - m)$. The work is distributed across threads (Thread 0 through Thread 7 shown), i.e., the elementwise exponentiation step is parallelized across threads.

points.title: Stable softmax workflow: three-stage pipeline (MAX → SUM → normalize)
points.body_markdown:
The full pipeline for the input vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}$:

1. **MAX reduction**: compute $m = \max_i x_i$.
2. **Elementwise exponentiation with max-subtraction**: compute $\exp(x_i - m)$ for each element, then **SUM reduction**: $s = \sum_i \exp(x_i - m)$.
3. **Elementwise normalization**: output $z_i / s$ to produce the softmax.

The document also shows the start of an `expKernel` with the standard thread-index pattern `int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;`.

points.title: Naive stable softmax kernel: structure and dependencies
points.body_markdown:
The naive stable softmax kernel assigns one block per softmax vector (`row = blockIdx.x`), with `input = x + row * N` and `output = y + row * N`. It uses shared variables `m` and `d` shared by all threads in the block.

- **Pass 1** (sequential, thread 0 only): find the maximum $m = \max_i x_i$.
- **Pass 2** (sequential, thread 0 only): compute the normalizer $d = \sum_j \exp(x_j - m)$.
- `__syncthreads()` waits until `m` and `d` are ready.
- **Pass 3** (parallel across threads): compute final values with a strided loop `for (int j = threadIdx.x; j < N; j += blockDim.x)`, setting `output[j] = expf(input[j] - m) / d`.

The dependency structure: $m = \max_{i \in A} x_i$ and $d = \sum_{j=1}^{V}\exp(x_j - m)$ must both be known before any output $y_i = \frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j - m)}$ can be computed.

points.title: Stable softmax requires two reductions over two scans of the input
points.body_markdown:
The stable softmax pipeline needs:

1. **MAX reduction** → $m$ (first scan of the input).
2. **Compute exponentials and SUM reduction** → $s = \sum_i \exp(x_i - m)$ (second scan of the input).
3. **Normalize**: $\text{softmax}_i = \frac{\exp(x_i - m)}{s}$.

Every output needs both $m$ and $s$, so the naive approach requires two passes over the input. The document also shows the incremental forms $m_{j-1} = \max_{1 \leq i \leq j-1} x_i$ and $d_{j-1} = \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} e^{x_i - m_{j-1}}$, and the update $d_j = \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} e^{x_i - m_{j-1} + m_{j-1} - m_j} + e^{x_j - m_j}$.

points.title: Online softmax: state variables and their meaning
points.body_markdown:
Online softmax processes elements one at a time, carrying a running state. The transition takes input $m_{j-1}$, $\hat{d}_{j-1}$, $x_j$ and outputs $m_j$, $d_j$:

- $x_j$: the current input element being processed.
- $m_{j-1}$: the maximum of the first $j-1$ input elements.
- $m_j$: the maximum of the first $j$ input elements.
- $\hat{d}_{j-1}$: the previously stored normalizer for the first $j-1$ elements, computed using the **old** maximum $m_{j-1}$.
- $d_{j-1}$: the previously stored normalizer for the first $j-1$ elements, computed using the **new** maximum $m_j$.
- $d_j$: the normalizer for the first $j$ elements, computed using the new maximum $m_j$.

points.title: Online softmax update rule
points.body_markdown:
The online softmax recurrence:

$$m_j = \max(m_{j-1}, x_j)$$

$$d_j = \sum_{i=1}^{j} e^{x_i - m_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} e^{x_i - m_{j-1} + m_{j-1} - m_j} + e^{x_j - m_j} = e^{m_{j-1} - m_j}\hat{d}_{j-1} + e^{x_j - m_j}$$

Key intermediate step: rescaling the old normalizer with the new maximum, $d_{j-1} = e^{m_{j-1} - m_j}\hat{d}_{j-1}$, so that $d_j = d_{j-1} + e^{x_j - m_j}$.

This lets the maximum and normalizer be updated **together in a single pass** over the input, instead of two separate scans.

points.title: Naive online softmax kernel
Parallel online softmax: combining two subsets' states
points.body_markdown:
For two disjoint subsets $A$ and $B$ with per-subset states:

- $m_A = \max_{i \in A} x_i$, $d_A = \sum_{i \in A} e^{x_i - m_A}$
- $m_B = \max_{i \in B} x_i$, $d_B = \sum_{i \in B} e^{x_i - m_B}$

The combined state for $A \cup B$ is $m = \max_{i \in A \cup B} x_i$ and $d = \sum_{i \in A \cup B} e^{x_i - m}$.

- $m_A$, $m_B$: maxima of sets $A$ and $B$; $m$: maximum of $A$ and $B$.
- $d_A$, $d_B$: previously stored normalizers for sets $A$ and $B$; $d$: new stored normalizer for $A \cup B$.

points.title: Parallel online softmax: the merge (⊕) operator
points.body_markdown:
The merge of two states is:

$$m = \max(m_A, m_B)$$

$$d = \sum_{i \in A \cup B} e^{x_i - m} = \sum_{i \in A} e^{x_i - m} + \sum_{i \in B} e^{x_i - m} = e^{m_A - m}\sum_{i \in A} e^{x_i - m_A} + e^{m_B - m}\sum_{i \in B} e^{x_i - m_B} = d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m}$$

Defining the associative combine operator:

$$(m_A, d_A) \oplus (m_B, d_B) = \left(m,\ d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m}\right)$$

This operator allows partial softmax states to be computed independently and then merged.

points.title: Parallel online softmax kernel: splitting work across threads
points.body_markdown:
The parallel online softmax kernel splits the vector at `mid = N / 2` and uses shared state `mA, dA, mB, dB, m, d`:

- **Thread 0** computes the online state $(m_A, d_A)$ over the first half `[0, mid)` using the same running update loop.
- **Thread 1** computes the online state $(m_B, d_B)$ over the second half `[mid, N)`.
- After `__syncthreads()`, **thread 0** merges the two states: `m = fmaxf(mA, mB); d = dA * expf(mA - m) + dB * expf(mB - m);`
- After a second `__syncthreads()`, all threads compute the final values in parallel with the strided loop: `output[j] = expf(input[j] - m) / d`.

This implements the combine operator $(m_A, d_A) \oplus (m_B, d_B) = (m,\ d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m})$ in code, with the two halves representing "one subset" and "another subset" of the input.

points.title: Naive attention computation and its cost
points.body_markdown:
Attention is defined as:

\[
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
\]

The naive implementation proceeds in three materialized steps:

\[
S = QK^{T}, \quad P = \text{softmax}(S), \quad O = PV
\]

### Why naive attention is slow

- It materializes the full score matrix \(S = QK^{T}\) and the probability matrix \(P = \text{softmax}(S)\).
- This causes high HBM traffic: write \(S\), read \(S\), write \(P\), read \(P\).
- Time and memory grow quadratically with sequence length: \(O(N^2)\).

points.title: FlashAttention idea 1: tiled GEMM
points.body_markdown:
Instead of materializing the full \(N \times N\) matrix, FlashAttention computes \(QK^{T}\) and \(PV\) block by block.

- Blockwise computation of \(Q_i K_j^{T}\).
- The full score matrix is never materialized.

points.title: FlashAttention idea 2: online softmax
points.body_markdown:
Running statistics are maintained while scanning blocks, rather than computing softmax over a fully materialized score matrix.

The combination rule for two block statistics \((m_A, d_A)\) and \((m_B, d_B)\) is:

\[
(m_A, d_A) \oplus (m_B, d_B) = (m,\; d_A e^{m_A - m} + d_B e^{m_B - m})
\]

points.title: Why FlashAttention is faster
points.body_markdown:
- No full attention matrix is stored in HBM.
- Much lower memory traffic.
- It computes exact attention, not an approximation.

points.title: Scope of the teaching kernel vs. real FlashAttention-1
points.body_markdown:
The explained core algorithmic idea is tiled GEMM plus online softmax:

- Avoid writing the full \(S = QK^{T}\) and \(P = \text{softmax}(S)\).
- Maintain running \(m\) and \(l\) while scanning tiles.

A small teaching kernel shows the math, not production scheduling.

### What real FlashAttention-1 adds

- One fused kernel: \(QK^{T} \rightarrow\) online softmax \(\rightarrow PV\).
- Careful SRAM/shared-memory/register tiling.
- Backward pass with recomputation to save memory.
- Causal mask, dropout, variable length, and occupancy details.

points.title: FlashAttention evolves with GPU architecture
points.body_markdown: FlashAttention evolves with GPU architecture.

This chapter reviews the key technical points from Tutorial 5, covering CXL memory expansion, memory tiering and pooling, PCIe foundations, CXL architecture and fabrics, real CXL prototypes and performance, and several appendix topics.

## TB-scale memory demand and stranded capacity motivate memory expansion

- Databases, large indexes and AI state can require TB-scale memory capacity.
- A larger resident working set can avoid expensive data movement.
- Fixed CPU-to-memory ratios can strand capacity beside busy resources.
- VM consolidation helps, but some capacity can remain unavailable to other hosts.

## Workload activity is uneven, motivating heterogeneous memory

- Page activity is uneven and changes over time.
- DRAM can serve active data while capacity memory or SSD holds colder data.

## CXL adds a host-accessible memory target beyond conventional DIMMs

- CXL adds a host-accessible memory target beyond conventional DIMMs.
- Software decides how applications receive and use the added capacity.

## PCIe topology: root complex, switches and endpoints

- The Root Complex connects the CPU and memory system to PCIe devices.
- Switches extend the tree to endpoints such as NICs, GPUs and storage.

## MMIO and DMA are the two device-access models

- MMIO: the CPU accesses a device's mapped register or memory window.
- DMA: the device accesses buffers in host memory.

## PCIe reads, writes and completions

- A read sends MRd and receives data in one or more CplD packets.
- Multiple outstanding requests can cover the round-trip delay.
- Posted memory writes do not receive a successful transaction-layer Completion TLP.

## CXL reuses PCIe infrastructure with three protocol roles

- CXL reuses the PCIe physical infrastructure and device-discovery foundation.
- CXL.io, CXL.cache and CXL.mem serve different protocol roles.

## CXL device types

- Type 1 and Type 2 devices can cache host memory.
- Type 3 supplies host-accessible memory through CXL.mem.

## A CPU load targeting a mapped CXL range

- A miss targeting a mapped CXL range follows the host's memory path.
- The endpoint serves the request and the returned line can enter CPU caches.

## HDM decoding: HPA to DPA (noninterleaved)

- Example: host base 0x40000000, HPA 0x40001240, device base 0 → DPA = HPA − host base = 0x1240.
- Root and switch decoders select paths while preserving HPA.
- The endpoint translates the address into its device-local range.

## Interleaving across devices

- Ways choose the number of participating targets; granularity sets the stripe size.
- Parallel requests can use multiple paths, while one small load targets one stripe.
- Original Intel example: two-way interleave at 2 KiB granularity.

## CXL fabrics: pooling and fabric management

- The Fabric Manager binds resources into a host virtual hierarchy.
- Ordinary memory requests follow the configured data path.
- Port roles: RP (root port), USP/DSP (upstream/downstream ports), EP (endpoint), FM (Fabric Manager).

## Multilevel CXL fabrics (CXL 3.0)

- CXL 3.0 adds multilevel switching and fabric-attached resources.
- Placement selects hop count and the shared links that carry traffic.

## DirectCXL hardware organization

- Four FPGA hosts and four memory devices; host CPU 100 MHz, CXL/PCIe IP 250 MHz.
- The prototype integrates hosts, memory blades and a custom CXL switch.
- Its system topology and the 1:1 latency experiment are different configurations.

## DirectCXL: from allocation to load/store

- The driver allocates an HDMI segment and exposes a namespace.
- After mmap, ordinary memory instructions access the mapped range.

## Link budget vs. useful bandwidth

- Transport budget, memory payload and application bandwidth are different quantities.
- CXL memory payload throughput is lower than the transport budget.
- Compare one link with one channel, then account for the full system configuration.
- PCIe 5.0 ×16: 32 GT/s × 16 × 128/130 ÷ 8 ≈ 63.0 GB/s per direction.
- DDR5-4800, 64 data bits: 4.8 GT/s × 64 ÷ 8 = 38.4 GB/s shared by reads/writes.

## Real CXL devices differ in latency and bandwidth

- The host and device implementation matter; CXL-D uses a separate machine.
- These are real Type 3 devices operating in CXL 1.1 mode.

| Device | Implementation | Link | Idle latency | Matrix BW |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CXL-A | ASIC, DDR4 | ×8 | 214 ns | 24 GB/s |
| CXL-B | ASIC, DDR5 | ×8 | 271 ns | 22 GB/s |
| CXL-C | FPGA, DDR4 | ×8 | 394 ns | 18 GB/s |
| CXL-D | ASIC, DDR5 | ×16 | 239 ns | 52 GB/s |

- A/B/C: SPR2S or EMR2S; D: separate EMR2S-prime. Matrix BW does not specify a traffic mix.

## Loaded latency rises toward saturation

- A foreground latency thread runs alongside 31 traffic generators.
- Latency rises as demand approaches a path's sustainable service rate.
- MLC delay sweep: 0–20K cycles; X-axis logarithmic; different device curves include different host setups.

## CXL latency and CPU prefetching

- CXL's longer access latency reduces L2PF timeliness and coverage.
- This leads to more aggressive L1PF prefetch and an increasing number of delayed L1 hits.
- Longer fills can reduce prefetch timeliness and coverage on the evaluated CPUs.
- The paper links available counter measurements to its interpretation of cache stalls.
- Findings are specific to the evaluated Intel platforms (SPEC CPU 2017 workloads).

## Beluga: a built CXL memory pool

- Two GPU servers connect to an 8 TB CXL 2.0 memory pool.
- The evaluation uses 16 H2O GPUs and a matched 2 TB cache budget.
- Physical deployment and evaluated configuration differ: 8 TB installed, 2 TB used for fair comparisons.

## Beluga: access paths and correctness

- CPU loads, DSA transfers and GPU copy kernels reach the same pool.
- Beluga uses software-managed sharing; there is no hardware coherence across host caches.
- Software must make writes visible and prevent stale reads across hosts.

## Beluga: KVCache placement and reuse

- A miss computes and stores KVCache for later reuse.
- A hit resolves a block address and loads KVCache from the pool.
- Workflow includes vLLM integration and CXL-based metadata RPC.

## Beluga: gather and scatter transfers

- Gather writes pack scattered GPU regions into contiguous pool blocks.
- The dense-transfer benchmark reports 36.2% lower write latency than MoonCake.
- The percentage describes writes in the tested configurations (Figure 14(a)).

## Real hardware vs. NUMA emulation

- Two setups in Beyond Hotness (OSDI 2025); different hosts and local-memory baselines.
- Local DRAM on real-CXL host: 114 ns, 218 GB/s; on emulation host: 90 ns, 49 GB/s.
- NUMA emulation controls an existing socket path rather than implementing CXL hardware.
- Keep the host baseline and measurement method when comparing reported results.

| Target tier | Platform / path | Latency | Bandwidth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Real ASIC expander | Sapphire Rapids, PCIe 5.0 ×8 | 271 ns | 26 GB/s |
| Emulated CXL tier | Skylake remote DRAM | 190 ns | 17 GB/s |

## Pond's topology latency budget

- Ports, flight time, retimers and switches contribute different costs.
- These are Pond's analytical budgets, not a measurement of every device.

## Worked HPA/DPA interleaving example

- Noninterleaved mapping subtracts the host window base in this example.
- Interleaving selects a target, then packs each target's stripes into DPA.
- Illustrative two-way, 256 B stripes; host base 0x40000000; device bases are zero.

| Host physical address | Target | Device physical address |
|---|---|---|
| 0x40000040 | Device 0 | 0x00000040 |
| 0x40000140 | Device 1 | 0x00000040 |
| 0x40000240 | Device 0 | 0x00000140 |
| 0x40000340 | Device 1 | 0x00000140 |

## CC-NIC: coherent descriptors

- CC-NIC carries readiness inside descriptors instead of separate head/tail registers.
- Cache transfers combine notification with descriptor delivery.
- Access types shown: local access, PCIe MMIO write, PCIe DMA read, PCIe DMA write, cache transfer.
- Coherent NIC-interface design evaluated using Intel UPI; figures compare transmit and signaling paths.

## HydraRPC: shared-memory rings

- Each RPC connection uses request and response queues in shared CXL memory.
- A 64-bit entry carries a data offset and an arrival flag.
- HydraRPC is an FPGA CXL prototype with a CXL 1.1+ driver; software controls cache visibility and ordering.

## NTSocks: the NTB fast path

- NTSocks evaluated two back-to-back servers using PCIe NTB; it is not a CXL prototype.
- Remote writes publish data to a peer buffer; the receiver reads locally.
- Socket semantics add buffering, queues and software processing.

## CXL 3.0 back-invalidation

- CXL 3.0 mechanism requiring suitable host, device and fabric support.
- A sharing device tracks which hosts hold a cache line.
- Exclusive ownership waits for conflicting cached copies to be invalidated.

## Beluga: end-to-end behavior

- Beluga sustains low TTFT and TPOT over a wider request-rate range.
- The experiment replays a populated cache, making KVCache reads the main bottleneck.
- Populated-cache rerun on two servers with 16 H20 GPUs; both systems receive a 2 TB pool budget.

documents.markdown:
This tutorial explains DeepEP, a communication library for expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that optimizes token dispatch and combine operations. It details the underlying GPU communication infrastructure, including NVLink and RDMA domains, as well as GPU-Initiated RDMA (IBGDA) for high-performance data transfer. The document contrasts two distinct dispatch paths: a low-latency approach using fixed receive slots and atomic reservations, and a high-throughput approach that pipelines RDMA and NVLink transfers. It further breaks down the high-throughput pipeline into specific roles such as senders, coordinators, and forwarders to manage buffer ownership and token counts. Finally, the tutorial provides a source map linking the Python APIs to the underlying GPU kernels.

## MoE Dispatch and Combine

- **Dispatch** moves each token to its selected experts before expert computation.
- **Combine** returns expert outputs and reduces them with routing weights.

## Expert IDs vs. GPU Ranks

- Routing selects **global expert IDs**; an expert ID is **not** a GPU rank.
- **Contiguous placement** maps expert `e` to rank `floor(e / L)` and local expert `e % L`, where `L` is the number of local experts per rank.
- Example with `L = 9`:
  - `rank = expert_id / 9`
  - `local_expert = expert_id % 9`

| Global expert ID | Destination GPU rank | Local expert ID |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | 0 | 8 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 |
| 287 | 31 | 8 |

## NVLink and RDMA Domains

- **NVLink** connects local GPU peers.
- **RDMA** connects GPU memory through NICs.
- The throughput path **composes** these domains rather than treating every hop alike.

## GPU Direct RDMA

- The NIC reads or writes **registered GPU memory** without a host-memory staging copy.
- Direct data movement still requires setup, valid memory mappings, and synchronization.

## GPU-Initiated RDMA with IBGDA

- **CPU proxy submission**: the CPU submits work on behalf of the GPU.
- **GPU submission with IBGDA**: GPU threads prepare work queue entries and notify the NIC through a doorbell.
- CPU setup establishes resources; the GPU can then issue communication **in the kernel**.

## Two Dispatch Paths

- **Low latency**: use fixed receive slots and publish counts after issuing token writes.
- **High throughput**: exchange layout information and pipeline RDMA with NVLink forwarding.
- Self-rank delivery can use a local-copy branch.

## Low-Latency Dispatch: Stages and Buffer Lifetimes

- **Before repeated dispatch**: create communication resources and register reusable storage.
- **Each invocation**: prepare → submit → notify → receive and pack.
- Stage token data, issue writes, publish counts, then pack the received messages.
- A buffer stays live until its readers and the communication protocol have finished.

## Low-Latency Dispatch: Fixed Receive Slots

- Receive buffer layout: `rdma_recv_x[local expert][source rank][slot]`.
- Reserve a separate receive slice for every **local-expert and source-rank pair**.
- Known addresses let payload writes start **before** a receiver-side count exchange.

## Low-Latency Dispatch: Packing Tokens into Registered Buffers

- Stage each token with **source identity** and, when enabled, **FP8 scaling factors**.
- The communication buffer gives the NIC registered addresses, keys, and stable storage.

## Low-Latency Dispatch: Mapping Token Sends to Warps

- Example launch: 96 CTAs × 960 threads; scheduling determines physical SM placement.
- A CTA cooperatively stages a token; selected warps issue its expert-directed writes.
- A separate **counting warp** tracks the experts assigned to that CTA.

## Low-Latency Dispatch: Reserving Slots with Atomics

- A partition belongs to one source rank.
- Slot reservation code:
  ```
  slot = atomicAdd(&reserve[e], 1);
  peer = e / 9;
  local_e = e % 9;
  put_nbi(remote[local_e][rank][slot], staged_token, peer);
  ```
- Each concurrent sender receives a **different slot**.
- One atomic increment allocates a unique slot among local sends to the same expert.
- Source-rank slices separate GPUs; the atomic separates concurrent warps on one GPU.

## Low-Latency Dispatch: Publishing Readiness to the Receiver

- Sender GPU sequence:
  1. Post payload WRITEs.
  2. Publish local issued progress.
  3. Wait until local requests are issued.
  4. Post count AMO: `-(n + 1)`.
- Receiver wait loop:
  ```
  while ((flag = load_acquire(count)) == 0) {}
  n = -flag - 1;
  ```
- `n = 0` still publishes `-1`, so the receiver can finish waiting.
- The local finish counter records **issued sends**, not remote payload completion.
- A count AMO follows payload writes on the same QP; encode `n` tokens as `-(n + 1)`.

## Low-Latency Dispatch: Receiving and Packing Expert Inputs

- Decode count and reserve output space:
  ```
  n = -ready_flag - 1;
  begin = atomicAdd(&packed_count[local_e], n);
  ```
- Wait for a nonzero count flag, decode `n`, and reserve `n` contiguous output positions.
- Pack source slices into each expert's valid prefix while preserving return metadata.

## High-Throughput Dispatch: RDMA-to-NVLink Forwarding

- RDMA connects the **same local GPU index across nodes**; NVLink reaches the final local ranks.
- A token crosses RDMA **once per destination node**, then its rank mask drives local forwarding.
- Path: same token → one remote node → several final GPU ranks.

## High-Throughput Dispatch: Notify and Dispatch Kernels

- **Notify kernel** establishes the layout:
  - Exchange token counts.
  - Compute receive prefixes and output sizes.
- **Dispatch kernel** moves the tokens:
  - Use the prepared layout to pipeline RDMA and NVLink transfers.
- Notify exchanges counts and builds prefixes; the runtime then allocates the receive tensors.
- Dispatch uses that metadata to move payloads through the RDMA and NVLink pipeline.

## High-Throughput Dispatch: Channels

- A channel partitions input token indices and owns independent communication progress.
- Select the subset destined for one peer from the partitioned source-token index range.
- `C_h = 10` launches 20 CTAs: one sender/receiver CTA and one forwarder CTA per channel.
- A channel is a **software pipeline partition**; a QP is **transport state**.

## High-Throughput Dispatch: Exchanging Token Counts

1. Exchange per-node / per-rank counts over RDMA.
2. Gather the final-rank / expert counts within the NVLink domain.
- Counts follow the payload route: exchange across an RDMA rail, then distribute through NVLink.
- Node counts deduplicate each token within a destination node; rank and expert counts stay distinct.

## High-Throughput Dispatch: Sender and Coordinator

- **Sender CTA**: load token chunks; publish progress to the coordinator.
- **Forwarder CTA**: 1 coordinator warp is active; 7 warps retire.
- Sender warps pack token data and routing metadata, then publish contiguous ready progress.
- A coordinator in the same CTA observes shared progress and issues chunked RDMA writes.

## High-Throughput Dispatch: Forwarder and NVLink Receiver

- Flow: RDMA receive → forwarding progress → NVLink receiver consumes its local buffer.
- Forwarder warps inspect destination bits and copy arrived tokens into each local rank's NVLink ring.
- NVLink receiver warps copy ready tokens to final offsets and release consumed ring slots.

## High-Throughput Dispatch: Buffer Ownership and Reuse

- RDMA stages through separate send/receive regions; NVLink writes into the receiver's data ring.
- Reuse follows **consumer release**: remote forwarders release RDMA slots; final receivers release NVLink slots.
- Ring state: `head` is released by the consumer; `tail` is arrived and published.

| Location | Writer | Reader |
|---|---|---|
| Receiver data / tail | Forwarder | NVLink receiver |
| Forwarder head | NVLink receiver via IPC | Forwarder |

## High-Throughput Dispatch: The Complete Communication Pipeline

- Pipeline: input → sender packing → RDMA ring → NVLink forwarding → compact receive tensor.
- Each stage publishes readiness downstream and returns reusable capacity upstream.

## DeepEP Source Map

- `Buffer.get_dispatch_layout()` builds route counts; `Buffer.dispatch()` selects the communication path.
- C++ manages tensors and launches; CUDA kernels implement notify, dispatch, and queue progress.

| Layer | File | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Python API | `deep_ep/buffer.py` | `get_dispatch_layout` / `dispatch` / `low_latency_dispatch` |
| Native runtime | `csrc/deep_ep.cpp` | Resource setup and kernel selection |
| GPU kernels | `layout.cu`; `internode.cu`; `internode_ll.cu` | Layout, staging, forwarding and packing |
| Device transport | `ibgda_device.cuh` | WQE construction and NIC submission |
documents.intro_markdown: This tutorial explains DeepEP, a communication library for expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that optimizes token dispatch and combine operations. It details the underlying GPU communication infrastructure, including NVLink and RDMA domains, as well as GPU-Initiated RDMA (IBGDA) for high-performance data transfer. The document contrasts two distinct dispatch paths: a low-latency approach using fixed receive slots and atomic reservations, and a high-throughput approach that pipelines RDMA and NVLink transfers. It further breaks down the high-throughput pipeline into specific roles such as senders, coordinators, and forwarders to manage buffer ownership and token counts. Finally, the tutorial provides a source map linking the Python APIs to the underlying GPU kernels.

points.body_markdown:
- **Dispatch** moves each token to its selected experts before expert computation.
- **Combine** returns expert outputs and reduces them with routing weights.

points.title: Expert IDs vs. GPU Ranks
points.body_markdown:
- Routing selects **global expert IDs**; an expert ID is **not** a GPU rank.
- **Contiguous placement** maps expert `e` to rank `floor(e / L)` and local expert `e % L`, where `L` is the number of local experts per rank.
- Example with `L = 9`:
  - `rank = expert_id / 9`
  - `local_expert = expert_id % 9`

| Global expert ID | Destination GPU rank | Local expert ID |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 8 | 0 | 8 |
| 9 | 1 | 0 |
| 287 | 31 | 8 |

points.title: NVLink and RDMA Domains
points.body_markdown:
- **NVLink** connects local GPU peers.
- **RDMA** connects GPU memory through NICs.
- The throughput path **composes** these domains rather than treating every hop alike.

points.title: GPU Direct RDMA
points.body_markdown:
- The NIC reads or writes **registered GPU memory** without a host-memory staging copy.
- Direct data movement still requires setup, valid memory mappings, and synchronization.

points.title: GPU-Initiated RDMA with IBGDA
points.body_markdown:
- **CPU proxy submission**: the CPU submits work on behalf of the GPU.
- **GPU submission with IBGDA**: GPU threads prepare work queue entries and notify the NIC through a doorbell.
- CPU setup establishes resources; the GPU can then issue communication **in the kernel**.

points.title: Two Dispatch Paths
points.body_markdown:
- **Low latency**: use fixed receive slots and publish counts after issuing token writes.
- **High throughput**: exchange layout information and pipeline RDMA with NVLink forwarding.
- Self-rank delivery can use a local-copy branch.

points.title: Low-Latency Dispatch: Stages and Buffer Lifetimes
points.body_markdown:

- A buffer stays live until its readers and the communication protocol have finished.

documents.markdown:
The course project asks students to build an end-to-end agent system on TACC. This chapter reviews the required system architecture, the deliverables and execution path, the recommended exploration directions, the sample project, and the project milestones.

## End-to-end agent system architecture on TACC

The project requires a **student-built application** composed of these connected parts:

- **User interface** — sends a request and receives a response.
- **Application backend** — handles the request API, including input, streaming, and session state.
- **State / memory** — stores session state.
- **Model-serving backend** — an endpoint feeds a queue, which feeds a model worker; the model is reached through an API.
- **Agent workflow** — cycles through task context, model call, observation, and tool action.
- **Model client** — issues requests and receives responses from the model.
- **Tool adapter** — performs a call and returns a result.
- **Tools / data sources** — search, DB, APIs, files, code, browser; the system must use at least one relevant capability.
- **Logging + evaluation** — traces, errors, and metrics.

## Required execution path

The required flow runs from **task** to **user interface** (submit, monitor, review) to **application backend** (agent workflow, model API, tools/data) to a **visible result** (answer, artifact, or completed action).

## Selecting a task or scenario

Choose one concrete use case—for example, coding, research, tutoring, or data analysis.

## Building the frontend

Provide an interface for task input, visible progress, and review of the final result.

## Building the backend

Implement the backend: agent workflow, model API, and tool/data integration.

## Evaluation: logs, traces, test cases, results

Test representative cases, report metrics, and analyze at least one failure. The evaluation chain is logs/traces → test cases → results.

## Demo and final presentation

Prepare a tested demo and present the task, system, evaluation, and limitations, including setup, configuration, and known limitations.

## Exploration direction: task learning and adaptation

Improve performance for a specific task, domain, or user group. The task-evaluation metric should quantify improvement over a baseline.

## Exploration direction: system efficiency

Reduce latency or resource use without unacceptable task-quality loss. The system metric should quantify gains versus baseline without degrading task quality.

## Possible topic: trip planning agent

A traveler needs a practical trip that fits their budget, interests, and available time. The agent compares transport, stays, and activities, checks constraints, and revises the plan with the user. Output: a day-by-day itinerary, itemized budget, source links, and alternative options.

## Possible topic: literature research agent

A student exploring a research topic needs to understand key methods, findings, and open questions. The agent finds and reads papers, compares methods and evidence, and follows up on missing information. Output: a cited literature review and a paper comparison table linked to supporting passages.

## Possible topic: job search and application assistant

A graduate needs to find suitable roles and prepare applications that reflect their experience. The agent reads job postings, matches requirements to a résumé, and tailors materials using verified experience. Output: a job shortlist with match reasons, application drafts, and a checklist of next steps.

## Other project ideas

Other project ideas are welcome, provided the team defines a clear user need and a useful result.

## Sample project: STORM

STORM is an open-source system that researches a topic and writes an article with citations. Example input: "The Future of Work". Output: an organized article with a detailed outline and source citations. Possible course extensions: improve question selection; reduce latency and model calls.

The sample output's table of contents covers:

- Evolution of Work (rise of remote work; impact of automation and AI; generational differences and adaptation challenges; the role of technology in shaping workplaces)
- Major Trends Shaping the Future of Work (remote work; automation and AI; hybrid work models; telehealth and digitalization in healthcare; impact on employment and skills; challenges and opportunities)
- The Role of Education and Training in the Future of Work (skills demand in a digital era; lifelong learning and upskilling; reducing inequality through education)
- Technological Advancements Supporting the Future of Work (AI and automation; remote work technologies; security and data protection; gig economy platforms)

## Sample content: remote work trend

Remote work is enabled by technological advancements and changing attitudes toward work-life balance. During the COVID-19 pandemic it proved highly effective, with a reported 47% increase in productivity during lockdown periods in early 2020 [9]. Industries such as marketing, accounting, finance, and healthcare have embraced remote work models, driven by digitization of work processes and telehealth services [10]. The shift offers greater flexibility, increased productivity, and access to global talent [3].

## Sample content: automation and AI trend

AI automates repetitive tasks, improves decision-making, and creates new employment opportunities [11]; for example, AI algorithms can read diagnostic scans with high accuracy, assisting doctors in diagnosis and treatment selection [12]. Challenges include job displacement and the need for retraining and upskilling programs [11]. Certain occupations—tax preparers, real estate brokers, and cashiers—are highly vulnerable to automation, with over a 95% chance of computerization [13].

## Sample content: hybrid work models

Hybrid models combine remote and in-office work and are becoming increasingly popular. Technology makes it easier to take work to people rather than bringing people to a centralized location, enabling more flexible long-term remote or hybrid models [14]. A 2016 study by Vodafone found that three-quarters of companies worldwide have already switched to flexible working options [15].

## Sample content: telehealth and healthcare digitalization

Healthcare has shifted toward remote work, driven by telehealth services and digitization of health records [10]. This allows remote consultations and more efficient management of patient information, contributing to better health outcomes and improved access to care.

## Sample content: impact on employment and skills

As automation and AI integrate into sectors, the mix of occupations and required skills evolves: some jobs may be automated away while others emerge, requiring new skills and educational backgrounds [12]. The McKinsey study predicts job growth in healthcare, IT, management, and education, driven by rising consumption, aging populations, and technological deployment [16].

## Sample content: challenges and opportunities

The transition toward automated and remote work presents both opportunities and challenges. Technology innovations offer solutions, particularly for employee mental health and productivity [17]. Strategies promoting productive employment and decent work are crucial for a sustainable future of work, helping mitigate inequalities and ensuring people can find work in a digitalized economy.

## Project milestones

1. **Team formation** — 3–5 students per team; confirm all members and align on shared interests and working expectations.
2. **Topic selection and proposal (due October 29)** — choose a focused task or scenario; submit a two-page proposal covering motivation, proposed system, and evaluation plan.
3. **Project development** — implement and evaluate the proposed system; refine scope and approach based on progress and feedback.
4. **Final presentation** — present the completed system and evaluation results, give a short demo, and submit the final code repository.
